יהושע בן נון.event: יהושע בן נון is placed in Egypt at birth by inference: Joshua 24:29 gives his age at death as 110, while the project's Codex chronology places his death in 1245 BCE. Neither the biblical text nor archaeology supplies a precise birthplace, so this Egyptian marker represents the narrative generation rather than a known town.

At Rephidim, יהושע בן נון first appears as the commander selected by Moshe to fight Amalek in Exodus 17:8–16. Rephidim's location is disputed; the coordinates are only a conventional Sinai approximation.

יהושע בן נון serves as Moshe's attendant in the Sinai narratives, accompanying him partway toward the mountain in Exodus 24:13 and remaining associated with the Tent of Meeting in Exodus 33:11. The marker uses the traditional Jebel Musa area; the location of biblical Sinai is unresolved.

From Kadesh-barnea, Hoshea son of Nun represents Ephraim among the twelve scouts; Moshe calls him Yehoshua, and he and Kalev reject the majority's despairing report. See Numbers 13:8–16 and Numbers 14:6–38. Ein Qudeirat is a widely discussed identification for Kadesh-barnea, but not an uncontested certainty.

On the plains of Moab opposite Jericho, Moshe publicly designates יהושע בן נון as his successor by divine command, places authority upon him, and commissions him before Elazar and the community. See Numbers 27:12–23 and Deuteronomy 31:1–8.
After Moshe's death, יהושע בן נון assumes leadership at Shittim, sends two scouts toward Jericho, and prepares Israel to cross the Jordan. See Joshua 1 and Joshua 2.

יהושע בן נון leads the crossing of the Jordan and establishes the first camp at Gilgal, where memorial stones are erected and the Passover is observed. See Joshua 3, Joshua 4, and Joshua 5. The precise location of this Gilgal is uncertain.

The conquest narrative places יהושע בן נון at Jericho and then Ai. Joshua 6 describes Jericho's fall; Joshua 7 and Joshua 8 describe defeat and eventual victory at Ai. Tell es-Sultan is ancient Jericho, but the identification and chronology of Ai remain disputed.
At Mount Ebal and opposite Mount Gerizim, יהושע בן נון builds an altar, writes or displays the Torah, and reads the covenant blessings and curses before the assembled people in Joshua 8:30–35.

Following the treaty with Gibeon, יהושע בן נון marches from Gilgal to defend the city against a southern coalition. The battle and the poetic sun-and-moon passage are recorded in Joshua 9 and Joshua 10; al-Jib is the standard identification of ancient Gibeon.

The northern campaign culminates at Hazor, described as the leading city of the northern coalition in Joshua 11. Hazor is securely identified archaeologically, but responsibility for its Late Bronze Age destruction remains debated; see the Bible Odyssey Hazor overview.

After the principal campaigns, יהושע בן נון works with Elazar and the tribal heads to apportion territories from Gilgal. The process begins in Joshua 13 and continues through the allotment narratives.
At Shiloh, the Tent of Meeting is established and יהושע בן נון directs the survey and allocation of the remaining territories in Joshua 18:1–10. The site is identified with Khirbet Seilun.

The community grants יהושע בן נון Timnath-serah in the Ephraimite hill country, where he builds and settles according to Joshua 19:49–51. Khirbet Tibnah is a common scholarly identification; other burial traditions also exist.

At Shechem, יהושע בן נון delivers a final historical address, renews the covenant, and erects a witness stone in Joshua 24:1–28. Tell Balata preserves the remains generally identified with ancient Shechem.

יהושע בן נון dies aged 110 and is buried at Timnath-serah north of Mount Gaash according to Joshua 24:29–31. The year 1245 BCE follows this project's traditional Codex chronology and is not an independently established archaeological date.

Moses.event: Moses is born in Egypt during the Israelite enslavement under Pharaoh.
Moses flees Egypt after killing an Egyptian and settles in Midian.
Moses encounters the burning bush at Mount Sinai and receives the divine mission to redeem Israel.
Moses leads the Exodus from Egypt and receives the Torah at Mount Sinai.
Moses defeats Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan during Israel’s approach to Canaan.
Moses dies on the seventh of Adar in the plains of Moab after delivering his final teachings to Israel.

Aaron.event: Aaron is born in Egypt among the enslaved Israelites.
Aaron assists Moses during the Exodus and speaks before Pharaoh on behalf of Israel.
Aaron is consecrated as the first High Priest at Mount Sinai.
Aaron continues leading Israel’s priesthood during the wilderness wanderings.
Aaron dies on Mount Hor on the first of Av during the fortieth year after the Exodus.

דוד המלך.event: דוד המלך is placed at Bethlehem at birth by inference. The biblical narrative identifies him as a son of ישי of Bethlehem, while the project's birth year is derived from his reported age and reign; see I Samuel 16:1–13 and II Samuel 5:4–5. No source gives a precise birth date.

At Bethlehem, דוד המלך, the youngest son of ישי and a shepherd, is privately anointed by שמואל הנביא. He is subsequently described as a skilled musician brought into שאול המלך's service; see I Samuel 16.
In the Valley of Elah narrative, דוד המלך defeats the Philistine champion Goliath and enters public military life. The text locates the opposing camps between Socoh and Azekah; see I Samuel 17.

At שאול המלך's court in Gibeah, דוד המלך becomes a successful commander, forms a covenant with יהונתן, marries מיכל and becomes the target of repeated royal violence. See I Samuel 18–20. Tell el-Ful is commonly identified with biblical Gibeah, though the site's detailed interpretation is debated.

Fleeing the court, דוד המלך reaches the priestly settlement of Nob, receives consecrated bread and Goliath's sword from אחימלך, and continues toward Philistine territory. The episode and its lethal consequences for the priests appear in I Samuel 21:2–10 and 22:6–23. Nob's exact location is uncertain; the marker is a conventional northern-Jerusalem approximation.

At the cave or stronghold of Adullam, דוד המלך gathers relatives, debtors and distressed followers into an armed band. See I Samuel 22:1–5. The marker follows the widely accepted Adullam region, not a securely identified individual cave.

דוד המלך relieves Keilah from a Philistine attack but leaves when divine consultation warns that the town would surrender him to שאול המלך. See I Samuel 23:1–13; Khirbet Qila is the usual site identification.
In the wilderness and strongholds of Ziph, דוד המלך evades שאול המלך, meets יהונתן for their final recorded covenant, and is betrayed by local informants. See I Samuel 23:14–29 and 26.
At the strongholds of En-gedi, דוד המלך spares שאול המלך inside a cave and appeals to their encounter as proof that he does not seek the king's life. See I Samuel 24.

In the Carmel–Maon district, דוד המלך's conflict with נבל is defused by אביגיל; after נבל's death, דוד marries her. See I Samuel 25. This is Carmel in the southern Judean hills, not Mount Carmel near Haifa.

Philistine king Achish grants Ziklag to דוד המלך, who operates there for sixteen months with his followers. After an Amalekite raid, he recovers the captives and distributes spoil among Judean allies. See I Samuel 27 and 30. Ziklag's archaeological location remains disputed, so the coordinates are approximate.

After שאול המלך and יהונתן die, דוד המלך laments them, moves to Hebron and is anointed king over Judah at age thirty. The text assigns him seven years and six months there; see II Samuel 1:17–27 and 2:1–11.
Following the collapse of the rival northern regime, representatives of Israel covenant with דוד המלך at Hebron and anoint him king over Israel. See II Samuel 5:1–5.

דוד המלך captures the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, establishes the City of David as his capital and receives building assistance from Hiram of Tyre. See II Samuel 5:6–12. The historical scale of Davidic Jerusalem and the united polity is debated in current scholarship.

From Jerusalem, דוד המלך confronts Philistine incursions in the Valley of Rephaim and at Baal-perazim, consolidating the new capital's security. See II Samuel 5:17–25. The precise battlefield boundaries cannot be reconstructed.

After an interrupted first attempt, דוד המלך brings the Ark into Jerusalem with public celebration. He then receives נתן הנביא's oracle that his dynasty will endure, while a son will build the Temple. See II Samuel 6 and 7.

While the army besieges Rabbah, דוד המלך commits adultery with בת שבע and arranges אוריה's death. נתן הנביא confronts him with a parable, and the narrative makes this abuse of royal power a turning point in his household. See II Samuel 11 and 12.

During אבשלום's revolt, דוד המלך leaves Jerusalem, crosses the Jordan and establishes himself at Mahanaim. His forces defeat the rebellion, but he mourns אבשלום despite the political victory. See II Samuel 15–19. Mahanaim's location is uncertain; the marker represents a proposed Transjordanian area.
After a census and plague, דוד המלך purchases the threshing floor of ארונה and builds an altar at the place later associated with the Temple. See II Samuel 24:18–25 and I Chronicles 21:18–30.

In his final days, דוד המלך confirms שלמה as successor during אדוניה's attempted accession. He dies after a forty-year reign and is buried in the City of David. See I Kings 1 and 2:1–12. The year follows the project's traditional chronology, not the conventional scholarly date around 970 BCE.

ר׳ יהודה בן שמואל אבן בלעם.event: ר׳ יהודה בן שמואל אבן בלעם is born around the beginning of the eleventh century into a respected family in Toledo. The year 1000 is a conventional map anchor rather than a documented birth date; the only substantial medieval biographical notice, preserved by ר׳ משה אבן עזרא, establishes Toledo origin but not an exact year. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the scholarly author profile in the Posen Library.

By the middle or later eleventh century, ר׳ יהודה בן שמואל אבן בלעם has left his native Toledo and settled in Seville, the only securely attested relocation in his life. The displayed year is approximate because the surviving medieval account gives no date. Seville becomes the principal geographical setting for his grammatical, exegetical and poetic career. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Around the later eleventh century, ר׳ יהודה בן שמואל אבן בלעם produces Judeo-Arabic biblical commentaries and concise grammatical treatises on homonyms, particles and denominative verbs. His works repeatedly engage earlier philologists and contain particularly sharp disagreement with ר׳ משה אבן ג׳יקטילה. The year marks his documented period of activity, not his death or the securely dated completion of a single book. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel authority record.

In his later career, ר׳ יהודה בן שמואל אבן בלעם increasingly applies rabbinic and halakhic hermeneutics within philological biblical commentary, while continuing to write in Arabic. Evidence places him within the intellectual world of the later eleventh century, so the old record's assertion that he died in 1070 is unsustainable. His precise final year and death place remain unknown. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the textual overview in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי.place: Qalʿat Bani Hammad, Hammadid realm (present-day Algeria)
ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי.event: ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי is born in 1013 at Qalʿat Hammad, now identified with the Hammadid capital Qalʿat Bani Hammad in present-day Algeria. Older reference works mistakenly placed a similarly named village near Fez; modern scholarship also calls him הקלעי after his actual birthplace. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Hebrew geographical discussion at דעת.

As a young scholar, ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי studies in Kairouan, then the leading western center of Talmudic learning. ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד later identifies his teachers as ר׳ חננאל בן חושיאל and ר׳ נסים בן יעקב; because the Rif himself does not name them as teachers, the relationship is reported as medieval biographical testimony rather than direct autobiography. The displayed year is approximate. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי.place: Fez, Maghrawa realm (present-day Morocco; residence debated)
ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי.event: According to the standard reconstruction, by about 1045 ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי has settled in Fez, where he teaches, answers legal questions and develops ספר ההלכות; the nisbah al-Fasi means “of Fez.” Some modern Hebrew scholarship argues that the family name may instead preserve ancestry from Fez and questions whether his own residence there is proven. This qualified point follows the principal reference tradition without concealing the debate. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the contrary research summary at דעת.

ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי.place: Fez to Córdoba, Morocco and al-Andalus
ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי.event: At approximately seventy-five, ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי is denounced to the government by opponents on a charge whose nature is not preserved. Forced to leave his North African base in 1088, he crosses to al-Andalus and spends several months in Córdoba. Sources do not justify embellishing the accusation or his route. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and Enciclopedia Italiana.

ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי moves from Córdoba to Lucena and becomes head of its yeshivah in 1089, following the death of ר׳ יצחק אבן גיאת. Lucena becomes his final home and the center from which he teaches a distinguished generation of students. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and Treccani.

During his Lucena leadership, ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי teaches students including ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש, ר׳ יהודה הלוי, ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד and ר׳ ברוך אבן אלבאליה. The displayed year is a midpoint for relationships extending across several years, not a precisely dated class. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ יצחק בן יעקב אלפסי dies in Lucena in 1103, close to ninety years old. Before his death he designates his foremost student ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש to succeed him rather than his own learned son ר׳ יעקב. Hebrew poets, including ר׳ משה אבן עזרא, commemorate him in elegies. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Italian chronology in Treccani.

ר׳ שלמה בן יהודה אבן גבירול.event: ר׳ שלמה בן יהודה אבן גבירול is probably born in Málaga in 1021 or 1022 to a family displaced from Córdoba during the collapse of the caliphate. His poetic signature al-Mālaqī securely identifies Málaga as his native affiliation, although the exact year is reconstructed. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

As a child, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול moves to Zaragoza, where he receives an extensive Hebrew and Arabic education. Orphaned young and frequently ill, he depends upon court-connected patrons while developing as poet, grammarian and philosopher. The year is an approximate childhood marker; see Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Stanford Encyclopedia.

By approximately sixteen, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול is already composing complex Hebrew poetry, including an אזהרות enumerating the commandments. His self-description as a sixteen-year-old with the heart of an eighty-year-old belongs to stylized self-praise but reflects extraordinary precocity. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול composes elegies after the death of ר׳ האי גאון in 1038, demonstrating how news from the eastern Geonic world reached Andalusian literary circles. His principal local patron is the learned courtier ר׳ יקותיאל בן יצחק. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Court intrigue and a coup lead to the killing of ר׳ יקותיאל בן יצחק in 1039. ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול answers with two major elegies, including one regarded among the finest works of medieval Hebrew secular poetry. The loss also removes his main political and financial protection. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the historical discussion from the Institución Fernando el Católico.

At about nineteen, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול completes הענק, a four-hundred-line didactic poem on Hebrew grammar. Only a fraction survives, but later scholars admired it as an important contribution to Hebrew philology. The year is derived from his approximate birth and stated age; see Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Around 1045, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול writes the Judaeo-Arabic תיקון מידות הנפש, connecting twenty character traits with the senses and bodily qualities. His mother also dies around this time, and worsening conflict with Zaragoza's communal elite appears to precede his departure. The exact sequence is reconstructed rather than securely dated day by day. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Stanford Encyclopedia.

After leaving Zaragoza, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול is traditionally placed for a time in Granada under the patronage of ר׳ שמואל הנגיד. Poems of praise and later satire suggest a relationship that eventually deteriorated, but the dates and duration of residence are uncertain; Granada is therefore marked as probable rather than certain. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the biographical caution in the Stanford Encyclopedia.

During his poorly documented final decade, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול composes his philosophical dialogue מקור חיים and major Hebrew religious poetry. The work's Arabic original is lost, but its Latin translation as Fons Vitae later makes “Avicebron” influential among Christian scholastics. No precise composition city is securely known. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

By his final years, ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול has composed כתר מלכות, a forty-part devotional meditation moving from divine attributes and cosmic spheres to confession and repentance. Its composition date and city cannot be fixed, so the marker is regional. Read the text at Sefaria, consult the National Library of Israel manuscript record, and see the Posen Library introduction.

ר׳ שלמה אבן גבירול most likely dies in Valencia in 1057 or 1058, still in his thirties. Other medieval traditions date his death as late as 1070. The story that an envious poet murdered him and buried him beneath a fig tree is a much later legend, not historical evidence. See the Stanford Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה.event: ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה is born in Córdoba in 1035 into an established Andalusian Jewish family. A later family tradition traced the lineage deep into Roman-period Iberia, but that origin legend cannot be independently verified. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the family overview in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה.place: Córdoba or Lucena, al-Andalus; study location uncertain
ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה.event: In youth, ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה studies with a learned visitor from Périgord remembered as ר׳ פריגורש and develops expertise in Talmud, mathematics and astronomy. The report comes through his grandson ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד; neither the teacher's identity nor the precise location and year are independently established, so Córdoba remains only the cautious anchor. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה becomes associated with the learned court circle first supported by ר׳ שמואל הנגיד and then by ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד. The patronage gives him access to rabbinic books and the mathematical-astronomical culture of Granada; the year marks the transition between the two Nagids rather than a documented arrival date. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

At about thirty, ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה begins the unfinished Talmudic commentary קופת הרוכלים and dedicates his calendrical-astronomical מחברת סוד העיבור to ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד. The second work demonstrates the place of mathematical astronomy within Andalusian Jewish scholarship, although its text is lost. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the contextual biography of ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד.

After ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד is killed and Granada's Jewish population attacked, ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה spends heavily to recover the dispersed Nagid family library and relocates to Córdoba. The preservation effort becomes the nucleus of his own important library. See the modern Encyclopaedia Judaica biography and the older Jewish Encyclopedia account.

Al-Muʿtamid ibn ʿAbbād brings ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה into the Seville court in 1069 as astronomer and astrologer and appoints him rabbi and nasi over the Jews of the kingdom. He uses his palace access to support Jewish communal interests and builds Seville's scholarly resources around his recovered library. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Jewish Virtual Library summary.

During his long Seville tenure, ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה combines court science with communal judgment and halakhic correspondence. His son ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה is born in Seville in 1077. Two responsa by the father survive, while later manuscript research also preserves aspects of his legal dispute with ר׳ יצחק אלפסי. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library research record on the exchanged criticisms and responses.

The Almoravid conquest removes al-Muʿtamid from Seville in 1091 and ends the court in which ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה had served. Sources place his death in Granada three years later; his relocation belongs to this political transition, although its exact date and circumstances are not directly documented. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia; the dating of the Seville regime's fall is confirmed by Encyclopaedia Britannica.

ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה dies in Granada in 1094. According to the later family narrative of his grandson ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד, he instructs his seventeen-year-old son ר׳ ברוך to reconcile with and study under ר׳ יצחק אלפסי; ר׳ יצחק אלפסי receives the youth as a son. The broad reconciliation is plausible family memory, but the reported speech is not a contemporary transcript. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the historical biography of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי.

ר׳ יהוסף בן שמואל הלוי הנגיד.event: ר׳ יהוסף בן שמואל הלוי הנגיד is born in Granada on the evening beginning 11 Tishrei 4796, conventionally converted to 15 September 1035. The unusually precise time survives in his editorial notice attached to his father's poetry. See the National Library of Israel authority record and the discussion of his editorial preface in the Hebrew University study of the dīwān.

At eight and a half, ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד begins collecting and editing the Hebrew poetry of his father, ר׳ שמואל הנגיד. He copies poems and supplies Arabic headings, dates and contextual notices, continuing for about twelve years. See the Hebrew University article and Cambridge's reconstructed-dīwān project.

ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד marries the only daughter of ר׳ נסים בן יעקב of Kairouan, joining the scholarly households of Granada and Kairouan. A visit by ר׳ נסים to Granada has been proposed, but the evidence does not prove it, so no movement of either man is assumed beyond the marriage's Granadan setting. See Encyclopaedia Judaica on ר׳ נסים and the source-critical discussion in Islamic Cultures, Islamic Contexts.

After the death of ר׳ שמואל הנגיד in 1055 or 1056, the approximately twenty-year-old ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד succeeds him as vizier to Bādīs ibn Ḥabbūs and as nagid of Granada's Jews. Sources agree on the succession but diverge sharply in judging his character and administration. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, the historical framing in the Journal of Medieval Iberian Studies, and the primary Zirid tradition preserved in The Tibyān.

As nagid and head of an academy, ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד patronizes scholars and supports ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה and ר׳ יצחק אבן גיאת. Arabic poets also praise his generosity. The year represents a continuing period of patronage rather than a single dated transaction. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and its biography of ר׳ יצחק אבן אלבאליה.

ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה dedicates his calendrical-astronomical work עיבור to ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד in 1065, evidence of the scientific and rabbinic patronage surrounding his court. See the Jewish Encyclopedia biography of ר׳ יצחק אבן אלבאליה.

During 1066, court conflict intensifies around ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד. The later Zirid memoir אלתביאן accuses him of controlling Bādīs through informants and plotting with al-Muʿtaṣim of Almería; those charges may preserve real factional manoeuvring but come through a dynastic source with a strong retrospective agenda. They must therefore be attributed, not stated as established fact. Compare the translated primary source, The Tibyān, with the source analysis in Mateusz Wilk's study of memory and politics.

Anti-Jewish agitation also becomes explicit. Abū Isḥāq al-Ilbīrī's polemical poem attacks ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד and Granada's Jews collectively, condemning Jewish wealth and authority over Muslims. Historians debate its immediate causal role, but it documents a religious and social language through which court resentment was redirected against an entire minority. See A Companion to Islamic Granada and the critical survey of Arabic sources.

ר׳ יהוסף בן שמואל הלוי הנגיד.place: Royal palace and Jewish quarter, Granada
ר׳ יהוסף בן שמואל הלוי הנגיד.event: On 30 December 1066, a Muslim crowd storms the royal palace, discovers and kills ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד, publicly displays his body, and attacks Granada's Jewish population. The violence is both a political overthrow and a collective anti-Jewish massacre. Sources agree that many Jews were killed but do not permit the conventional figure of four thousand deaths to be treated as verified demographic data. See the source-critical study Memory and Politics: Anti-Jewish Tumult in Granada in 1066, the broader context in the Journal of Medieval Iberian Studies, and the older Jewish account in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ יהוסף בן שמואל הלוי הנגיד.place: Lucena, al-Andalus (family refuge after his death)
ר׳ יהוסף בן שמואל הלוי הנגיד.event: After the killing, the unnamed wife of ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד—daughter of ר׳ נסים בן יעקב—and their young son ר׳ עזריה escape to Lucena, where the Jewish community supports them. ר׳ עזריה later dies young. This is a posthumous family movement included to show the immediate geographical consequence of his fall; see the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica on ר׳ נסים בן יעקב.

ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת.event: ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת is born in Lucena in 1038 into an established Jewish family. Lucena's large and unusually prominent Jewish community provided the setting for his education and later academy. See the National Library of Israel authority record, the literary biography from Oxford Academic/Liverpool University Press and the Encyclopaedia Judaica family entry.

In his young adulthood, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת receives support and esteem from ר׳ שמואל הנגיד and later ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד. When ר׳ שמואל dies in 1055 or 1056, ר׳ יצחק composes an Aramaic elegy, demonstrating both personal connection and mastery of learned memorial poetry. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

After ר׳ יהוסף הנגיד is killed and Granada's Jewish community is attacked in 1066, his widow and young son ר׳ עזריה take refuge in Lucena. ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת shelters and supports them, remembers the family's earlier patronage and writes two elegies for ר׳ יהוסף. He hopes ר׳ עזריה may later lead the community, but the young man dies around age twenty. See the modern Encyclopaedia Judaica account and the older Jewish Encyclopedia biography.

Following the crisis of 1066, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת becomes rabbi and head of Lucena's academy. He teaches, judges, answers legal questions and builds the city into a major centre linking Geonic learning with the emerging scholarship of al-Andalus. The precise appointment year is inferred from the post-1066 succession rather than preserved in an appointment document. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, Oxford Academic and the National Library biography.

At the Lucena academy, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת trains a distinguished circle that includes ר׳ משה אבן עזרא, ר׳ יוסף אבן סהל and ר׳ יוסף אבן צדיק. Their later poetry and scholarship, including elegies for their teacher, show the breadth of his influence. The year represents sustained teaching rather than a single enrollment date. See the National Library of Israel and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

During his mature leadership, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת composes the halakhic corpus probably called הלכות כלולות, now partially preserved under the editorial titles שערי שמחה and מאה שערים. The work organizes festival and mourning law while conserving numerous Geonic rulings otherwise lost. The year is approximate. See the modern manuscript study in Ginzei Qedem, the National Library catalogue and a digitized halakhic manuscript.

ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת develops major Judaeo-Arabic exegetical projects: the Talmud commentary כתאב אלסראג or ספר הנר, and כתאב אלזהד, his translation and philosophical commentary on Ecclesiastes. Fragments show his dependence on Geonic traditions and ר׳ חננאל בן חושיאל alongside independent organization and interpretation. The year is an approximate map marker. See the peer-reviewed Ginzei Qedem study, the National Library bibliography for ספר הנר and the NLI author portal.

By the final decade of his life, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת has produced hundreds of sacred poems—selihot, bakashot, elegies, qerovot, ma'amadot and a Yom Kippur Avodah. His verse integrates science and philosophy into Hebrew liturgical expression and spreads through North African, Italian and eastern Mediterranean rites. See the National Library's curated poetry profile, the academic study on Oxford Academic and a primary poem record in the Academy of the Hebrew Language Historical Dictionary.

Seriously ill at age fifty-one, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת travels from Lucena to Córdoba for medical treatment in 1089 and dies there on the Sabbath. His attendants carry his body back overnight for burial with his ancestors in Lucena. ר׳ יצחק אלפסי subsequently succeeds him as head of the Lucena academy. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the National Library biography.

After his death in Córdoba, ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת is returned to Lucena and buried with his ancestors. His students mourn him in Hebrew verse, while the academy, halakhic writings and extensive piyyut corpus preserve his standing as a formative bridge between Geonic learning and the Spanish Rishonim. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry and the National Library of Israel profile.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Troyes, County of Champagne, Kingdom of France
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: ר׳ שלמה יצחקי is born in Troyes in 1040 to a father named ר׳ יצחק. Later legends elaborate his ancestry and childhood, but the secure biographical record begins with Troyes and the conventional birth year. See the National Library of Israel biography and Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Mainz, Holy Roman Empire; study period approximate
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: Around the age of twenty, ר׳ שלמה יצחקי leaves Troyes for the Rhineland academies and studies in Mainz, principally within the traditions taught by ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה and the pupils of ר׳ גרשום מאור הגולה. Sources differ on the exact sequence and duration of his Mainz and Worms studies, so 1059 is an approximate map anchor. See the National Library of Israel and the reference account in Encyclopædia Britannica.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Worms, Holy Roman Empire; study period approximate
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: During the same formative Rhineland period, ר׳ שלמה יצחקי studies in Worms under ר׳ יעקב בן יקר—whom he regarded as a central teacher—and ר׳ יצחק בן אליעזר הלוי. These academies supplied textual traditions and legal methods later embedded throughout his commentaries. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry on ר׳ יעקב בן יקר and the National Library of Israel biography.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Troyes, County of Champagne, Kingdom of France; return approximate
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: After roughly a decade of study associated with Mainz and Worms, ר׳ שלמה יצחקי returns to Troyes. He serves the local community as teacher, dayan, and halakhic respondent, apparently without treating scholarship as a salaried court office. The exact return year is reconstructed rather than documented. See the Hebrew account at the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Troyes, County of Champagne, Kingdom of France; academy activity approximate
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: By this period, ר׳ שלמה יצחקי leads an academy in Troyes and circulates explanatory notebooks—קונטרסים—on Scripture and Talmud. Students copy, question, and transmit the texts, helping explain both their rapid influence and the layered textual history of some commentaries. The year is representative, not a documented foundation date. See the National Library of Israel and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Troyes, County of Champagne, Kingdom of France; mature teaching period
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: In his mature Troyes school, ר׳ שלמה יצחקי teaches students and family members whose work will develop into the Tosafist tradition. His scholarly descendants include ר׳ שמואל בן מאיר and ר׳ יעקב בן מאיר, while compilations such as מחזור ויטרי preserve rulings and customs from his circle. The year marks continuing activity. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and its entry on מחזור ויטרי.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Troyes, County of Champagne, Kingdom of France
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: During the First Crusade, ר׳ שלמה יצחקי remains associated with Troyes while the Rhineland communities and academies of Mainz and Worms—where he had studied—are devastated by massacres. Later tradition attributes laments to him, but historians note that his surviving writings contain no unambiguous explicit description of the 1096 persecutions; the event is therefore framed as historical impact, not eyewitness travel. Compare the National Library of Israel account with the source-critical observation in The Jews and the Crusaders.

ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.place: Troyes, County of Champagne, Kingdom of France
ר׳ שלמה יצחקי.event: ר׳ שלמה יצחקי dies in Troyes in 1105. A notice in the printed commentary to Makkot marks where his explanation ceased and was continued by his student and son-in-law ר׳ יהודה בן נתן. He was buried in Troyes, but the medieval cemetery and precise grave were subsequently lost; a modern memorial stands in the area rather than an authenticated tomb. See the National Library of Israel and Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני.event: ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני is born in Barcelona in 1043. His geographical byname—אלברגלוני or הברצלוני—identifies the city, and modern authority records consistently preserve this birth year. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica biography and the National Library of Israel authority record.

A Genizah fragment describes ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני as a pupil of a scholar identified as ר׳ חנוך בן משה and has therefore been used to place part of his formation in Córdoba. The identification conflicts with the conventional chronology of the famous Cordoban ר׳ חנוך, whose reported death precedes ר׳ יצחק's 1043 birth; the notice may reflect a different chronology, indirect discipleship or mistaken identification. The year 1060 and Córdoba marker are therefore explicitly provisional. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

By his mature career, ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני has settled permanently in the Mediterranean port of Dénia, where he is remembered as a dayyan. Sources also connect him, probably through marriage, with the Ibn Laktush family, although the exact relationship is uncertain. The displayed year is approximate and precedes his securely dated work there. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia, and the National Library biographical essay.

At age thirty-five, ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני completes his Hebrew translation of ר׳ האי גאון's Arabic Book of Buying and Selling, known as ספר המקח והממכר. The work makes Geonic commercial law available beyond Arabic-reading communities and remains in later print circulation. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Posen Library creator biography.

During his Dénia period, ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני composes Talmudic explanations and the celebrated Shavuot אזהרות beginning איזה מקום בינה. Its 145 stanzas enumerate commandments according to הלכות גדולות and end with deftly integrated biblical quotations. The year is an approximate literary marker because the poem itself is not securely dated. See the National Library's detailed account of the אזהרות and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In his later Dénia career, ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני continues as judge, translator and poet. ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד later ranks him among the distinguished Spanish authorities named יצחק, and ר׳ יהודה אלחריזי praises his ability to weave biblical verses into legal poetry. This year represents continuing activity rather than a single documented incident. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library's אזהרות essay.

ר׳ יצחק בן ראובן אלברגלוני dies in Dénia, traditionally dated to approximately 1113. Authoritative modern records confirm that Dénia remained his residence until death but often leave the year unspecified; accordingly, 1113 is shown as an approximate conventional endpoint rather than an exact date. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the open-ended National Library authority record.

ר׳ בחיי בן יוסף אבן פקודה.event: ר׳ בחיי בן יוסף אבן פקודה is shown in Zaragoza from the project's conventional starting year of 1050. This is not a documented birth event: his birth year and birthplace are unknown, while Zaragoza is the securely transmitted center of his activity. Compare the cautious dating in the Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy with the Zaragoza tradition summarized by the modern Hebrew critical translation.

ר׳ בחיי בן יוסף אבן פקודה is traditionally identified as a dayan, or Jewish judge, in Zaragoza. His title al-Dayyan supports the role, but no surviving appointment record supplies a precise year; 1075 is an approximate map marker within his probable period of activity. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica biography and the Kotar/CET scholarly edition overview.

Around 1080, ר׳ בחיי בן יוסף אבן פקודה composes the Judaeo-Arabic כתאב אלהדאיה אלא פראיץ׳ אלקלוב, later famous in Hebrew as חובות הלבבות. The book reorganizes Jewish religious life around the relationship between outward 'duties of the limbs' and inward 'duties of the hearts.' Circa 1080 is a modern scholarly estimate, not a dated colophon. See the peer-reviewed Harvard Theological Review study, Stanford University Press and the CET educational anthology.

The ten-gate architecture of חובות הלבבות guides the reader from divine unity and reflection through service, trust, sincerity, humility, repentance, self-examination and abstinence to love of God. ר׳ בחיי בן יוסף אבן פקודה combines biblical and rabbinic foundations with rational inquiry and Arabic ethical and pietist traditions, insisting that outward deeds require inward intention. The year is an interpretive map marker, not a separate dated event. Read the book's introduction on Sefaria, the Routledge analysis and the academic monograph A Sufi-Jewish Dialogue.

ר׳ בחיי בן יוסף אבן פקודה is shown at the project's conventional endpoint of 1120. Neither his death year nor death place is known, so this is not evidence that he died in Zaragoza in 1120. What is secure is the survival and immense influence of his book; in 1161, after his lifetime, ר׳ יהודה בן שאול אבן תיבון began the Hebrew translation that made it a classic. See the Jewish Encyclopedia's translation history, a National Library of Israel manuscript record and the Routledge overview.

ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד.event: ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד is placed at Qalʿat Banī Ḥammād from the conventional map year 1050. This is not a documented birth event: his birth date and birthplace are unknown. The secure evidence is that he lived in this Hammadid capital in present-day Algeria and was active in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the National Library of Israel authority record and the UNESCO site record for Qalʿat Banī Ḥammād.

In the scholarly circle of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי, ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד becomes an outstanding student-colleague rather than a merely passive pupil. Their legal discussions sometimes lead ר׳ יצחק אלפסי to accept his view. The year is approximate, representing their period of overlap before ר׳ יצחק אלפסי left North Africa. See the scholarly Encyclopaedia Judaica biography and the National Library record for the collected writings.

ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד's corrections and additions contribute to the later recension of הלכות הרי״ף. Some annotations remain identifiable as his; others entered the transmitted text from manuscript margins. This makes him an unusually important witness to how a medieval legal code was revised and copied. The date is an approximate scholarly marker. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the JTS bibliography of medieval commentary, responsa and codes.

ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד.place: Qalʿat Banī Ḥammād; later location uncertain
ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד.event: When ר׳ יצחק אלפסי leaves North Africa and ultimately establishes himself at Lucena, ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד's own route becomes uncertain. Later proposals place him in Lucena, Provence or continuously at Qalʿat Ḥammād, but none is secure enough to map as a journey. This marker therefore remains at his documented North African base. Compare the cautious Encyclopaedia Judaica account with the traditions summarized by Yeshiva.org.il.

Around the turn of the century, ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד develops the earliest known commentary and supplement to הלכות הרי״ף. It explains the code, restores omitted material, answers critics and sometimes challenges its rulings from Geonic and North African tradition. Later labels—הגהות, השגות, תוספות, תשובות and תשלום הלכות—probably describe the functions of this lost corpus rather than five securely separate books. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and a translated Bava Kamma example in the Posen Library.

In the early twelfth century, ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד's surviving comments show work across Mishnah, Tosefta, Talmud, textual variants and practical law. His commentary on Pirkei Avot examines literary sequence and ethical reasoning; his legal fragments include the influential rejection of compulsory intoxication on Purim. The year is representative rather than exact. See the curated Posen Library Avot selection, Posen Library Bava Kamma selection and the modern collected edition.

ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד.place: Qalʿat Banī Ḥammād; teaching location uncertain
ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד.event: ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן פרחון is identified as a pupil of ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד, supporting the latter's role in Hebrew linguistic as well as halakhic study. The evidence does not establish where their instruction occurred, so Qalʿat Ḥammād remains only the safest geographic anchor. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel research index.

ר׳ אפרים מקלעת חמאד is shown at the conventional endpoint 1120; neither his death year nor death place is known. His writings survive indirectly through quotations and especially through the scholars of Provence and Catalonia, including ר׳ אברהם בן דוד מפושקיירא, ר׳ זרחיה הלוי, ר׳ יהונתן הכהן מלוניל, ר׳ יצחק בן אבא מארי and ר׳ משה בן נחמן. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library catalogue for the 1976 reconstruction of his corpus.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא is born around 1055 into a prominent Jewish family in Granada. The precise year varies across modern references between about 1055 and 1060; 1055 is the project's conventional anchor. See the Real Academia de la Historia, the Spanish Ministry of Culture's Museo Sefardí, and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.place: Lucena, Taifa-era al-Andalus; study date approximate
ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: As a young scholar, ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא studies Jewish tradition and liturgical poetry at Lucena under ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת. The sources establish the teacher and city but not his exact enrollment years, so 1072 is an approximate formative marker. See the Real Academia de la Historia and the Museo Sefardí.

By the 1080s, ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא has returned to Granada and participates in Jewish and Muslim courtly literary circles. He holds an honored position, cultivates Arabic and Hebrew learning and develops the poetry later assembled in ספר הענק. The displayed year represents this established period rather than a single dated appointment. See the Real Academia de la Historia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.place: Granada, Taifa of Granada; date approximate
ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: In Granada, ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא recognizes and encourages the younger ר׳ יהודה הלוי, invites him into the city's literary circle and begins a lasting friendship and poetic correspondence. The relationship is secure, but the meeting year is approximate. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Real Academia de la Historia.

The Almoravid capture of Granada around 1090 destroys the courtly setting of ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא's early life and disperses his family. Sources state that he remains for a time under difficult circumstances before eventually escaping; they do not establish an immediate journey on the conquest date. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.place: Christian northern Iberia, represented by Castile; exact itinerary unknown
ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: After hardship in Granada, ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא escapes into Christian-ruled Spain and begins a prolonged exile. His poems describe wandering, dependence on patrons and longing for Granada, but do not permit a reliable city-by-city route; the central Castile marker is regional and explicitly approximate. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Real Academia de la Historia.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.place: Christian northern Iberia; precise residence unknown
ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: During exile, ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא writes praise poems for patrons, elegies, complaints, philosophical verse and sacred poetry. His many seliḥot establish the title הסלח, while his verse repeatedly records estrangement, old age and homesickness. The year is a representative literary marker, not a dated residence. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.place: Christian northern Iberia; precise residence unknown
ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: In advanced old age, after 1135, ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא composes the Judaeo-Arabic כתאב אלמחאצ׳רה ואלמד׳אכרה, known as ספר העיונים והדיונים or שירת ישראל. Written in response to eight questions, it preserves and analyzes Andalusian Hebrew poetics at a time when that Arabic literary culture was dispersing. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library record for the critical text and translation.

ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.place: Christian Iberia; death place unknown and year approximate
ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא.event: ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא dies away from Granada sometime after 1138, conventionally placed around 1140. Neither the exact year nor the city is securely known, so this marker is only a functional endpoint for the map and not a claimed burial location. See the circa-1138 dating of the Real Academia de la Historia, the 1055–1140 cataloguing of the National Library of Israel, and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא.place: Crown of Aragon (birthplace uncertain; Barcelona used as conventional anchor)
ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא.event: ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא is born around 1065 somewhere in northeastern Iberia. Barcelona is conventional, while scholarly proposals also include Huesca, Soria or another Aragonese locality; no surviving source fixes the birthplace. The map therefore uses Barcelona as a qualified regional anchor. See the National Library of Israel authority record and the source-critical biography of the Real Academia de la Historia.

By his mature career, ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא lives and works in Christian Barcelona while drawing deeply on Arabic mathematics and astronomy. The titles הנשיא and the Arabic-derived office behind “Savasorda” indicate communal and public responsibilities, possibly judicial, fiscal or administrative, but their exact scope cannot be recovered. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers.

During the early twelfth century, ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא collaborates with Plato of Tivoli in conveying Arabic mathematical and astronomical works into Latin. The displayed year is an approximate marker for a multi-year translation partnership, not a dated appointment. Their collaboration makes Barcelona an important point of contact among Arabic, Hebrew and Latin scientific cultures. See the Max Planck Institute-hosted scientific biography and Enciclopedia Italiana.

In 1122–1123 ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא completes ספר העבור, the earliest Hebrew monograph devoted wholly to the Jewish calendar. The work explains cycles, intercalations and calendrical calculations and creates Hebrew terminology capable of transmitting Arabic mathematical astronomy. See the digitized National Library of Israel edition and MacTutor History of Mathematics.

In the 1120s, ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא develops a broad Hebrew scientific corpus, including צורת הארץ, חשבון מהלכות הכוכבים, astronomical tables and the surviving portions of יסודי התבונה ומגדל האמונה. The year is an approximate literary marker because several texts lack secure completion dates. See the National Library manuscript record and the Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers.

ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא.place: Barcelona, with intellectual ties to Provence
ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא.event: By about 1130 ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא has written works expressly for Hebrew readers in Provence who lacked access to Arabic science, and he also develops the philosophical הגיון הנפש and historical-astrological מגילת המגלה. Older biographies infer that he lived for a time in southern France; modern scholarship notes that an intended Provençal audience does not by itself prove residence, so the marker remains at Barcelona. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Hebrew overview at Kotar.

ר׳ אברהם בר חייא הנשיא probably dies by 10 April 1136, when a manuscript scribe appends a memorial formula to his name. His death place is not known; Barcelona and Provence are conventional possibilities. A disputed identification with a translator active in 1143 would require a later death, so 1136 is retained as the best-supported canonical endpoint rather than an unquestioned exact date. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, National Library authority record and the Real Academia de la Historia.

ר׳ יהודה הלוי.event: Around 1075, ר׳ יהודה הלוי is born, probably in Tudela, then a Muslim-ruled frontier city. Toledo was the traditional identification, but modern research generally prefers Tudela; the year itself is approximate. See the National Library of Israel and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

As a gifted young poet, ר׳ יהודה הלוי sends verse to ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא, who invites him to Granada and introduces him to the city's Hebrew-Arabic literary circle. The displayed year is approximate because the surviving poetry establishes the relationship more securely than its exact beginning. See the Hebrew CET biography and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

By the opening decades of the twelfth century, ר׳ יהודה הלוי is associated with Christian-ruled Toledo, where he practises medicine and writes poetry while moving within the wider learned networks of Iberian Jewry. The year represents a documented phase rather than a precisely dated appointment. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

Evidence from poetic headings and later reconstruction places ר׳ יהודה הלוי in Córdoba during the 1120s. His mature career combines medicine, Hebrew verse, correspondence and close relationships with scholars including ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש; not every city named in later summaries can be dated securely. See the Magnes Press scholarly preview and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ יהודה הלוי.place: Iberian Peninsula; map anchor at Córdoba
ר׳ יהודה הלוי.event: Around 1138–1140, shortly before leaving Iberia, ר׳ יהודה הלוי completes or brings near completion his Judaeo-Arabic defence of Judaism, later called ספר הכוזרי. Recent reassessment of Geniza letters favours this concentrated late period of composition rather than an unsupported decades-long writing itinerary; Córdoba is only a regional map anchor, not a claimed printing place. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the National Library of Israel.

In 1140, ר׳ יהודה הלוי reaches Alexandria on his journey toward the Land of Israel and receives an elaborate welcome from Egyptian Jewish scholars and communal leaders. Geniza letters and poems document his arrival, companions and repeated efforts by admirers to host him. See the Oxford Academic study of the pilgrimage and Cambridge Genizah Research Unit.

Late in 1140, ר׳ יהודה הלוי travels from Alexandria to Fustat, where the merchant-scholar Halfon ben Netanel and other members of the Jewish elite receive him. Five surviving letters to Halfon, several in the poet's own hand, illuminate this Egyptian stage and his determination to continue eastward. See the Cambridge Genizah Research Unit and the National Library of Israel manuscript catalogue.

ר׳ יהודה הלוי.place: Egyptian Mediterranean coast; embarkation associated with Alexandria
ר׳ יהודה הלוי.event: In May 1141, ר׳ יהודה הלוי boards a ship bound for the Land of Israel. Contemporary evidence confirms the departure but not his arrival. A Geniza letter dated 12 November indicates that he had died, probably in July or August; his exact place of death and burial remain unknown. This marker uses Alexandria, his securely documented Egyptian port, and does not claim that he died there. The later tale that a horseman killed him at Jerusalem's gates is not contemporary evidence. See the Cambridge Genizah Research Unit, the National Library of Israel, and the Oxford Academic study.

ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב אבן צדיק.event: Around 1075, ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב אבן צדיק is probably born in Córdoba. The surviving medieval notices do not provide a precise birth date, and some modern Spanish references prefer approximately 1080; 1075 is therefore a conventional map year rather than a documented date. See the National Library of Israel authority record, the Real Academia de la Historia, and the Spanish-language biography.

Probably during his youth, ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב אבן צדיק studies at the Lucena academy under ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אבן גיאת, alongside the circle that also formed poets and scholars such as ר׳ משה בן יעקב אבן עזרא and ר׳ יוסף אבן סהל. The teacher-pupil relationship is transmitted by biographical sources, but the displayed year is an approximation. See the National Library of Israel biography of ר׳ יצחק אבן גיאת and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In 1138, ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב אבן צדיק is appointed a dayan of Córdoba's Jewish community and serves in that office until his death. Older sources say that he sat alongside ר׳ מימון הדיין, father of ר׳ משה בן מימון. The marker uses Córdoba's historic Jewish quarter because the precise location of the twelfth-century court is unknown. See Jewish Encyclopedia, Encyclopedia of Philosophy, and the Real Academia de la Historia.

During ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב אבן צדיק's mature Córdoba career, his writing unites communal judgment, Hebrew poetry and philosophical investigation. He exchanges verse with ר׳ יהודה הלוי, and a poem associated with ר׳ יהודה הלוי's eastward journey belongs to this relationship. The precise date and identification of every poem are debated, so 1140 represents the closing phase of their documented literary circle rather than a certain meeting day. See Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In 1149, ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב אבן צדיק dies in Córdoba after approximately eleven years as a communal dayan. No reliable source identifies his exact death date, residence, court building, grave or cemetery, so the marker remains at the historic Jewish quarter rather than claiming a specific building or burial plot. See the Real Academia de la Historia, Jewish Encyclopedia, and Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה.event: ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה is born in Seville in 1077, the son of ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה, then a court astronomer and leading Jewish communal official under al-Muʿtamid. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the contextual biography of ר׳ יצחק אבן אלבאליה.

The fall of al-Muʿtamid's Seville kingdom ends the court setting in which ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה grew up. His father's final years and death are placed in Granada, making Granada the cautious location for the family's transition; the precise year of ר׳ ברוך's own move is not independently recorded. See the biographies of ר׳ ברוך and ר׳ יצחק אבן אלבאליה in Encyclopaedia Judaica.

At seventeen, following his father's death, ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה travels to Lucena to seek reconciliation with ר׳ יצחק אלפסי and enter his academy. The later family narrative in ספר הקבלה says that ר׳ יצחק אלפסי received him as a son; its broad outline is historically valuable, while its detailed deathbed dialogue remains retrospective. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד's ספר הקבלה.

During nine years of study in Lucena, ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה learns under ר׳ יצחק אלפסי together with his contemporary ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש. The displayed year marks the middle of a continuing apprenticeship, not a separately dated event. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia biography of ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש.

After the death of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי in 1103, ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה concludes his nine-year Lucena period. ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש succeeds to the Lucena academy, while ר׳ ברוך establishes his mature career in Córdoba as dayyan and head of a yeshivah. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the account of the Lucena succession in the Encyclopaedia Judaica biography of ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש.

In Córdoba, ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה leads an academy, serves as judge and teaches many students. His nephew ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד spends his formative years in his household and receives instruction spanning rabbinics, Bible, Hebrew poetry and Greek-Arabic and Jewish philosophy. The year is an approximate marker within their teacher-student relationship. See Encyclopaedia Judaica on ר׳ ברוך and its biography of ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד.

ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה belongs to the learned and poetic circle of ר׳ יהודה הלוי and ר׳ משה אבן עזרא. A poem by ר׳ יהודה הלוי praises him through wordplay on the name ברוך, evidence of his standing among Andalusian Jewish intellectuals; the displayed year represents an ongoing association rather than a securely dated meeting. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה dies in 1126 after serving as Córdoba's dayyan and academy head. ר׳ משה אבן עזרא and ר׳ יהודה הלוי commemorate him in elegies, confirming both his death and his close place in their intellectual circle. Some later Hebrew summaries render the corresponding Hebrew year as 1127; this record follows Encyclopaedia Judaica's 1126. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש.place: Seville, Taifa of Seville; birthplace probable
ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש.event: ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש is born in 1077, probably in Seville. Some older scholarship proposed Granada, so the city is a strong traditional identification rather than an absolute certainty. He first studies within the scholarly circle of ר׳ יצחק בן ברוך אבן אלבאליה. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel authority record.
At approximately twelve, ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש leaves Seville for Lucena and enters the academy of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי. This begins fourteen years of intensive study. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

During his long apprenticeship, ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש studies under ר׳ יצחק אלפסי alongside his contemporary and close friend ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה. The displayed year marks continuing study, not a separately documented incident. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Shortly before his death, ר׳ יצחק אלפסי ordains the twenty-six-year-old ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש, praises his exceptional understanding, and appoints him successor over the Lucena academy despite the presence of his own learned son. ר׳ יוסף begins a thirty-eight-year tenure as its head. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

As the new academy head, ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש consolidates Lucena's position as the principal Talmudic centre of Muslim Spain. His friend ר׳ יהודה הלוי composes poetry celebrating his accession and maintains a close intellectual relationship with him. The year is approximate within the opening phase of his leadership. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

From Lucena, ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש writes responsa—primarily in Judaeo-Arabic—and develops Talmudic commentaries that ultimately cover at least half the Talmud. His surviving writings include substantial but incomplete novellae on Bava Batra and Shevuot. The year represents continuing authorship rather than a precisely dated publication. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library catalogue record for his responsa.

ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש sends, through language formulated by ר׳ יהודה הלוי, a letter seeking contact with the scholars of Provence. It is the earliest surviving document attesting formal scholarly ties between the Spanish and Provençal rabbinic centres; its exact year is not supplied, so 1120 is an approximate map position. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Among the many students of ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש is apparently ר׳ מימון הדיין. Through ר׳ מימון, his methods and rulings profoundly shape ר׳ משה בן מימון, who later praises his Talmudic understanding while never claiming a personal teacher-student meeting. The year is an approximate marker of the teaching relationship. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In the later decades of his leadership, ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש continues issuing decisions and training scholars whose teachings circulate through Spain and Provence. His novellae later enter the works of ר׳ מאיר הלוי אבולעפיה, ר׳ משה בן נחמן, ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן אדרת and ר׳ יום טוב בן אברהם אשבילי, frequently without explicit attribution. The year is representative, not event-specific. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ יוסף בן מאיר הלוי אבן מיגאש dies in Lucena in 1141 after thirty-eight years as head of its academy. His incomplete surviving commentaries, responsa, students and extensive quotation by later Rishonim make his teaching a decisive bridge from ר׳ יצחק אלפסי to the classical Spanish halakhic tradition. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel authority record.

ר׳ חייא אלדאודי.event: Later reference and Al-Daudi family traditions place the birth of ר׳ חייא אלדאודי in Babylonia around 1085 and connect him genealogically with the Babylonian exilarch חזקיה. No contemporary document establishing the year, town or complete lineage has been identified, so the point is a regional map anchor near Baghdad—not a claim that he was born in Baghdad itself. Compare the tradition summarized in Israel Ben-Dor, “The Al-Daudi Family—Between Babylonia, Spain, Morocco and the Land of Israel”, with the much narrower contemporary-literary evidence summarized by the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ חייא אלדאודי.place: Iberian Peninsula (exact place and date unknown)
ר׳ חייא אלדאודי.event: By an unknown point in the first half of the twelfth century, ר׳ חייא אלדאודי is associated with the Iberian Hebrew liturgical world. His recoverable output consists of seliḥot, including one that explicitly adds אלדאודי to the signature חייא. Because the sources do not securely identify a composition city, this deliberately approximate marker is placed centrally on the peninsula rather than at an invented residence. See the Jewish Encyclopedia's source-critical notice.

ר׳ חייא אלדאודי dies in Castile in 1154 according to the standard bibliographical notice. Later Al-Daudi family history specifies León, but that precision is not supplied by the Jewish Encyclopedia and is therefore displayed as a later tradition rather than certainty. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the qualified family-history discussion in Sharsheret Hadorot, vol. 11.

Meir ben Samuel.event: Meir ben Samuel is born in northern France during the formative era of Ashkenazic rabbinic scholarship.
Meir ben Samuel marries Jochebed, daughter of Rashi, linking him to the leading scholarly family of medieval Ashkenaz.
Meir ben Samuel becomes active in the rabbinic academy of Ramerupt and contributes to the emerging Tosafist tradition.
Meir ben Samuel educates his sons Rabbenu Tam, Rashbam, and Isaac ben Meir, who become leading Tosafist scholars.
Meir ben Samuel dies in Ramerupt after helping establish one of the central scholarly dynasties of Ashkenazic Judaism.

Samuel ben Meir.event: Samuel ben Meir is born in Ramerupt into the scholarly family of Rashi during the formative era of Ashkenazic Judaism.
Samuel ben Meir studies under Rashi and the early Tosafist circles in northern France.
Rashbam emerges as a leading Tosafist scholar and develops his distinctive approach to biblical interpretation emphasizing peshat.
Rashbam composes influential commentaries on the Torah and portions of the Talmud that shape later Jewish scholarship.
Samuel ben Meir dies after becoming one of the foundational scholars of the Tosafist and exegetical traditions.

ר׳ אברהם בן מאיר אבן עזרא.event: ר׳ אברהם בן מאיר אבן עזרא is probably born at Tudela around 1089; other scholarly reconstructions give 1092–1093 and an older tradition names Toledo. Tudela lay within the northern reaches of Muslim Iberia and is the birthplace preferred by the National Library of Israel and recent scholarship. See the National Library of Israel and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

During his first five decades in Iberia, ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא earns a precarious living chiefly as a Hebrew poet and develops a close literary and intellectual friendship with fellow Tudelan ר׳ יהודה הלוי. Claims about a formal family relationship are disputed, and his exact sequence of Iberian residences cannot be reconstructed securely. This regional marker uses Tudela rather than inventing a specific move. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the National Library poetry catalogue.

By 1140 ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא has left Iberia and is in Rome, beginning the itinerant Hebrew-writing phase from which most of his scholarly corpus survives. He composes מאזנים and biblical commentaries for readers who lack Arabic, turning Andalusian grammar, exegesis and science into portable Hebrew learning. The Almohad advance forms the historical background, although his precise personal reason and departure route remain uncertain. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Stanford Encyclopedia.

In 1145 ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא is documented at Lucca, where he continues biblical, grammatical and scientific writing. His dated compositions and astronomical observations make Lucca a secure station rather than a conjectural itinerary point. See the scholarly chronology by Shlomo Sela and Gad Freudenthal and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

During 1145–1147 ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא works successively in Mantua and Verona. Biographical tradition connects a serious illness at Mantua with his renewed determination to explain the Torah according to peshat; his writings securely attest the northern Italian phase even where individual anecdotes remain less certain. Verona is used as the displayed endpoint of this short movement. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Enciclopedia Italiana.

At Béziers around 1147–1148, ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא composes the first coordinated version of his Hebrew astrological corpus, including ראשית חכמה and specialized books on judgments, nativities, interrogations and elections. He also writes on divine names for local patrons. This phase systematically translates Arabic scientific concepts into Hebrew. See the Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

By 1154 ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא is in Rouen, producing revised scientific works and continuing his biblical commentaries. Older scholarship sometimes read a corrupted Hebrew place-name as Rhodes, Rodez or Dreux; the modern chronological reconstruction identifies Rouen for major compositions of this northern French phase. See Sela and Freudenthal’s chronological study and the discussion in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

In 1158–1159 ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא is securely documented in London. For his student ר׳ יוסף בן יעקב ממורוויל he composes יסוד מורא וסוד תורה; his אגרת השבת explicitly places its dream narrative in London on 14 Tevet 4919. These writings mark the northernmost certain station of his travels. See the manuscript-based study Ibn Ezra in England and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Around 1160 ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא is again in southern France and is associated with Narbonne, where he translates or transmits an Arabic astronomical treatise. His presence helped introduce the linguistic and scientific inheritance of al-Andalus to the scholars of Provence. See the Enciclopedia Italiana and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ אברהם בן מאיר אבן עזרא.place: Death place uncertain (Rome shown as one scholarly reconstruction)
ר׳ אברהם בן מאיר אבן עזרא.event: Manuscript evidence supports the death of ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא in 1167 at about seventy-five years old, although an influential older chronology gave 1164. His death place is not securely known: Rome, northern Spain, England and the Land of Israel occur in competing traditions. Rome is used only as a cartographic anchor because one scholarly itinerary places him there again in 1166–1167—not as a claim of certainty. See Itamar Kislev’s peer-reviewed chronological reassessment and the cautious National Library biography.

Eliezer ben Nathan.event: Eliezer ben Nathan is born in Mainz in the Rhineland during the rise of Ashkenazic rabbinic scholarship.
Eliezer ben Nathan studies under the disciples of Rashi and becomes associated with the emerging Tosafist tradition.
Eliezer ben Nathan emerges as a leading halakhic authority in Mainz and the wider Rhineland Jewish communities.
Eliezer ben Nathan witnesses the anti-Jewish violence accompanying the Second Crusade and records the suffering of Rhineland Jewry in liturgical compositions.
Eliezer ben Nathan composes halakhic works and responsa that become foundational sources for later Ashkenazic authorities.
Eliezer ben Nathan dies in Mainz after helping shape the development of medieval Ashkenazic Jewish law.

ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי.place: Córdoba, Almoravid al-Andalus (birthplace probable, not certain)
ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי.event: ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי is born around 1110, probably in Córdoba. Older reference works sometimes say Toledo, while current scholarship stresses that the exact birthplace is unknown; Córdoba is the strongest geographical anchor because his maternal family and education are securely associated with the city. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

In his formative years, ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי is educated in the Córdoba household of his maternal uncle ר׳ ברוך בן יצחק אבן אלבאליה, who combines rabbinic leadership with philosophical learning. The displayed year is an approximate midpoint in an extended education that ended no later than his uncle's death in 1126. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי.place: Córdoba to Toledo, al-Andalus and the Kingdom of Castile
ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי.event: After the Almohad conquest transforms southern Iberia and drives many Jews and Christians from Almohad territory, ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי leaves the Andalusian south and settles in Christian Toledo. The sources do not preserve a dated travel diary, so 1148 marks the historical displacement and probable relocation rather than a documented day of arrival. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Spain's Museo Sefardí.

Around 1160–1161 in Toledo, ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי writes the Judeo-Arabic אלעקידה אלרפיעה, later preserved as האמונה הרמה and האמונה הנשאה. It is the first systematic Jewish Aristotelian treatise, using the thought of al-Farabi and especially Ibn Sina to examine physics, metaphysics, prophecy, free will and ethics in relation to Scripture. See the Ben-Zvi Institute critical-edition description and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי completes ספר הקבלה, using the succession of teachers and academies from antiquity through the Geonim and Spanish centers to defend the authority of rabbinic tradition against Karaite objections. Related chronicles form the larger historical project now edited as דורות עולם. See the National Library of Israel catalogue and critical edition and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

During his Toledo years, ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי may also have been the Jewish philosopher-translator called Avendauth, who worked with Dominicus Gundissalinus on Latin translations of Ibn Sina. The shared intellectual profile and recent research provide substantial support, but no indisputable proof establishes that the two names designate one person; this is therefore recorded as a scholarly hypothesis, not a separate certain career. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and its cited translation scholarship.

ר׳ אברהם אבן דאוד הלוי dies in Toledo around 1180. ר׳ יהודה בן שלמה הכהן, writing in Toledo in the first half of the thirteenth century, is the earliest known source to report that he died a martyr; because no reliable account preserves the perpetrators or circumstances, the map does not invent them. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the older Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין.event: ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין is born around 1110 into a Cordoban scholarly family whose remembered lineage included several generations of judges. No birth document survives, and Córdoba is inferred from the family's established association rather than proven as an exact birthplace. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

As a young scholar, ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין studies at Lucena under ר׳ יוסף הלוי אבן מיגאש, the leading disciple of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי. The displayed year is approximate because the period of study is not dated; it necessarily precedes ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש's death in 1141. This relationship becomes central to the halakhic education that ר׳ מימון transmits to his son. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel.

By the middle decades of the twelfth century, ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין serves as a dayan of Córdoba and teaches his children, especially ר׳ משה בן מימון. His judicial role continues the family's Cordoban legal tradition. The year represents his documented mature career rather than a precisely dated appointment. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library biography of ר׳ משה בן מימון.

ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין.place: Córdoba and the family's uncertain Iberian displacement
ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין.event: The Almohad conquest of Córdoba in 1148 ends secure public Jewish life and confronts ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין and his family with conversion, flight or death. Traditional biographies describe about a decade of wandering through Iberia; newer reconstruction allows that they remained near Córdoba for much of this period while outwardly conforming. Because no precise itinerary is established, no invented Spanish towns are plotted. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the overview in Moses Maimonides: Biographic Outlines.

Around 1160 ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין and his family settle in Fez, where Jews living under Almohad coercion often practiced privately. He composes אגרת הנחמה in Judaeo-Arabic to reassure persecuted Jews that Israel's covenant and the Torah remain valid, and he warns against reliance on the messianic predictions of ר׳ משה דרעי. See the National Library record for אגרת הנחמה, Eliezer Schlossberg's Hebrew study and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In spring 1165 ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין leaves Morocco by sea with his family; after a dangerous voyage they reach Acre. Evidence for the family journey derives principally from dated autobiographical notices by ר׳ משה בן מימון. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, the National Library of Israel and the translated itinerary in the Guide for the Perplexed introduction.

On 12 October 1165, according to the dated family itinerary, ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין reaches Jerusalem with ר׳ משה בן מימון and their party and prays at the site of the Temple. The journey also included a visit associated with the patriarchal tombs, but the surviving notice does not justify inventing a longer residence. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the primary itinerary translated in the Guide for the Perplexed introduction.

ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין.place: Final location uncertain: Land of Israel or Fustat, Egypt
ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין.event: The final stage of ר׳ מימון בן יוסף הדיין's life is disputed. One tradition says that he died in the Land of Israel, perhaps in 1165 or 1166, and later associates his burial with Tiberias; another scholarly reconstruction has him accompany the family to Egypt and die at Fustat around 1166, while some references allow a date as late as 1170. Fustat is shown as the probable family destination, not a certain death site. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and Moses Maimonides: Biographic Outlines.

ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי.event: By October or November 1164, ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי has assumed office as gaon and head of ישיבת גאון יעקב in Baghdad. His birth and earlier itinerary are unknown, so the map begins with this first secure institutional anchor rather than inventing a birthplace or place of study. See the Princeton Geniza Project, drawing on Marina Rustow's Encyclopedia of Jews in the Islamic World entry, and the Hebrew history of the Baghdad academy.

In Ḥeshvan 1478 Seleucid (1166 CE), the court of ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי issues a strongly worded Judaeo-Arabic responsum concerning inheritance and protection of an orphan's share. The dated Geniza copy provides direct evidence for his functioning court and legal reach. See the manuscript, transcription and metadata in the Princeton Geniza Project, T-S 13J9.7.

During the tenure of ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי, ר׳ בנימין מטודלה visits Baghdad and names him head of the principal academy among ten centres of full-time Jewish learning. This is an approximate date within ר׳ בנימין's journey, not a precisely dated meeting. See the translated Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela and the Hebrew institutional discussion in Project Ben-Yehuda.

Around the period of ר׳ פתחיה מרגנסבורג's eastern journey, ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי presides over an academy described as drawing a large body of advanced students and authorizing judges across Babylonia, Assyria, Damascus, Persia and Media. ר׳ פתחיה also reports that the gaon's unnamed daughter, learned in Bible and Talmud, taught male pupils from inside the house while they listened outside. The year and reported numbers are approximate and should be treated as a traveler's testimony. See the Princeton Geniza Project and the Hebrew quotation in Project Ben-Yehuda.

Around 1190–1191, ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי becomes a central critic of ר׳ משה בן מימון. Questions concerning bodily resurrection, including material arriving from Yemen, lead him to compose a treatise arguing against implications attributed to משנה תורה. ר׳ משה replies sharply in correspondence and in איגרת תחיית המתים.
