The dispute joins theology to rivalry over transregional rabbinic authority. See the Posen Library, the Library of Congress manuscript description and the Hebrew discussion at Yeshiva.org.il.

Before Rosh Hashanah in 1193, ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי sends a letter to Erbil invoking his Levitical descent as a foundation of the academy's authority. The event is mapped at Baghdad because that is his documented institutional seat; Erbil is the recipient community, not evidence that he traveled there. See the institutional analysis in the Johns Hopkins University dissertation and the broader document corpus in the Princeton Geniza Project.

A writ of appointment bearing the signature of ר׳ שמואל בן עלי הלוי places him alive in 1197, later than the traditional death date of 1194. His death year and burial place are consequently left unknown. His son-in-law ר׳ זכריה בן ברכאל appears as his successor in the academy's leadership. See the updated biographical record of the Princeton Geniza Project and the older conventional chronology in Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Abraham ben David of Posquières.event: Abraham ben David is born in Narbonne in Provence, a major center of Jewish learning.
Abraham ben David studies under leading Provençal rabbis and develops his expertise in Talmudic scholarship.
Abraham ben David establishes a prominent yeshiva in Posquières, attracting students from across Provence and Spain.
Abraham ben David composes critical glosses on Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, becoming one of the principal medieval critics of Maimonidean legal codification.
Abraham ben David dies in Posquières after shaping the development of Provençal Talmudic scholarship and Jewish legal thought.

ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה.event: ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה is conventionally placed at birth around 1130 in Tudela, a significant Jewish centre on the Ebro in the Kingdom of Navarre. His father's name, יונה, and his native city come from the anonymous prologue to ספר המסעות; the year is approximate. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, the National Library of Israel and the translated primary prologue.

ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה.place: Tudela and the Ebro route toward Zaragoza
ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה.event: Around 1165–1166, according to a widely accepted reconstruction, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה leaves Tudela and follows the Ebro corridor through Zaragoza, Tortosa, Tarragona and Barcelona. Alternative scholarship begins the journey as early as 1159–1160, so 1165 is a map anchor rather than an exact departure date. His purpose is not stated and proposed identities as merchant, pilgrim or communal investigator remain hypotheses. See the University of Manchester study and the Auñamendi Basque Encyclopedia.

On the west-to-east European route, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה passes through Girona and Narbonne and records the Jewish communities and scholars of Béziers, Montpellier, Lunel, Posquières, Saint-Gilles, Arles and Marseille. The year is approximate; the ordered itinerary, not an individual calendar date, is secure. See the route and translated text in the Fordham Medieval Sourcebook and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

After sailing from Marseille toward Genoa, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה travels through Pisa and Lucca to Rome, whose monuments and Jewish community he describes in unusual detail. He then follows the Italian peninsula through Campania and Apulia to the Adriatic crossing at Otranto. The year is an approximate itinerary marker. See the primary itinerary and contents and the scholarly Literature of Travel and Exploration.

Traveling by Corfu and the Greek coast through Corinth, Thebes and Thessaloniki, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה reaches Constantinople. His account describes the imperial capital, Hagia Sophia, ceremonial life, commerce and the constrained position of its Jewish population. The sequence is secure, but the year is approximate. See the Fordham edition of the itinerary and Literature of Travel and Exploration.

After crossing the Aegean and moving along the coasts of Anatolia, Syria and Lebanon, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה reaches the Land of Israel and describes Acre, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Hebron and other biblical sites. Jerusalem is a probable personal visit, although modern scholars warn that errors and difficult Crusader-period travel conditions make some individual Holy Land stops uncertain. The year is approximate. See Literature of Travel and Exploration and the National Library of Israel.

Proceeding through Damascus, Aleppo, Harran and Mosul, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה reaches Baghdad, where he gives an extensive account of the caliphate, the exilarch and the city's academies and Jewish population. Baghdad is generally accepted as a firsthand destination. Reports extending toward Central Asia, India and China increasingly depend on informants and are therefore not mapped as his personal movements. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the critical University of Manchester study.

On the return journey, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה is probably in Egypt around 1171, describing Fustat, Cairo and Alexandria in substantial detail. The exact route between Mesopotamia and Egypt is debated, and descriptions of India, China and other distant lands are not proof that he visited them. See Literature of Travel and Exploration and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

From Alexandria, ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה sails toward Sicily and records Messina and Palermo, the final places in his itinerary treated with the density characteristic of firsthand observation. Later brief notices about Germany, Bohemia and northern France are generally treated as reported information rather than proof of visits. The year is approximate. See Literature of Travel and Exploration and the Fordham Medieval Sourcebook.

In the Jewish year 4933 (1173 CE), ר׳ בנימין בן יונה מטודלה returns with his travel notes to Castile. An anonymous editor's prologue says that the resulting Hebrew book preserves what he saw and what he learned from trustworthy people. The source does not say that he died in 1173, despite that date's frequent later use as a death year; his subsequent life is unknown. See the translated primary prologue, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the University of Manchester chronology review.

ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן פרחון.event: ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן פרחון is conventionally placed at birth around 1130 in Qal'a, identified by Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia as Calatayud in Aragon. The date is an authority-file approximation, and some modern Hebrew accounts instead connect the name Qal'a with Qal'at Bani Hammad in North Africa; the marker therefore records the prevailing identification rather than certainty. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Wikimedia authority data.

By the later 1150s, ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן פרחון has left Iberia and reached Salerno. In the preface to his lexicon he explains that local readers knew the Hebrew dictionary of ר׳ מנחם בן סרוק but lacked access to the Judaeo-Arabic grammatical and lexical achievements of Andalusian scholars; this intellectual need motivates his Hebrew synthesis. The year 1155 is only an approximate pre-1160 map anchor, not a documented arrival date. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

On 1 Kislev 4921, in late 1160, ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן פרחון completes מחברת הערוך in Salerno. Written in Hebrew, its grammatical introduction and root lexicon make the philology of ר׳ יהודה חיוג׳ and ר׳ יונה אבן ג׳נאח accessible beyond the Arabic-reading Jewish world. The work also preserves original exegetical, ritual and historical notes. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel catalogue.

ר׳ משה בן מימון.event: ר׳ משה בן מימון is born in Córdoba, conventionally on 14 Nisan 4898 (1138), into the family of the dayan ר׳ מימון בן יוסף. Older scholarship and catalogues sometimes use 1135. He receives his foundational Torah education from his father, within an Andalusian legal tradition linked to ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש and ר׳ יצחק אלפסי; claims that he personally studied with ר׳ יוסף אבן מיגאש are chronologically impossible. See the National Library of Israel and the Biblioteca Nacional de España.

ר׳ משה בן מימון.place: Córdoba and the family's Andalusian exile
ר׳ משה בן מימון.event: The Almohad capture of Córdoba forces the family of ר׳ משה בן מימון to leave the city as the new regime removes the protected legal status traditionally accorded to Jews and Christians and imposes conversionist pressure. The family's movements during the following decade are poorly documented; Almería and other Iberian locations are proposed, but the map does not invent a continuous route. See the Biblioteca Nacional de España and the National Library of Israel.

By approximately 1159–1160, ר׳ משה בן מימון and his family are living in Fez. Here he continues פירוש המשנה and writes or completes works associated with persecution, especially אגרת השמד. Medieval Muslim biographical testimony alleges an outward conversion to Islam, while Jewish sources and modern scholars debate the episode; the record therefore does not present it as settled fact. See the Biblioteca Nacional de España, the Hebrew Maimonides Heritage Center and the scholarly biography by Moshe Halbertal.

On 4 Iyar 4925, ר׳ משה בן מימון and his family leave Fez by sea; after a dangerous voyage they reach Acre on 3 Sivan 1165. His own commemorative account records the storm and arrival. Later that year he visits Jerusalem and Hebron before continuing to Egypt. See the Hebrew chronology and primary quotations at the Maimonides Heritage Center and the National Library of Israel.

In the autumn of 1165, ר׳ משה בן מימון visits Jerusalem and prays at the holy site he calls the Great and Holy House; on 9 Marḥeshvan he goes to Hebron and the Cave of Machpelah. The exact identification of the Jerusalem prayer location should not be expanded beyond his wording into an unsupported architectural claim. See the documented dates at the Maimonides Heritage Center and the National Library's Hebrew biography.

After a short stay in Alexandria, ר׳ משה בן מימון settles permanently in Fustat, the commercial and Jewish centre adjoining Cairo. He completes פירוש המשנה around 1168, serves as a dayan, develops a transregional responsa practice and begins the sustained legal work culminating in משנה תורה. See the National Library of Israel and Cambridge's account of his Egyptian autograph manuscripts.

Around 1169–1170, David, the younger brother and commercial supporter of ר׳ משה בן מימון, dies in an Indian Ocean shipwreck while carrying family capital. ר׳ משה later describes prolonged grief; economic responsibility and his existing medical learning help push medicine from scholarship into an intensive profession. The shipwreck is not mapped abroad because its exact location is uncertain and ר׳ משה was not present. See the National Library of Israel and the scholarly biographical overview in PubMed Central.

In 1172, ר׳ משה בן מימון writes אגרת תימן to Jews facing persecution and a destabilizing messianic claimant. The event remains mapped at Fustat, where he wrote; Yemen is the destination of the letter, not evidence of his physical presence. See the manuscript and work survey at the National Library of Israel and the broader account at My Jewish Learning.

By approximately 1177–1178, ר׳ משה בן מימון completes the main recension of משנה תורה, a fourteen-book Hebrew codification of the whole halakhic system. He continues revising the text, and its lack of explicit source citations provokes criticism from figures including ר׳ אברהם בן דוד מפושקיירא and the Baghdad circle. See Oxford Bibliographies, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Cambridge's autograph evidence.

By the mid-1180s, ר׳ משה בן מימון is an established physician connected to the Ayyubid ruling elite, particularly the powerful administrator al-Qāḍī al-Fāḍil. The familiar statement that he was Saladin's personal physician is often overstated; the secure evidence places him within the courtly medical circle. His surviving letter to ר׳ שמואל אבן תיבון describes exhausting daily travel between Fustat and Cairo and a heavy patient load. See Cambridge University's biographical account, the Hebrew CET biography and the critical medical editions at Brill.

Around 1190, ר׳ משה בן מימון completes מורה הנבוכים for his advanced student ר׳ יוסף בן יהודה אבן שמעון. Soon afterward, controversy over resurrection and criticism from the Baghdad academy of ר׳ שמואל בן עלי lead him to issue מאמר תחיית המתים in 1191. During portions of his Egyptian career he also exercises the functions associated with Head of the Jews, though the exact dates and formal title are debated. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, the Library of Congress manuscript and the National Library of Israel.

On 20 Tevet 4965 (13 December 1204), ר׳ משה בן מימון dies in Fustat. His son ר׳ אברהם בן הרמב״ם succeeds to communal leadership and develops an influential pietist synthesis. A powerful tradition holds that ר׳ משה's remains were carried to Tiberias, where his tomb is venerated, but some scholarship argues that he remained buried in Egypt; Fustat is therefore the secure death marker and Tiberias a separately acknowledged burial tradition. See the National Library of Israel and the summary of the burial dispute at the Tomb of Maimonides reference page.

Hillel ben Eliakim.event: Hillel ben Eliakim is born in the Byzantine Empire, likely within the Jewish scholarly communities of Greece.
Hillel ben Eliakim becomes active as a biblical commentator and scholar within the Byzantine Jewish world.
Hillel ben Eliakim draws upon earlier Sephardic and eastern exegetical traditions circulating through the eastern Mediterranean.
Hillel ben Eliakim composes Hebrew biblical commentaries noted for philological and interpretive analysis.
Hillel ben Eliakim dies after contributing to the preservation of medieval Byzantine Jewish biblical scholarship.

Samuel ibn Tibbon.event: Samuel ibn Tibbon is born in Lunel in Provence into a family of prominent translators and scholars.
Samuel ibn Tibbon studies philosophy, medicine, and Hebrew philology within the intellectual circles of Provence.
Samuel ibn Tibbon travels to the Land of Israel and the eastern Mediterranean while deepening his engagement with philosophical scholarship.
Samuel ibn Tibbon completes his influential Hebrew translation of Maimonides' 'Guide for the Perplexed'.
Samuel ibn Tibbon composes philosophical commentaries and translations that help spread Aristotelian thought among European Jews.
Samuel ibn Tibbon dies after transforming the transmission of Jewish philosophy into the Hebrew-speaking world.

ר׳ עזריאל בן מנחם מגירונה.event: ר׳ עזריאל בן מנחם מגירונה is placed in Girona from the conventional map year 1160. This is not a securely documented birth date: authoritative modern references say that no personal details survive and identify him only as active in the early thirteenth century. The conventional date is retained for filename and map compatibility. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Bibliothèque nationale de France catalogue, and the Jewish Encyclopedia's Girona entry.

Around the opening of the thirteenth century, ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה belongs to the emerging Girona kabbalistic centre. A preserved letter from his teacher ר׳ יצחק סגי נהור to Girona appears to criticize the disclosure of esoteric teachings to wider audiences. The evidence establishes the relationship but does not prove a separate journey by ר׳ עזריאל to Provence, so the point remains at Girona. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Theological Seminary overview.

ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה develops שער השואל, a question-and-answer exposition of the ten sefirot. It distinguishes the unknowable אין סוף from the revealed sefirotic life of divinity and adapts Neoplatonic reasoning to explain emanation, unity and creation. The year is an approximate activity marker rather than a dated publication. See a fifteenth-century witness in the National Library of Israel Ktiv catalogue and the analysis in Encyclopaedia Judaica.

During his Girona activity, ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה writes or develops commentaries on ספר יצירה, talmudic aggadah and the liturgy. His prayer interpretations understand acts such as answering אמן as channels for divine emanation. Because overlapping texts circulated under the names of ר׳ עזרא בן שלמה and ר׳ משה בן נחמן, modern attribution depends on terminology and manuscript comparison rather than printed title pages alone. See the Jewish Theological Seminary, BnF description of the critical corpus, and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה sends a substantial epistle from Girona to Burgos answering kabbalistic questions. This documents correspondence, not physical travel to Burgos. Some manuscripts assign the letter to ר׳ יעקב בן יעקב הכהן of Soria, but textual scholarship restores it to ר׳ עזריאל. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the recent reassessment in Tarbiz.

By the mature phase of Girona Kabbalah, the poet ר׳ משולם בן שלמה דפיירה praises ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה as a leader of the city's kabbalists and as his teacher. ר׳ עזריאל's thought also closely parallels early kabbalistic formulations by ר׳ משה בן נחמן, although recent scholarship treats a direct teacher–student relationship as plausible rather than proven. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Hebrew University study הקבלה בגרונה במאה השלוש עשרה: עזריאל ורמב״ן, הערכה מחודשת.

The year 1238 is retained only as a conventional endpoint used by some modern catalogues for ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה; it is not a securely documented death year and may reflect the longstanding confusion with ר׳ עזרא בן שלמה. No reliable death place or burial site is known. Compare the cautious Encyclopaedia Judaica biography with the conventional dates in the Bibliothèque nationale de France catalogue.

David Kimhi.event: David Kimhi is born in Narbonne in Provence into a family of prominent Jewish scholars and grammarians.
David Kimhi studies Hebrew grammar, philosophy, and biblical interpretation under the guidance of his family in Provence.
David Kimhi begins composing influential grammatical and biblical works that spread throughout Jewish communities in Europe.
David Kimhi becomes involved in defending the philosophical legacy of Maimonides during the Maimonidean controversies.
David Kimhi dies in Provence after shaping the future of Hebrew grammar and biblical commentary.

Eleazar of Worms.event: Eleazar of Worms is born in Mainz in the Rhineland, a major center of medieval Ashkenazic Judaism.
Eleazar of Worms studies under Judah ben Samuel of Regensburg and becomes associated with the Hasidei Ashkenaz movement.
Eleazar of Worms settles in Worms and emerges as a leading authority in Jewish law, ethics, and mysticism.
Eleazar of Worms's wife and daughters are murdered during anti-Jewish violence, an event that profoundly shapes his pietistic writings.
Eleazar of Worms composes mystical, ethical, and halakhic works that become foundational texts of Ashkenazic pietism.
Eleazar of Worms dies in Worms after becoming one of the foremost mystical scholars of medieval Ashkenaz.

ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.place: Burgos, Kingdom of Castile; probable birthplace
ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.event: ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה is born around this time, probably at Burgos, into the prominent Abulafia family. The National Library of Israel uses 1170, while reference works offer approximate dates from about 1165 to 1180; the marker therefore represents a documented regional tradition, not a precise birthplace and date. See the National Library of Israel authority record and Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.place: Toledo, Kingdom of Castile; move approximate
ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.event: By the end of the twelfth century, ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה is associated with Toledo after moving there with his father, ר׳ טודרוס בן יהודה הלוי אבולעפיה. Toledo—not a recoverable modern street address—became the center of his academy, court service, writing, and communal authority. The year is an approximate map anchor because the sources do not preserve a dated itinerary. See the biographical synthesis and cited scholarship in Meir ha-Levi Abulafia.

From Toledo, ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה writes to the sages of Lunel challenging formulations attributed to ר׳ משה בן מימון on bodily resurrection and the interpretation of rabbinic aggadah. This is correspondence, not evidence that he travelled to Lunel. The exchange opens the first Maimonidean controversy and is preserved through ספר האגרות. See the National Library of Israel and this source study of the controversy.

By approximately his mid-thirties, ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה serves among Toledo’s three dayyanim and heads a yeshiva. His judicial work and teaching establish Toledo as the secure geographical center of his mature career; the year is representative rather than an attested appointment date. See the biographical accounts in Meir Abulafia and Meir ha-Levi Abulafia.

During the early thirteenth century, ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה develops the Talmudic project later known as יד רמה. The exact dates of individual tractates cannot be securely fixed, so 1210 marks an active Toledo teaching and writing phase rather than a claimed publication year. Surviving witnesses include Bava Batra, Sanhedrin, Kiddushin, and fragments on Gittin. Consult the National Library manuscript record, the Ktiv Gittin-fragment record, and Sefaria’s work record.

After the death of his father, ר׳ טודרוס בן יהודה הלוי אבולעפיה, ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה succeeds to the communal honorific nasi in Toledo. The title reflects the family’s elite communal standing alongside his established judicial and scholarly authority. See the contemporary-biographical summary in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.place: Toledo, Kingdom of Castile; year approximate
ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.event: When opponents seek to renew the campaign against ר׳ משה בן מימון in the 1230s, ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה declines to participate despite his earlier criticism. The episode shows that his 1202 objections should not be collapsed into every later anti-Maimonidean movement. The map remains at Toledo because the evidence concerns correspondence and policy, not travel. See Meir Abulafia and the fuller bibliographical account in Meir ha-Levi Abulafia.

ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.place: Toledo, Kingdom of Castile; death-place disputed
ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה.event: ר׳ מאיר בן טודרוס הלוי אבולעפיה dies in 1244, conventionally on 18 Nisan 5004 (29 March). Toledo is used because it was his securely documented career center and some references place his death there; another modern account gives Burgos. The disagreement is retained rather than assigning false certainty. Compare the date in the Jewish Encyclopedia, Toledo in the German biographical record, and Burgos in the English biographical record.

ר׳ יהודה בן יוסף אבן אלפכאר.event: ר׳ יהודה בן יוסף אבן אלפכאר is born in Toledo during the last third of the twelfth century. The displayed year 1170 is a conventional approximate marker rather than an exact date. He belongs to a prominent family originally from Granada and established in Toledo, including his court-physician father ר׳ יוסף אלפכאר. See the Real Academia de la Historia biography and the Jewish Encyclopedia family entry.

By the reign of Ferdinand III, ר׳ יהודה אלפכאר is an eminent physician, learned communal figure and politically connected member of Toledo Jewry. Reference works describe him as physician-in-ordinary to Ferdinand III, although surviving evidence is clearer about his Toledo influence than about the precise terms of his royal appointment. See the Real Academia de la Historia and Jewish Encyclopedia.

During the renewed controversy over the writings of ר׳ משה בן מימון, ר׳ דוד קמחי attempts to reach Toledo and enlist ר׳ יהודה אלפכאר for the Maimonidean party. Illness prevents the meeting, so the debate proceeds by letter. This point remains at Toledo because it maps ר׳ יהודה's documented location, not ר׳ דוד's route. See the dated historical introduction and primary text at Daat, the Encyclopaedia Judaica overview, and the Jewish Encyclopedia account.

ר׳ יהודה אלפכאר answers ר׳ דוד קמחי in highly crafted rhymed Hebrew prose. He attacks philosophical allegorization and the elevation of speculative premises over Scripture, while explicitly recognizing ר׳ משה בן מימון as a great but fallible human scholar. The surviving manuscript tradition opens one reply with ‘יגער ה׳ בך השטן, דוד הוא הקטן’. Read the textual study at Daat and consult the National Library of Israel catalogue for Frankfurt Ms. Oct. 99.

The correspondence establishes ר׳ יהודה אלפכאר as one of the major intellectual voices opposing the Maimonidean party. His medical and philosophical education complicates any simple picture of the opponents as enemies of all rational learning; the dispute concerns the authority and permissible reach of philosophy in interpreting Torah. His harsh treatment of ר׳ דוד קמחי, however, draws disapproval even from associates. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the scholarly controversy overview.

ר׳ יהודה בן יוסף אבן אלפכאר dies in 1235, probably in Toledo. His letters survive in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century manuscript witnesses and in later printed collections, making his polemic far better documented than the details of his private life or medical practice. See the Real Academia de la Historia, National Library catalogue for Vatican Ms. ebr. 507, and Frankfurt Ms. Oct. 99.

Solomon ben Abraham of Montpellier.event: Solomon ben Abraham of Montpellier is born in Provence during the flourishing of medieval Jewish intellectual culture.
Solomon ben Abraham becomes active as a rabbinic authority in Montpellier and aligns with traditionalist circles opposed to radical philosophical trends.
Solomon ben Abraham launches campaigns against the philosophical teachings associated with Maimonides and Aristotelian rationalism.
Solomon ben Abraham appeals to leading rabbinic authorities in Spain, including Solomon ben Aderet, seeking support for anti-philosophical decrees.
Solomon ben Abraham of Montpellier dies after becoming a central figure in the early Maimonidean controversies.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Girona, County of Barcelona, Crown of Aragon
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: ר׳ משה בן נחמן is born in Girona in 1194 and grows up within its Jewish community. His Girona origin is reflected in the appellation Gerondi and in his Catalan name, Bonastruc ça Porta. See the National Library of Israel biography and the scholarly overview in Encyclopaedia of Religion.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Barcelona and Girona, Crown of Aragon; study period approximate
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: As a young scholar, ר׳ משה בן נחמן studies the Talmudic traditions transmitted by ר׳ יהודה בן יקר in Barcelona and by ר׳ נתן בן מאיר מטרינקטייל, gaining access to the methods of the northern French Tosafists while retaining Spanish and Provençal learning. The year is a representative anchor because no dated student itinerary survives. See the biographical study in Encyclopaedia of Religion and the Encyclopaedia Judaica article.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Girona, Crown of Aragon; literary activity approximate
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: By the early thirteenth century, ר׳ משה בן נחמן has begun the halakhic and Talmudic writing that establishes his school, including מלחמות ה׳ in defense of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי and novellae that combine Sephardi learning with Tosafist analysis. The date marks a broad Girona period rather than a first-publication claim. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia of Religion.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Girona, Crown of Aragon; correspondence network
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: During the renewed controversy over the writings of ר׳ משה בן מימון, ר׳ משה בן נחמן attempts to mediate between defenders and opponents. He criticizes philosophical excesses but refuses a simple rejection of ר׳ משה בן מימון’s halakhic authority. His letters reach communities outside Girona, but correspondence is not treated as physical travel. See the National Library of Israel and the detailed account in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Royal Palace, Barcelona, Crown of Aragon
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: King James I orders ר׳ משה בן נחמן to defend Judaism in the Barcelona Disputation against the Dominican convert Pablo Christiani. Held in July 1263 before the royal court, the sessions concern messianic claims, the status of Jesus, and Christian readings of rabbinic aggadah. Two partisan records survive: רמב״ן’s Hebrew account and a shorter Latin account. See the University of Texas source introduction and the University of Konstanz primary-source edition.

After circulating his account of the disputation, ר׳ משה בן נחמן faces Dominican accusations of blasphemy. A royal tribunal imposes punishment while church pressure seeks a harsher sentence; the legal aftermath, rather than an immediate expulsion on the debate’s final day, explains his eventual departure. See Robert Chazan’s study, Barcelona and Beyond, and the documentary discussion in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Having left the Crown of Aragon, ר׳ משה בן נחמן reaches the port of Acre in 1267 and enters the Land of Israel. Acre becomes his principal eastern base and later teaching center; the surviving record does not securely reconstruct every stage of the Mediterranean voyage. See the National Library of Israel biography.

In Jerusalem, ר׳ משה בן נחמן encounters a severely diminished Jewish community, organizes communal prayer, and describes the city’s condition in a letter to his son. Tradition connects this renewal with the institution later called the Ramban Synagogue, though the present structure should not be treated as an unchanged thirteenth-century building. See the National Library of Israel and the preserved Jerusalem-letter discussion at Kotar.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Bethlehem and Hebron, Kingdom of Jerusalem
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: During his first period in the Land of Israel, ר׳ משה בן נחמן visits Bethlehem and Hebron. These visits belong to his documented encounter with biblical geography and should not be mistaken for permanent residence in either town. See the Hebrew biography and itinerary summary at the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן settles in Acre, gathers students, teaches, and continues revising פירוש התורה in light of texts, traditions, and geographical observations encountered in the Land of Israel. A surviving manuscript notice explicitly associates a late exposition with Acre. See the National Library manuscript record and the NLI biography.

ר׳ משה בן נחמן.place: Acre, Kingdom of Jerusalem; final base, death place uncertain
ר׳ משה בן נחמן.event: ר׳ משה בן נחמן dies around 1270 after spending his final years in the Land of Israel, with Acre his last securely documented scholarly base. His burial place is unknown; later traditions variously identify Acre, Haifa, Hebron, and Jerusalem, so no supposed tomb is presented as certain. See the National Library of Israel and the older source survey in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Yonah Gerondi.event: Yonah Gerondi is born in Girona in Catalonia during the flourishing of medieval Sephardic Jewish scholarship.
Yonah Gerondi studies under the French Tosafists and becomes immersed in advanced Talmudic scholarship.
Yonah Gerondi participates in opposition to the philosophical writings of Maimonides during the Maimonidean controversies.
Yonah Gerondi is profoundly affected by the public burning of Talmud manuscripts in Paris and reconsiders his earlier opposition to Maimonides.
Rabbeinu Yonah composes ethical and penitential works emphasizing repentance, humility, and spiritual discipline.
Yonah Gerondi dies after becoming one of the most influential ethical and halakhic voices of medieval Sephardic Judaism.

ר׳ יעקב בן ששת גירונדי.event: ר׳ יעקב בן ששת גירונדי is placed at Girona from the conventional map year 1200. This is not a documented birth date: neither his birth year nor his death year is known. The surname Gerondi identifies his association with Girona, and historical reference works describe him as a thirteenth-century kabbalist of the city. See the National Library of Israel authority record, Encyclopaedia Judaica, and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

By the middle decades of the thirteenth century, ר׳ יעקב בן ששת participates intellectually in Girona's kabbalistic circle alongside contemporaries such as ר׳ משה בן נחמן and ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה. He repeatedly uses teachings associated with ר׳ יצחק סגי נהור but does not identify him as his own teacher, so direct discipleship remains unproved. See the scholarly discussion by Joseph Dan, Tel Aviv University and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Around 1240, ר׳ יעקב בן ששת composes משיב דברים נכוחים, a systematic response to מאמר יקוו המים by ר׳ שמואל אבן תיבון. Across thirty chapters he defends creation, providence, prayer and recompense through kabbalistic interpretation while demonstrating an ambivalent, informed engagement with science rather than blanket hostility to it. The date is approximate. Consult the National Library catalogue for the critical edition, Revue des Études Juives review, and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Approximately in this period, ר׳ יעקב בן ששת writes שער השמים, also known from its opening as משה קיבל. Its elaborate rhymed prose presents traditions concerning the sefirot and divine names and combines mystical exposition with polemic against philosophical approaches. The precise composition year is not secure. See the National Library of Israel manuscript record and Jewish Encyclopedia.

During his mid-thirteenth-century activity, ר׳ יעקב בן ששת is also associated by modern scholarship with ספר האמונה והבטחון. The work circulated for centuries under the name of ר׳ משה בן נחמן; comparison with משיב דברים נכוחים supports attribution to ר׳ יעקב, though its complicated manuscript history should not be hidden. The displayed year is representative, not an exact publication date. See the public-domain National Library edition and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

יצחק מקורבייל (Sefer Mitzvot Katan – Sma.event: Born in Corbeil, France, into a prominent rabbinic family.
Active in French rabbinic circles; influenced by Tosafist methodology and the Semag.
Compiled the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (Smak), a condensed, practical halakhic code based on the Semag.
Died in Corbeil, France. His Smak remained a standard halakhic text for centuries in Ashkenazic yeshivot.

מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג (Maharam of Rothe.event: Born in Worms, part of medieval Germany, into a distinguished rabbinic family.
Studied under Rabbi Yechiel of Paris and other Tosafists in France; influenced by the Paris Talmud disputation (1240).
Returned to Germany, teaching and serving as rabbi in various communities, including Rothenburg, Wurzburg, and Mainz.
Attempted to emigrate to Eretz Yisrael with many followers, but was captured and imprisoned by Emperor Rudolf I near Ensisheim.
Died in prison in Ensisheim after seven years of captivity. His body was held for ransom and only buried years later in Worms by Alexander ben Shlomo Wimpfen, who paid the ransom.

ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.place: Toledo, Kingdom of Castile; probable workshop location
ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.event: Around 1245–1255, ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל copies the monumental three-volume Hebrew Bible now preserved in Marseille as Bibliothèque municipale MS 1626. Institutional cataloguing assigns the manuscript to central Castile and identifies Toledo as the probable place of manufacture. Toledo is therefore a strong codicological localization, though the surviving record does not supply a modern building or street. See the Biblissima manuscript catalogue and its IIIF digitization record.

ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.place: Toledo and Burgos scribal network, Kingdom of Castile
ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.event: By the middle of the thirteenth century, ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל is situated within the Ben Israel family network of specialist biblical scribes working principally in Toledo and Burgos. The evidence defines a workshop and kinship network rather than a securely dated personal move between the two cities, so the marker remains at Toledo and does not invent a journey to Burgos. See Katrin Kogman-Appel’s reconstruction of the family workshops in Jewish Book Art Between Islam and Christianity.

ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.place: Toledo, Kingdom of Castile; documentary association
ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.event: A documentary reconstruction of the Ben Israel family records ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל in 1282, extending his attested presence beyond the production date of the Marseille Bible. The source does not justify attaching a new office, residence, or journey to this notice; it confirms continuing activity within the Castilian scribal milieu. See the family diagram and documentary discussion in Kogman-Appel’s study.

ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.place: Toledo, Kingdom of Castile; place uncertain
ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל.event: A tombstone dated 1297 has been associated by scholarship with ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל, providing the likely endpoint of his documented life. The publication’s family reconstruction supplies the date but does not warrant a precise modern burial-site coordinate; Toledo is retained as the center of his known professional network and the location is explicitly uncertain. See the genealogical and documentary reconstruction in Jewish Book Art Between Islam and Christianity.

ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי מברצלונה (הרא״ה).event: Around 1235, ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי is probably born in Girona into a distinguished scholarly family descended from ר׳ זרחיה הלוי, בעל המאור. The exact birth year is conventional and the birthplace probable rather than certain. See Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

By the middle of the thirteenth century, ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי studies with his elder brother ר׳ פנחס הלוי and with ר׳ משה בן נחמן. In this Catalan school he encounters ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת, later his colleague and principal halakhic opponent. The year is approximate. See Jewish Encyclopedia.

By his mature career, ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי is identified with Barcelona, hence הרא״ה מברצלונה. He teaches, decides law and develops the independent method later transmitted especially by ר׳ יום טוב בן אברהם אשבילי. The starting year is approximate. See the National Library of Israel and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In 1284/1285, the king appoints ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי rabbi in Zaragoza to help end continuing communal dissension. The authority of his rulings there remained strong for generations. See Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Around 1286—placed by some older reconstructions closer to 1291—ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי spends a short period in Toledo before returning to Barcelona. The evidence supports only a brief residence, not a long rabbinic tenure. See Jewish Encyclopedia and its history of Jewish Toledo.

After returning to Barcelona, ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי remains a leading independent authority. In the late thirteenth century he writes בדק הבית, a close critique of תורת הבית by ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת; the latter responds in משמרת הבית. The composition year is unknown, so 1290 is approximate. See Sefaria and the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי מברצלונה (הרא״ה).place: Place of death unknown; Barcelona is the final documented base
ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי מברצלונה (הרא״ה).event: ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי dies sometime before 1303; neither the exact year nor place is securely documented. The coordinate retains Barcelona only as his final well-supported base and is not proof that he died there. A reported late move to Montpellier derives from a likely textual misreading and is omitted. See Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

רשב״א.event: Born in Barcelona, Crown of Aragon; studied under Nachmanides and Yonah Gerondi
Issued responsa to Moravia, earliest evidence of Jewish presence in Austerlitz and Třešť
Documented as banker and communal leader in Barcelona
Became chief rabbi of Barcelona’s Main Synagogue; widely recognized as authority for Spanish and European Jewry
With Barcelona rabbinate, issued ban forbidding study of philosophy/metaphysics before age 30 (except medicine)
Died in Barcelona; left major halachic and Talmudic works and over 3,000 responsa

Moses de Leon.event: Moses de Leon is born in León in Christian Spain during the rise of medieval Kabbalistic thought.
Moses de Leon becomes active in the Jewish scholarly and mystical circles of Castile.
Moses de Leon begins composing and circulating mystical writings associated with early Kabbalistic traditions.
Moses de Leon disseminates the 'Zohar', presenting it as an ancient mystical revelation attributed to Shimon bar Yochai.
Moses de Leon dies in Ávila after helping establish the textual foundations of classical Kabbalah.

Menachem Meiri.event: Menachem Meiri is born in Perpignan in Provence during the flourishing of medieval Jewish scholarship.
Menachem Meiri studies under leading Provençal rabbis and becomes immersed in Talmudic and philosophical scholarship.
Menachem Meiri begins composing his systematic commentaries on the Babylonian Talmud.
Menachem Meiri produces philosophical and ethical writings emphasizing rational interpretation and moral universalism.
Menachem Meiri's Talmudic works gain recognition for their clarity, organization, and comprehensive legal analysis.
Menachem Meiri dies in Perpignan after becoming one of the most important rabbinic scholars of medieval Provence.

Abba Mari ben Moses ben Joseph.event: Abba Mari ben Moses ben Joseph is born in Lunel, Provence.
Abba Mari becomes active among the Jewish scholars of Montpellier and grows concerned over the spread of Aristotelian rationalism.
Abba Mari begins corresponding with Rabbi Solomon ben Aderet of Barcelona, urging intervention against philosophical extremism.
Abba Mari participates in the anti-rationalist campaign that culminates in rabbinic decrees restricting philosophical studies among the youth.
Abba Mari relocates to Perpignan following the expulsion of Jews from France under Philip IV and compiles the polemical correspondence later published as 'Minḥat Ḳenaot'.

Mordecai ben Hillel.event: Mordecai ben Hillel is born in the Holy Roman Empire during the height of the Tosafist period of Ashkenazic scholarship.
Mordecai ben Hillel studies under Meir of Rothenburg and other leading Tosafist authorities.
Mordecai ben Hillel begins compiling halakhic rulings and Tosafist traditions into his major legal work.
Mordecai ben Hillel's halakhic compilation becomes widely circulated among Ashkenazic Jewish communities.
Mordecai ben Hillel and members of his family are killed during the Rintfleisch massacres in Germany.

Yom Tov of Seville.event: Yom Tov of Seville is born in Seville during the flourishing of medieval Sephardic Jewish scholarship.
Yom Tov of Seville studies in Barcelona under Solomon ben Aderet and Aaron HaLevi.
The Ritva emerges as a leading Talmudic scholar within the Catalonian rabbinic academies.
The Ritva composes influential novellae on the Talmud synthesizing Sephardic and Ashkenazic legal traditions.
Yom Tov of Seville dies after becoming one of the major rabbinic authorities of medieval Spanish Jewry.

Asher ben Jehiel.event: Asher ben Jehiel is born in the Rhineland region of the Holy Roman Empire, likely in Cologne.
Asher ben Jehiel studies under Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg and emerges as a prominent Ashkenazic Talmudist.
Asher ben Jehiel becomes involved in communal rabbinic leadership amid increasing pressures on German Jewry.
Asher ben Jehiel flees Germany and settles in Toledo, where he is appointed chief rabbi and head of a major yeshiva.
Asher ben Jehiel composes influential halakhic rulings and Talmudic commentaries that bridge Ashkenazic and Sephardic traditions.
Asher ben Jehiel dies in Toledo after becoming one of the most authoritative halakhic voices of medieval Judaism.

Jacob ben Asher.event: Jacob ben Asher is born in Cologne in the Holy Roman Empire into the family of the prominent rabbinic authority Asher ben Jehiel.
Jacob ben Asher studies under his father and leading Ashkenazic scholars in the Rhineland.
Jacob ben Asher relocates with his family to Toledo following increasing persecution of Jews in Germany.
Jacob ben Asher begins composing the 'Arba'ah Turim', systematically organizing Jewish law into four major sections.
Jacob ben Asher's legal rulings and halakhic methodology gain wide influence among both Sephardic and Ashkenazic communities.
Jacob ben Asher dies in Toledo after producing one of the foundational codes of Jewish law.

יעקב בן אשר (Ba'al HaTurim).event: Born in Cologne, Holy Roman Empire, during his father’s wanderings (or possibly in Spain).
Moved with his father, the Rosh, to Toledo, Castile, after expulsion of Jews from parts of Germany.
Settled in Toledo. Became a leading posek (decisor), developing the structure of his code, the Arba'ah Turim.
Died in Toledo, Castile. Buried there near his father, the Rosh.

Gersonides.event: Levi ben Gershon is born in Bagnols-sur-Cèze in Provence during the flourishing of medieval Jewish philosophy.
Gersonides becomes active in the intellectual circles of Provence, studying philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, and Talmud.
Gersonides composes portions of 'Milhamot HaShem', his major philosophical work reconciling Aristotelianism with Judaism.
Gersonides conducts astronomical observations and develops scientific instruments that gain attention among contemporary scholars.
Gersonides completes influential biblical commentaries noted for their philosophical and rationalist interpretation.
Gersonides dies in Provence after becoming one of the foremost Jewish philosophers and scientists of the medieval period.

David Abudarham.event: David Abudarham is born in Seville in Christian Spain during the later period of Sephardic Jewish scholarship.
David Abudarham studies under Rabbi Jacob ben Asher and becomes immersed in halakhic and liturgical scholarship.
David Abudarham composes his major commentary on the Jewish liturgy, systematically explaining prayers, blessings, and synagogue customs.
David Abudarham's liturgical commentary begins circulating widely among Sephardic Jewish communities in Spain.
David Abudarham dies in Seville after establishing one of the foundational medieval commentaries on Jewish prayer.

ר' וידאל די טולוסה (Vidal of Tolosa, Mag.event: Born in Tolosa or possibly in Barcelona, in the Crown of Aragon.
Studied Torah and halakha in the Spanish yeshivot, in the intellectual climate of the Rishonim.
Began writing his Maggid Mishneh commentary on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah, clarifying sources and addressing critiques.
Passed away in Spain; his Maggid Mishneh became foundational for later study and psak.

Nissim of Gerona.event: Nissim of Gerona is born in Barcelona during the flourishing of medieval Catalonian Jewish scholarship.
Nissim of Gerona becomes active in the rabbinic academies of Catalonia and gains recognition for his Talmudic scholarship.
Nissim of Gerona emerges as one of the leading halakhic authorities of Spanish Jewry and heads an important yeshiva.
The Ran composes influential novellae on the Talmud and develops philosophical sermons addressing theology and ethics.
The Ran responds to growing communal and political pressures affecting Jewish life in Christian Spain.
Nissim of Gerona dies after becoming one of the most influential rabbinic scholars of medieval Sephardic Judaism.

Hasdai Crescas.event: Hasdai Crescas is born in Barcelona during the flourishing of medieval Sephardic Jewish culture.
Hasdai Crescas studies under Rabbi Nissim ben Reuben and becomes established as a leading rabbinic scholar.
Hasdai Crescas is appointed to positions of communal and royal authority within the Jewish communities of the Crown of Aragon.
Hasdai Crescas witnesses the anti-Jewish massacres of 1391, during which his son is killed, profoundly shaping his later writings.
Hasdai Crescas composes 'Or Adonai', a major critique of Aristotelian philosophy and defense of Jewish theology.
Hasdai Crescas dies after becoming one of the most influential Jewish philosophers of late medieval Spain.

Joseph Albo.event: Joseph Albo is born in the Crown of Aragon during the final century of medieval Sephardic Jewish culture in Spain.
Joseph Albo studies under Hasdai Crescas and becomes influenced by Jewish critiques of Aristotelian philosophy.
Joseph Albo participates in the Disputation of Tortosa, one of the most significant public religious confrontations between Jews and Christians in medieval Spain.
Joseph Albo composes portions of 'Sefer Ha-Ikkarim', outlining the fundamental principles of Jewish belief.
Joseph Albo's philosophical writings circulate among Sephardic Jewish scholars confronting theological and communal crises.
Joseph Albo dies after becoming one of the major Jewish theologians of late medieval Spain.

Israel Isserlein.event: Israel Isserlein is born in Regensburg during a turbulent period for Ashkenazic Jewry in Central Europe.
Israel Isserlein studies under leading German and Austrian rabbinic authorities and gains recognition for his halakhic scholarship.
Israel Isserlein settles in Wiener Neustadt and establishes a prominent yeshiva attracting students from across Central Europe.
Israel Isserlein composes influential halakhic responsa and legal rulings addressing the customs and challenges of Ashkenazic communities.
Israel Isserlein completes 'Terumat HaDeshen', one of the foundational legal works of late medieval Ashkenazic Judaism.
Israel Isserlein dies in Wiener Neustadt after becoming one of the principal halakhic authorities of Ashkenazic Jewry.

Isaac Abravanel.event: Isaac Abravanel is born in Lisbon into a prominent Sephardic Jewish family connected to royal and financial circles.
Isaac Abravanel rises to prominence as a financier and advisor in the Portuguese royal court.
Isaac Abravanel flees Portugal after political accusations and settles in Castile in Christian Spain.
Isaac Abravanel unsuccessfully attempts to prevent the expulsion of Spanish Jewry and departs Spain following the Alhambra Decree.
Isaac Abravanel enters the service of the Kingdom of Naples while continuing his biblical and philosophical writings.
Isaac Abravanel settles in Venice after the political collapse of Naples and continues writing major biblical commentaries.
Isaac Abravanel dies in Venice after becoming one of the foremost Sephardic intellectuals and statesmen of the late medieval Jewish world.

Abarbanel.event: Born in Lisbon, Portugal, into a wealthy and influential Jewish family.
Fled to Toledo, Spain, after being accused of treason in Portugal. Became financial advisor to King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella.
Expelled with Spanish Jewry during the Alhambra Decree. Tried unsuccessfully to prevent the expulsion by offering the crown a ransom.
Settled in Naples, Italy, where he began writing his major biblical commentaries.
Moved to Venice, where he advised the Venetian Republic and continued writing.
Died in Venice. Buried in Padua. His commentaries and messianic writings influenced generations.

יעקב פולאק (Rabbi Jacob Pollak).event: Born in Poland (possibly Prague or Kraków). Little is known of his early years.
Settled in Kraków; founded a yeshivah that attracted many students.
Served as chief rabbi of Kraków; pioneered the method of pilpul in Talmud study.
Expelled from Kraków; moved to Vienna and served as rabbi there.
Taught in Vienna; influenced a generation of students including Shalom Shachna of Lublin.
Died in Vienna; remembered as a founder of the Polish–Lithuanian rabbinic tradition.

Jacob Berab.event: Jacob Berab is born in Castile in Christian Spain during the final generation before the expulsion of Spanish Jewry.
Jacob Berab flees Spain following the Alhambra Decree and relocates to North Africa with other Sephardic exiles.
Jacob Berab studies and teaches in Egypt, gaining recognition as a leading Talmudic scholar.
Jacob Berab settles in Safed, which had emerged as a major center of Jewish scholarship under Ottoman rule.
Jacob Berab initiates an attempt to restore classical rabbinic semikhah in Safed, provoking significant halakhic controversy.
Jacob Berab becomes embroiled in disputes with the rabbinic leadership of Jerusalem over the legitimacy of renewed semikhah.
Jacob Berab dies in Safed after shaping the intellectual and halakhic life of early Ottoman Sephardic Jewry.

ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו.event: ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו is born at Cesena around the middle of the 1470s to Jacob di Rubino, in a Jewish banking family of Catalan origin with strong connections to Bologna. The exact year is unknown; circa 1475 is the conventional map date. See the archival Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

By 1498, ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו is living in Rome and pursuing medicine, philosophy, mathematics and philology. From 1498 to 1500 he gives Johannes Reuchlin private instruction in Hebrew and probably Maimonidean philosophy, a relationship remembered in Reuchlin's De rudimentis Hebraicis. See Treccani's archival biography and the Treccani Reuchlin entry.

ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו.place: Ferrara, Duchy of Ferrara; now Italy
ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו.event: In 1501 ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו is documented at Ferrara, where he receives his medical degree. He is already married to Allegra, from the prominent Norsa banking family. This was a documented study and qualification visit, not his permanent settlement. See the source-based account in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani.

After his medical qualification, ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו returns to Rome and remains closely connected with the city until 1527. He practises medicine, participates in banking interests and becomes a communal notable with relationships reaching papal court circles. The chronicle of דוד הראובני records him among leading Roman Jews during the latter's 1524 visit. See Treccani and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Following the Sack of Rome in 1527, ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו relocates to Bologna. There he practises medicine, shares in the credit enterprise of his brother ר׳ חננאל ספורנו, serves as a rabbi in the court of Avraham HaKohen and teaches a select circle. See the documented chronology in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani.

ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו publishes his philosophical אור עמים in Bologna in 1537 through the Hebrew press of the Associates of the Silk Art, whose revival he probably helped lead. His commentary on Pirkei Avot follows in a Bologna machzor in 1540, and the revised Latin Lumen gentium in 1548. See Treccani and the autograph manuscript record at the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו dies in Bologna in 1550, after making surviving wills in 1547 and 1549. Notarial records confirm the year. His brother ר׳ חננאל ספורנו later edits the Torah commentary for its first printing in Venice in 1567. Bologna's later expulsions and destruction of its Jewish cemetery mean that his burial place is no longer identifiable. See the archival Italian biography and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra.event: David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra is born in Spain shortly before the expulsion of Spanish Jewry.
David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra relocates with his family to North Africa following the expulsion of the Jews from Spain.
David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra settles in Cairo and rises to prominence as a leading halakhic authority in Egypt.
The Radbaz serves as chief rabbi of Cairo and head of a major yeshiva, issuing responsa consulted throughout the Jewish world.
The Radbaz relocates to Safed in Ottoman Palestine and joins the renowned circle of rabbinic scholars and mystics there.
David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra dies in Safed after becoming one of the most influential Sephardic halakhic authorities of the sixteenth century.

דוד בן שלמה אבן זמרא (Radvaz).event: Born in Spain, possibly Seville, shortly before the expulsion of 1492.
Expelled from Spain; family settled in North Africa, likely in Algiers.
Appointed Chief Rabbi of Egypt (Cairo). Served for nearly 40 years, leading Egyptian Jewry.
Migrated to Safed in the Land of Israel. Joined the circle of great sages including Rabbi Yosef Karo, the Ari, and Rabbi Moshe Cordovero.
Died in Safed; buried there. His thousands of responsa continue to influence halakhic rulings.

מאיר קצנלנבוגן.event: Born in Katzenelnbogen, Germany, into a distinguished rabbinic family connected to the Luria lineage.
Studied in Prague under Rabbi Jacob Pollak, one of the founders of the pilpul method of Talmudic learning.
Moved to Padua, Italy, and entered the yeshiva of Rabbi Judah Minz.
Succeeded Rabbi Abraham Minz as Chief Rabbi of Padua and became one of the foremost halachic authorities in Italy.
Became involved in the Bragadin-Giustiniani Hebrew printing dispute in Venice concerning publication rights to the Mishneh Torah.
Witnessed the aftermath of the burning of the Talmud in Italy under Pope Julius III following tensions surrounding Hebrew printing.
Passed away in Padua after decades of leadership, leaving behind influential responsa and a major rabbinic legacy.

יוסף קארו (Rabbi Yosef Karo).event: Born in Spain or Portugal, shortly before the expulsion of Jews from Iberia.
Exiled with his family following the expulsion of Jews from Spain and Portugal. Settled in the Ottoman Empire.
Lived in Nikopol (in present-day Bulgaria, then Ottoman Empire), where he began writing his commentary on the Tur, Beit Yosef.
Settled in Safed, Galilee. Became head of the rabbinic court, working alongside Rabbi Moshe of Trani and later Rabbi Moshe Cordovero and the Ari (Rabbi Isaac Luria).
Published the Shulchan Aruch in Venice, which together with Rabbi Moshe Isserles' glosses became the standard halakhic code.
Died in Safed, where he is buried. Revered as one of the greatest codifiers in Jewish history.

שלמה הלוי אלקבץ (Shlomo HaLevi Alkabetz).event: Born in Salonica (Thessaloniki), Ottoman Greece, into a family of Spanish exiles after the 1492 Expulsion.
Began studies in Talmud and Kabbalah; already recognized as a promising poet and mystic.
Traveled to Jerusalem, where he joined the mystical circles studying Zohar. Influenced by encounters with leading scholars.
Settled in Safed, becoming a leading figure in the emerging school of Kabbalah. Taught Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (the Ramak).
Composed Lecha Dodi, a hymn welcoming the Sabbath Bride, which became part of the universal Jewish liturgy.
Died in Safed, where he was buried alongside other kabbalists. Remembered as a central poet and mystic of the Golden Age of Safed.

שלמה לוריא (Maharshal).event: Born in Brisk (Brest-Litovsk), in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Studied in Poland, possibly Warsaw and nearby communities.
Appointed Rosh Yeshivah in Lublin; became renowned for his rigorous Talmudic method.
Led one of the largest yeshivot in Poland; trained students who became leaders across Europe.
Died in Lublin; buried in the Old Jewish Cemetery of Lublin, near the Maharam of Lublin.

שלום שכנא מלובלין (Rabbi Shalom Shachna.event: Born in Kraków, Poland, into a distinguished rabbinic family.
Studied under Rabbi Jacob Pollak in Kraków; absorbed the pilpul method.
Founded a yeshivah in Lublin, which became the most prominent center of Jewish learning in Poland.
Served as rabbi of Lublin and head of its yeshivah; attracted hundreds of students.
Taught Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema), who later became his son-in-law.
Died in Lublin; buried there. Left a lasting legacy through his yeshivah and disciples.

יהודה ליווא בן בצלאל (Maharal of Prague).event: Born in Poznań (or possibly Worms); later associated with Moravia and Prague.
Served as rabbi of Moravia, residing in various towns.
Appointed chief rabbi of Moravia, centered in Mikulov.
Became rabbi of Prague; established yeshivah and exerted strong communal leadership.
Led Prague community; legendary association with the creation of the Golem.
Visited Emperor Rudolf II in Prague; noted for philosophical and mystical discussions.
Returned to Prague rabbinate after disputes; continued teaching and writing.
Died in Prague; buried in the Old Jewish Cemetery, where his grave remains a pilgrimage site.

בצלאל אשכנזי (Shita Mekubetzet).event: Born in Cairo, Egypt, to a family of Ashkenazi origin that had settled in the Ottoman Empire.
Studied under Rabbi David ibn Abi Zimra (Radbaz) in Egypt, acquiring mastery in halakha and Talmud.
Moved to Safed, where he became part of the flourishing circle of Kabbalists and scholars. Counted among his students were the Arizal and Rabbi Chaim Vital.
Compiled the Shita Mekubetzet, collecting and preserving fragments of Rishonim's commentaries on the Talmud that might otherwise have been lost.
Died in Safed. His Shita Mekubetzet remains an indispensable tool for Talmudic study.

משה קורדובירו (Ramak).event: Born in Safed, Ottoman Galilee, a city that became a flourishing center of Jewish learning and Kabbalah.
Studied under his brother-in-law Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz (author of Lecha Dodi) and mastered halakhah and Kabbalah.
Became a disciple of Rabbi Yosef Caro, author of the Shulchan Aruch, while also delving deeply into Kabbalistic texts.
Established himself as the leading Kabbalist of Safed, attracting students from across the Jewish world.
Completed his magnum opus Pardes Rimonim, a systematic exposition of Kabbalah synthesizing earlier traditions.
Died in Safed. At his funeral, the young Arizal declared that a pillar of fire accompanied his bier, symbolizing his saintly stature.

הרב מרדכי יפה.event: Born in Prague or possibly Grodno (sources differ), into a learned Ashkenazi family.
Studied under leading rabbis of his time, including the Rema (Rabbi Moshe Isserles) and the Maharshal (Rabbi Shlomo Luria).
Around this time, after his marriage, the Levush returned to Prague and established a Yeshivah there.
The Levush was expelled from Bohemia with the rest of the Jews. The Levush goes to Venice to study Astronomy.
The Levush becomes Rav in Hrodna.
The Levush becomes Rav in Lublin ,where he served as one of the leaders of the Va'ad Arba Arzot.
The Levush becomes Rav in Kremenetz.
Served as rabbi and dayan in Prague; began work on his monumental Levushim.
Completed and began publishing the Levushim, a ten-volume halakhic code harmonizing the Shulchan Aruch with Ashkenazic custom.
Died in Prague, leaving behind his influential halakhic code, which was widely studied in Europe.

משה איסרליש (Rema).event: Born in Kraków, Poland, into a prominent rabbinic family.
Established a famous yeshiva in Kraków, attracting students from across Poland and beyond.
Wrote major halakhic works including responsa, Torat HaChatat, and glosses to Shulchan Aruch (HaMapah).
Died in Kraków. Buried in the Rema Cemetery near his synagogue, which still bears his name.

Arizal.event: Rabbi Yitzchak Luria Ashkenazi is born in Jerusalem to Rabbi Shlomo Luria Ashkenazi and a Sephardic mother.
After the death of his father, Rabbi Yitzchak Luria Ashkenazi moves with his mother to Cairo, Egypt, where he is raised in the home of his wealthy uncle Mordechai Francis.
Rabbi Yitzchak Luria Ashkenazi marries his cousin, the daughter of Mordechai Frances.
The Arizal begins years of intense mystical isolation on an island in the Nile, devoting himself to meditation, asceticism, and the study of the Zohar.
Rabbi Yitzchak Luria Ashkenazi moves to Safed in the Galilee, then the major center of Jewish mysticism in the Ottoman Empire.
The Arizal gathers a circle of disciples in Safed, including Rabbi Chaim Vital, and begins teaching the system later known as Lurianic Kabbalah.
Teachings concerning Tzimtzum, Shevirat HaKelim, Tikkun, gilgulim, and mystical kavvanot spread rapidly among the תלמידי המקובלים of Safed.
Rabbi Yitzchak Luria Ashkenazi dies in Safed during a plague epidemic at the age of 38, leaving behind a revolutionary spiritual legacy preserved primarily by Rabbi Chaim Vital.

ר׳ חיים ויטאל.event: ר׳ חיים ויטאל is born in Safed around 1 Cheshvan 5303 (1542; some older references print 1543) to Joseph Vital Calabrese, a scribe whose family came from Calabria in southern Italy. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica-derived biography and המכלול.

As a youth, ר׳ חיים ויטאל studies halakhah and Talmud in the academy of ר׳ משה אלשיך. He later enters the kabbalistic world associated with ר׳ משה קורדובירו and briefly pursues alchemy and other esoteric disciplines, which he subsequently regrets. See החכם היומי and the scholarly encyclopedia account.

When ר׳ יצחק לוריא settles in Safed, ר׳ חיים ויטאל becomes his principal disciple. For nearly two years he listens to, questions and records the האר״י's teachings on creation, divine emanation, exile, prayer, souls and reincarnation. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica account and Chabad's biography of the האר״י.

After the death of ר׳ יצחק לוריא in 1572, ר׳ חיים ויטאל organizes a circle that receives the master's teachings through him and begins the long work of arranging his notes. Other disciples, including ר׳ יוסף אבן טבול and ר׳ ישראל סרוג, do not accept his exclusive authority, producing competing channels of transmission. See המכלול and the scholarly biography.

ר׳ חיים ויטאל.place: Egypt and Ein al-Zeitun, Ottoman Empire
ר׳ חיים ויטאל.event: After a period in Egypt, ר׳ חיים ויטאל returns to Ottoman Palestine in 1577, visiting Ein al-Zeitun north of Safed before continuing to Jerusalem. The evidence supports travel through these places but not a long Egyptian rabbinate. See the referenced multilingual chronology and החכם היומי.

ר׳ חיים ויטאל establishes himself in Jerusalem, where he teaches and leads a yeshivah for roughly eight years while continuing to organize the Lurianic corpus. Later stories connect his departure with pressure from the Ottoman governor over a legendary opening of the Gihon; that supernatural framing is tradition rather than independently verifiable political documentation. See החכם היומי and the German biographical chronology.

Around 1585, ר׳ חיים ויטאל leaves Jerusalem for Damascus amid conflict with local Ottoman authority. This first Damascene stay is brief, because he returns to Safed the following year. See החכם היומי and המכלול.

ר׳ חיים ויטאל returns to Safed in 1586. During this later Safed period he receives rabbinic ordination from his former teacher ר׳ משה אלשיך and suffers a prolonged illness; copies of portions of his guarded manuscripts circulate without his full control. Sources differ on whether the ordination occurred immediately or closer to 1590–1594. See המכלול and the Encyclopedia of Religion account.

Around 1594, ר׳ חיים ויטאל settles permanently in Damascus. He teaches Kabbalah, gathers a restricted circle of students and is associated with the Sicilian Jewish congregation, while continuing to revise his writings and dream diary. See the history of Damascus Jewry and the referenced biography.

ר׳ חיים ויטאל dies in Damascus in 1620, traditionally on 30 Nisan 5380, while reportedly preparing to return to Safed. He is traditionally buried in Damascus's old Jewish cemetery. A later claim that his remains were secretly transferred to Israel has not been demonstrated, so the map retains Damascus as the historical burial place. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the burial-tradition assessment.

ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ.event: ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ is born around 1550 in Łęczyca, the Polish town from which the name Luntschitz derives. The National Library authority record identifies him as ר׳ שלמה אפרים בן ר׳ אהרן לונטשיץ. See the National Library of Israel, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the modern biographical synthesis in Shlomo Ephraim Luntschitz.

As a young scholar, ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ studies in Lublin under ר׳ שלמה לוריא (מהרש״ל), whose disciplined Talmudic and textual approach forms an important part of his intellectual background. The displayed year is approximate because the sources preserve the relationship but not an enrollment date. See the biographical summary and the scholarly study cited there, Leonard Levin’s Seeing with Both Eyes.

By this period, ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ is established as a preacher and scholar and serves as rosh yeshiva in Lviv. His first major work, עיר גיבורים, is printed at Basel in 1580; the printing location is not treated as proof that he personally resided in Basel. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the modern biographical summary.

ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ publishes עוללות אפרים, four parts of biblical and Talmudic ethical sermons, at Lublin in 1590. אורח לחיים follows there in 1595, confirming his growing reputation as a moralist and public preacher. See the detailed bibliography in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

During a life-threatening illness, the name שלמה is added to אפרים. In his introduction to כלי יקר, ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ relates this naming episode. The year follows the traditional chronology and is retained as approximate. See the Hebrew biographical account and the modern summary.

ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ publishes כלי יקר on the Pentateuch at Lublin. Its fusion of textual exegesis, midrash, ethical teaching and critique of communal failings makes it his defining work and a lasting component of מקראות גדולות. See the digitized bibliographical record at the National Library of Israel and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ is appointed rabbi and leading preacher in Prague after having served as rosh yeshiva in Lviv. He remains a central rabbinic figure there for the rest of his life, in the intellectual world shaped by ר׳ יהודה ליווא בן בצלאל (מהר״ל). See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the modern biographical synthesis.

In Prague, ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ publishes שפתי דעת, extending the homiletical project of כלי יקר. The following year he composes penitential liturgical poems commemorating the community’s deliverance after hostile forces entered Prague on 2 Adar 1611. See the bibliography and historical note in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ publishes עמודי שש, a collection of sermons that includes forceful criticism of sterile pilpul and educational priorities detached from ethical transformation. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the work summary.

ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ dies in Prague on Thursday, 7 Adar 5379 and is buried in the Old Jewish Cemetery. The gravestone date corresponds to 21 February 1619 Gregorian; the Jewish Encyclopedia’s 3 March reflects the contemporary calendar difference. See the gravestone-based date discussion, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the National Library authority record.

שמואל אליעזר איידלס (Maharsha).event: Born in Kraków, Poland, into a rabbinic family.
Served as rabbi and opened a yeshivah in Lwów (Lviv).
Became rabbi and rosh yeshivah in Lublin; gained fame as a leading Talmudist.
Appointed rabbi in Tykocin and later Ostroh; continued leading large yeshivot.
Served as rabbi in Kiev, contributing to Jewish scholarship in Eastern Europe.
Became rabbi of Ostroh; wrote and refined his Talmudic commentaries.
Died in Ostroh. Buried there; remembered as one of the greatest Talmudic commentators.

ר' אברהם די בוטון (Abraham de Boton, Lec.event: Born in Salonika, an important center of Sephardic Jewry in the Ottoman Empire.
Became a leading figure in the Salonika rabbinate; began writing Lechem Mishneh.
Moved to Adrianople (Edirne), where he established and led a major yeshiva.
Passed away in Adrianople; his Lechem Mishneh soon became a standard commentary on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah.

יואל סירקיש (Bach).event: Born in Kraków, Poland, into a scholarly rabbinic family.
Served as rabbi of Belz, where he established his reputation as a leading halakhist.
Appointed rabbi of Brest-Litovsk (Brisk), a major Jewish center in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Became rabbi of Kraków, one of the most prestigious posts in Poland.
Died in Kraków. Buried in the Old Jewish Cemetery. His Bayit Chadash became a cornerstone of halakhic study.

R' Yoshiyahu Pinto.event: R' Yoshiyahu Pinto is born in Damascus, Syria.
R' Yoshiyahu Pinto moves to Safed intending to settle, but soon suffers the death of his young son Joseph.
R' Yoshiyahu Pinto returns to Damascus after the loss of his son Joseph.
R' Yoshiyahu Pinto passes away in Damascus in February–March 1648 while serving as rabbi of the city.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: Born into a rabbinic family in Kraków during the height of Polish Jewish scholarship.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: Kraków in the late sixteenth century was one of the major centers of Jewish learning in Europe. The young David HaLevi Segal grew up in an environment deeply shaped by Talmudic scholarship and communal leadership.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).event: Studied under Rabbi Shlomo Ephraim of Luntschitz (the Keli Yakar) and became son-in-law of Rabbi Joel Sirkis (the Bach).
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: The Taz emerged from one of the greatest rabbinic networks of early modern Poland.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: His connection to both the Keli Yakar and the Bach placed him within the elite rabbinic circles of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. These relationships profoundly influenced his halakhic methodology and authority.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).event: Served as rabbi in various communities in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and began writing halakhic responsa.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: His reputation spread through responsa and rabbinic leadership across Eastern Europe.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: During these years, Rabbi David Segal developed the sharp analytical style that would later define the Turei Zahav. Communities increasingly turned to him for legal rulings and guidance.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).event: Appointed rabbi of Lwów (Lviv). Completed much of his Turei Zahav commentary.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: Lwów became the center of the Taz’s literary and rabbinic legacy.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: His commentary on the Shulchan Aruch, the Turei Zahav ('Rows of Gold'), became one of the foundational commentaries studied by generations of rabbinic scholars and yeshivot.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).event: Fled during the Khmelnytsky massacres; lost many family members and disciples.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: The Khmelnytsky uprising devastated Jewish communities across Eastern Europe.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: The massacres of 1648–1649 were among the greatest catastrophes in pre-modern Jewish history. The Taz personally suffered enormous tragedy, including the loss of family and students.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).event: Settled in Lublin for several years; continued rabbinic leadership and writing.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: Even after catastrophe, the Taz continued teaching and writing.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: Lublin was one of the great Jewish cities of Poland and became a refuge where Rabbi David Segal rebuilt his scholarly activity and communal influence.

דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).event: Died in Lwów. Buried there; remembered as one of the greatest halakhic authorities of his era.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).extract: The Taz’s rulings became permanently embedded in Jewish legal tradition.
דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav).read_more: Today, the Turei Zahav is printed in nearly every standard edition of the Shulchan Aruch. His influence continues across Orthodox Jewish learning and halakhic practice worldwide.

שבתי בן מאיר הכהן (Shabbatai ben Meir Ha.event: Born either in Amstibovo or Wilno (Vilnius), Lithuania.
Entered the yeshivah of Rabbi Joshua Höschel ben Joseph in Tykotzin.
Studied in Kraków under Naphtali Cohen.
Studied in Lublin under Rabbi Ya'acov ben Ephraim Hersch.
Published his magnum opus Siftei Kohen (Shakh) in Kraków.
Returned to Wilno (Vilnius), joined Beit Din under Rabbi Moses Lima.
Fled Wilno during the Northern War; stayed briefly in Lublin.
Resided in Prague after fleeing the war.
Died in Holešov, where his grave is still a pilgrimage site.

ר׳ שבתי משורר בס.event: ר׳ שבתי משורר בס is born in Kalisz in 1641 to ר׳ יוסף. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, the Posen Library and the POLIN Virtual Shtetl.

After his parents are killed in the 1655 persecutions at Kalisz, the fourteen-year-old ר׳ שבתי משורר בס takes refuge in Prague. He studies Talmud under ר׳ מאיר וֶרטֶרס, learns singing from ר׳ לייב שיר השירים and becomes a bass singer in the Altneuschul, the origin of the surnames Bass, Bassista and משורר. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Posen Library.

Between 1674 and 1679, ר׳ שבתי משורר בס undertakes a sustained research journey through Jewish centres and libraries in Poland, Germany and Holland. Recorded stops include Glogau, Kalisz, Krotoszyn, Leszno, Poznań, Worms and Amsterdam. This regional marker represents an itinerary, not a permanent residence. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Posen Library.

In Amsterdam, ר׳ שבתי משורר בס studies the crafts of Hebrew printing and proofreading. In 1680 he publishes שפתי חכמים, his explanation of רש״י on the Torah, and שפתי ישנים, the pioneering bibliography that catalogues more than two thousand Hebrew books. See YIVO Encyclopedia, Posen Library and the National Library of Israel.

After obtaining official permission, ר׳ שבתי משורר בס establishes his Hebrew press at Dyhernfurth. Its first known book appears in August 1689. The enterprise attracts Jewish compositors, correctors and craftsmen and contributes to the formation of a permanent Jewish community. See YIVO Encyclopedia, the POLIN Virtual Shtetl and the Jewish Encyclopedia.
A fire partly destroys the Dyhernfurth press, but ר׳ שבתי משורר בס and his family rebuild the printing enterprise. See the YIVO Encyclopedia.

Jesuit accusations that his publications contain anti-Christian passages lead to the arrest of ר׳ שבתי משורר בס and the confiscation of books from his press. He is ultimately acquitted, but the proceedings seriously disrupt the business. See YIVO Encyclopedia, Posen Library and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

Having returned to Poland, ר׳ שבתי משורר בס dies at Krotoszyn on 21 July 1718, corresponding to 22 Tammuz 5478. His descendants continue the Dyhernfurth printing house, while שפתי חכמים becomes a standard companion to רש״י. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, the Hebrew biographical entry and the POLIN Virtual Shtetl.

Chacham Tzvi (Rabbi Zvi Ashkenazi).event: Born in Moravia (probably Vienna or nearby)
Served as Chief Rabbi of Amsterdam

Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart.event: Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart is born in Breslau, Silesia (modern-day Wrocław, Poland).
Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart is appointed rabbi of the first Ashkenazic synagogue in London, the Great Synagogue at Duke’s Place.
Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart publishes Urim ve-Tummim, the first book printed entirely in Hebrew in London.
Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart passes away in London after serving as chief rabbi of the Ashkenazi community for over 50 years.

Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka.event: Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka is born in Zolkova, Galicia (modern-day Zhovkva, Ukraine).
Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka makes his first aliyah to the Land of Israel with his son Shimshon Chaim, but returns after a short period.
Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka leads the first organized group of Baal Shem Tov’s disciples on a second aliyah to the Land of Israel, eventually settling in Tiberias.
Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka passes away in Tiberias on 2 Tammuz 5525 and is buried in the Baal Shem Tov Students' Plot in the ancient cemetery.

Rabbi Joseph ben Emanuel Ergas.event: Rabbi Joseph ben Emanuel Ergas is born in Livorno, Italy, into a rabbinic family with connections to kabbalists and followers of Shabbatai Zevi.
Rabbi Joseph Ergas marries Sarah, who would bear him six children.
