Rabbi Joseph Ergas settles in Pisa, where he establishes the 'Noah Shalom' yeshiva and charitable institutions.
The Sabbatean Neḥemiah Ḥayyun arrives in Livorno; Rabbi Ergas refuses to endorse him and expels him from the city, marking him as a staunch opponent of Sabbateanism.
Rabbi Joseph Ergas publishes his polemical works Tokhaḥat Meguleh and Ha-Tzad Naḥash in London, responding to Sabbatean attacks.
Rabbi Joseph ben Emanuel Ergas passes away in Livorno on 3 Sivan 5490, leaving a legacy as a kabbalist and defender of rabbinic tradition.

ר׳ נתנאל וייל.event: ר׳ נתנאל וייל is born at Stühlingen in 1687 to ר׳ נפתלי צבי הירש וייל, in a family tracing its rabbinic lineage to ר׳ יעקב וייל (מהרי״ו). His father and a brother are murdered in 1692. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, LEO-BW and the Hebrew biographical account.

At ten, the orphaned ר׳ נתנאל וייל is brought by his mother to Fürth, then a major centre of Jewish learning. He is soon sent onward to Prague to live with his paternal uncle. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Hebrew biographical account.

In Prague, ר׳ ליפמן וייל raises his nephew ר׳ נתנאל וייל. The gifted youth is admitted to the yeshiva of ר׳ אברהם ברודא, becomes his outstanding disciple, and in 1708 marries the teacher’s niece פייגלא. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica via Jewish Virtual Library.

ר׳ נתנאל וייל.place: Metz and the western German yeshiva circuit
ר׳ נתנאל וייל.event: After his marriage, ר׳ נתנאל וייל accompanies his teacher ר׳ אברהם ברודא westward and continues studying in his yeshiva. Modern accounts associate this phase with Metz and Frankfurt, while the older Jewish Encyclopedia names Mayence; the marker is therefore deliberately regional and the date approximate. Compare the Encyclopaedia Judaica summary, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Hebrew biographical account.

Following the death of ר׳ אברהם ברודא, ר׳ נתנאל וייל returns to Prague. He serves as an assistant rabbi, leads advanced Talmud study and teaches a large body of pupils while living on a modest salary. He begins the scholarship that will become קרבן נתנאל. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, LEO-BW and the Hebrew biographical account.

Maria Theresa’s decree expelling the Jews of Prague and Bohemia uproots ר׳ נתנאל וייל. In 1745 he accepts the regional rabbinate of the Black Forest communities, headquartered at Mühringen, and writes much of his commentary on the רא״ש there. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, Encyclopaedia Judaica and Karlsruhe Stadtwiki.

ר׳ נתנאל וייל is appointed chief regional rabbi for the margraviates of Baden-Baden and Baden-Durlach, with his seat in Karlsruhe. He completes קרבן נתנאל and becomes one of the city’s most significant Jewish scholars. See the City of Karlsruhe, LEO-BW and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ נתנאל וייל publishes קרבן נתנאל, his commentary on the rulings of ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל for orders מועד and נשים. It is the first Hebrew book printed in Karlsruhe and later enters standard Talmud editions alongside the רא״ש. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the history of Karlsruhe’s Jewish community.

ר׳ נתנאל וייל dies at Rastatt on 7 May 1769 (traditionally 30 Nisan 5529) while still serving as Baden’s chief regional rabbi. He is buried in Karlsruhe, where his grave survives, and his son ר׳ ידידיה טיאה וייל continues his rabbinic legacy. See the City of Karlsruhe, Jewish Community of Karlsruhe and Wikimedia Commons documentation of his grave.

Rabbi Jonathan Eybeschutz.event: Born in Cracow (disputed, some say Prague)
Became Chief Rabbi of Altona, Hamburg, and Wandsbek

ר׳ חיים בן עטר (אור החיים הקדוש).event: ר׳ חיים בן עטר is born in Salé to ר׳ משה בן עטר and receives his earliest Torah education from his grandfather, ר׳ חיים בן עטר הזקן. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and Posen Library.

Political persecution forces the family from Salé to Meknes. The young ר׳ חיים בן עטר continues his education and learns the jewelry trade while the household stays with ר׳ משה די אבילה. See the Daily Sage archive.
After roughly three years in Meknes, the family returns to Salé, where ר׳ חיים בן עטר develops as a teacher in the Ben Attar study-house tradition. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Daily Sage.

Following his father-in-law's death, ר׳ חיים בן עטר faces worsening financial and legal pressures while continuing to teach. Sources vary on family details and exact timing; see Posen Library and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

While based in Morocco, ר׳ חיים בן עטר brings his Talmudic novellae חפץ ה׳ to print in Amsterdam. The publication is recorded by the Jewish Encyclopedia; the marker does not imply a documented Amsterdam visit.

Amid famine and instability, ר׳ חיים בן עטר teaches in Fez and is associated with the academy of ר׳ שמואל אלבז while preparing to leave Morocco. See the Daily Sage and Institute for Jewish Ideas and Ideals.
ר׳ חיים בן עטר passes through Algiers after leaving Morocco, an intermediate stage toward Italy and the Land of Israel. See the Daily Sage biography and scholarly overview.
ר׳ חיים בן עטר reaches Livorno, where patrons support his academy, publications and planned aliyah; he gathers the fellowship that will accompany him. See Posen Library and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

The commentary אור החיים is prepared for its Venice printing as ר׳ חיים בן עטר organizes departure from Italy. The 1742 edition is documented by the Jewish Encyclopedia. His precise physical stay in Venice is not securely dated.

ר׳ חיים בן עטר, his wives and approximately thirty disciples arrive by sea at Acre. Epidemics affecting Jaffa and Jerusalem lead the group to remain in the north. See Posen Library and the Institute for Jewish Ideas and Ideals.

During the delay in northern Palestine, ר׳ חיים בן עטר and his fellowship study among Galilean Jewish communities before moving to Jerusalem. Sources agree on an approximately year-long northern sojourn but vary over individual stops, so this marker is regional. See Posen Library.

ר׳ חיים בן עטר settles in Jerusalem and establishes מדרש כנסת ישראל for advanced revealed Torah and kabbalistic study. ר׳ חיים יוסף דוד אזולאי is among the scholars associated with his academy. See Posen Library and the Daily Sage.
ר׳ חיים בן עטר dies on 15 Tammuz 5503 (7 July 1743), aged about forty-seven, and is buried on the Mount of Olives. See Posen Library and Da'at Encyclopedia.

ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב.place: Okopy, Podolia, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Okopy, Ukraine
ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב.event: According to Hasidic tradition, ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב is born on 18 Elul 5458 (1698) at Okopy, a small fortified settlement in Podolia. Modern scholarship accepts Okopy as the likely birthplace but dates the birth only to about 1700; the displayed year is traditional, not documentarily certain. See Moshe Rosman, YIVO Encyclopedia, the National Library of Israel and the traditional Da'at entry.

During his early adult years, ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב works in several Podolian communities, reportedly as an elementary teacher, ritual slaughterer and circumciser, while acquiring knowledge of rabbinic literature, Kabbalah and herbal remedies. The source does not provide a secure year-by-year itinerary, so 1720 is an approximate career marker rather than a claimed date of relocation. See YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב.place: Kuty and the southeastern Podolian–Carpathian region; date approximate
ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב.event: In the southeastern Podolian–Carpathian region, ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב associates with mystical and ascetic practitioners including ר׳ משה מקיטוב and learns practical as well as contemplative Kabbalah and medicinal remedies. His wife Chana is the sister of ר׳ אברהם גרשון מקיטוב. The date is approximate because the biographical source establishes the relationships but not an exact move. See YIVO Encyclopedia.

By the 1730s, while active in Podolian towns including Tłuste, ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב is using the title baal shem or baal shem tov and gaining a reputation as a healer and spiritual intermediary. Later tradition describes a public 'revelation' around this period, but the contemporary evidence supports a gradual emergence rather than one precisely documented ceremony. See Moshe Rosman, YIVO Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב.place: Medzhybizh, Podolia, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Ukraine
ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב.event: ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב settles in Medzhybizh after the Jewish communal leadership provides him a house free of rent and tax. Czartoryski estate documents identify the privileged resident as a kabbalist in 1740 and subsequently as a baal shem and 'baal shem doctor,' supplying rare contemporary evidence for his residence and communal function. See YIVO Encyclopedia biography and the YIVO Medzhybizh entry.

In the famous narrative later preserved as אגרת הקודש, ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב reports a Rosh Hashanah visionary ascent and a messianic answer linking redemption to the spread of his teachings. The text was transmitted and printed only after his death, so this event is presented as an influential attributed testimony rather than a fully secure autograph record. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel.

At Medzhybizh, ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב leads a learned mystical circle and attracts visiting disciples including ר׳ יעקב יוסף מפולנאה, ר׳ דב בער ממזריטש, ר׳ פנחס מקוריץ and ר׳ נחמן מהורודנקה. His teachings circulate orally through this network and later appear in students' books, especially תולדות יעקב יוסף. See YIVO Encyclopedia and the Hebrew Da'at study.

ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב dies in Medzhybizh in 1760 and is buried in its Jewish cemetery. Hasidic tradition places his death on Shavuot, usually 6 Sivan 5520; the securely documented point is the year and town. His disciples subsequently turn the Medzhybizh circle into the expanding Hasidic movement. See YIVO Encyclopedia, the National Library of Israel and the geolocated Wikimedia Commons cemetery record.

Haham Isaac Nieto.event: Isaac Nieto is born in London, the son of Rabbi David Nieto.
Isaac Nieto is appointed Haham of the Portuguese congregation Sha'are Hashamayim (Bevis Marks) in London.
Isaac Nieto resigns his post as Haham and leaves London for several years.
Isaac Nieto travels to Gibraltar and establishes the Shaar Hashamayim congregation, becoming Gibraltar's first rabbi.
Isaac Nieto returns to London and is appointed Av Bet Din, serving alongside Rabbis Isaac de Valle and Jacob Coronel.
Isaac Nieto resigns after disputes in the Bet Din and is barred from acting as assessor.

ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.place: Lokachi, Volhynian Voivodeship, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Ukraine
ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.event: ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש is born at Lokachi in Volhynia, probably around 1704, to ר׳ אברהם, a poor teacher. His birth year is not securely known: scholarly and Hasidic sources variously propose 1698, 1704 and about 1710. See the Encyclopedia of Religion and the uncertainty survey by Bar-Ilan University's Chair for Hasidism.

ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.place: Lwów, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Lviv, Ukraine
ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.event: According to established Hasidic biographical tradition, the gifted young ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש is sent to the Lwów yeshivah of ר׳ יעקב יהושע פאלק, author of פני יהושע. The approximate year is a map aid rather than a documented enrollment date. See the Hebrew biographical account maintained by Bar-Ilan University's Chair for Hasidism.

By early adulthood, ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש has married at Turchyn and works as a teacher in a nearby village before serving as the town's maggid. He deepens his study of Kabbalah and adopts the severe ascetic disciplines characteristic of his early religious life. The date is approximate because the surviving sources establish the sequence but not a precise year. See Bar-Ilan's Hebrew biography and the Encyclopedia of Religion.

ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.place: Korets and Rivne, Volhynia; now Ukraine
ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.event: During the period before his Hasidic leadership, ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש serves successively as a maggid in Korets and Rivne. His preaching ability and advanced Talmudic and kabbalistic learning become central to his public identity. The date is approximate and represents an attested career phase rather than a securely dated appointment. See Bar-Ilan University's Chair for Hasidism.

ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.place: Medzhybizh, Podolia, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Ukraine
ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.event: Around the middle of the eighteenth century, the physically frail and intensely ascetic ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש travels to Medzhybizh and becomes a disciple of ר׳ ישראל בעל שם טוב. The precise first-visit year is unknown. The encounter redirects his religious path toward divine immanence, joy, transformation of material life and devekut rather than bodily mortification. See the scholarly interpretation in the Encyclopedia of Religion and the Hebrew biography from Bar-Ilan University.

ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.place: Mezhirichi, Volhynia, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Velyki Mezhyrichi, Ukraine
ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.event: After the 1760 death of ר׳ ישראל בעל שם טוב and a period of unsettled succession, ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש becomes the central leader of most of the emerging Hasidic movement at Mezhirichi. His court trains an elite fellowship and sends disciples into Volhynia, Podolia, Poland, Galicia, Lithuania and White Russia, transforming a regional revival into a networked movement. See the Encyclopedia of Religion and YIVO's history of Mezhyrichi.

ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.place: Hannopil, Volhynia, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Ukraine
ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש.event: During the 1772 epidemic at Mezhirichi, ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש relocates with his household to Hannopil with assistance from his disciple ר׳ משולם זושא מאניפולי. He dies there on 19 Kislev 5533—4 December Old Style / 15 December 1772 New Style—and is buried in the Hannopil Jewish cemetery. His death coincides with the first major communal bans against Hasidism. See the death chronology in the Encyclopedia of Religion, the epidemic tradition summarized in French Wikipedia, and the verified Wikimedia tomb record.

Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto (Ramchal).event: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto is born in Padua, Republic of Venice.
Moshe Chaim Luzzatto publishes his first major literary work, Leshon Limmudim, a treatise on Hebrew style and poetry.
Moshe Chaim Luzzatto leaves Italy under rabbinic pressure and settles in Amsterdam, where he writes his greatest works including Mesillat Yesharim and Derech Hashem.
Moshe Chaim Luzzatto immigrates to the Land of Israel and settles in Acre.
Moshe Chaim Luzzatto and his family die in a plague in Acre on 26 Iyar (16 May 1746).

Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk (Baal She.event: Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk is born, possibly in Fürth, Bavaria (alternative tradition: Pidhaytsi, Podolia).
Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk demonstrates kabbalistic powers at the castle of Count von Rantzau in Holzminden after narrowly escaping execution in Westphalia.
Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk settles in London, residing at Prescott Street and later Wellclose Square, becoming known as the Baal Shem of London.
Folklore recounts that Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk saved the Great Synagogue of London from fire by inscribing Hebrew words on its pillars.
Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk dies in London on 17 April 1782 and is buried in Alderney Road Cemetery, Mile End.

שמואל מרגליות (Shmuel Margolies).event: Born in Galicia (then part of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth).
Immigrated to New York; became rabbi of Congregation Shearith Israel, the first synagogue in America.
Became recognized as the leading halachic authority in the American colonies.
Died in New York; left a legacy as one of the earliest rabbinic figures in American Jewish history.

ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא.event: ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא is born at Opatów on 18 Heshvan 5474 (7 November 1713) to ר׳ יהודה הלוי לנדא and חיה. He studies first with his father and local teachers. See the Jewish Museum in Prague and Daʿat.

Shortly after marrying at about eighteen, ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא enters the elite kloyz at Brody, an important center of Talmudic and kabbalistic scholarship. In 1733 he becomes head judge of one of Brody's four Jewish courts and remains in its learned circle for about thirteen years. See the YIVO Encyclopedia and Daʿat.

ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא becomes chief rabbi and head of the Talmudic academy at Yampol in Volhynia. His sermons, responsa and communal judgments establish his wider reputation. This is Yampil in present-day Khmelnytskyi Oblast, correcting the former coordinate near Lviv. See YIVO and the Jewish Museum in Prague.

From Yampol, ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא writes אגרת השלום, proposing a settlement of the divisive amulet controversy between ר׳ יעקב עמדין and ר׳ יהונתן אייבשיץ while challenging procedural defects in the testimony. See YIVO Encyclopedia and Daʿat.

Following his election in late 1754, ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא assumes office as chief rabbi of Prague in 1755 and heads its prominent yeshivah. He guides the community through the Seven Years' War, Habsburg centralization and religious controversy. See the Jewish Museum in Prague and Oxford Academic.

At Prague, ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא publishes the first edition of נודע ביהודה, named in memory of his father ר׳ יהודה. It organizes decisions from his Brody, Yampol and Prague periods. See the Jewish Museum in Prague and the original title information at Wikisource.

ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא dies in Prague on 17 Iyar 5553 (29 April 1793). In accordance with his written wishes, his grave bears a restrained stone rather than an elaborate ohel; he is buried in the Jewish cemetery on Fibichova Street in Žižkov. See Daʿat, the Jewish Museum, and the Prague cemetery guide.

ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק.event: ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק is born in 1717 at Łopuchowo, a small village near Tykocin in Podlasie, to ר׳ אליעזר ליפמן and his wife. Some modern summaries give Tykocin itself; the village-level identification is preserved here while acknowledging that the surviving biography is largely based on later Hasidic sources. See the Hebrew biographical study at Daʿat, the regional summary from the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage in Poland, and the Łopuchowo geographic record.

By the mid-eighteenth century, ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק and his brother ר׳ משולם זושא מאניפולי undertake a voluntary wandering exile marked by poverty, ascetic disciplines and efforts to inspire repentance. The itinerary and dates are not securely documented, so this map point represents their home region rather than an invented route. The tradition and its evidentiary limits are discussed in the Hebrew scholarly account at Daʿat.

Around the 1760s, through the influence of his brother ר׳ משולם זושא מאניפולי, ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק joins the circle of ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש at Mezhirichi. He becomes one of the Maggid's important disciples and absorbs the teaching that would underlie his later model of Hasidic leadership. The year is approximate because the sources establish the relationship but not a precise arrival date. See YIVO Encyclopedia, the Polish Jewish Heritage route, and the Hebrew study at Daʿat.

After the death of ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש in 1772, ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק settles at Leżajsk in Galicia and emerges as the central organizer of early Hasidism in Poland and Galicia. His modest court attracts disciples whom he trains to lead communities across the region, while his teaching develops the tsaddik's responsibility for both the spiritual and material needs of followers. See the scholarly entry in the YIVO Encyclopedia and the Hebrew biography at Daʿat.

ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק dies at Leżajsk on 21 Adar 5547 (11 March 1787) and is buried in the town's Jewish cemetery. His son ר׳ אלעזר succeeds him locally and helps prepare his teachings for publication. The ohel over the burial place remains an identified pilgrimage site. See YIVO Encyclopedia, the Hebrew Daʿat encyclopedia, and the geotagged Wikimedia ohel record.

Rabbi Eliyahu ben Shlomo Zalman (Vilna G.event: Rabbi Eliyahu ben Shlomo Zalman, later known as the Vilna Gaon, is born in Sialiec near Brisk, in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.
The Vilna Gaon settles permanently in Vilna, dedicating his life to Torah study while declining formal rabbinic office.
The Vilna Gaon signs the first excommunication (cherem) against the Hasidic movement, marking the start of organized opposition (Mitnagdim).
The Vilna Gaon passes away in Vilna on 19 Tishrei 5558 (October 9, 1797). He is buried in the Vilna cemetery.

Rabbi Sar Shalom Mizraḥi Sharabi (Rashas.event: Rabbi Sar Shalom Sharabi (Rashash) is born in Sharab, Yemen.
Rabbi Sharabi stays in Damascus, where he debates leading sages over the minimum kezayit of matzah.
Rabbi Sharabi arrives in Jerusalem, joining the circle of kabbalists at Beit El Yeshiva and initially working in humility as a servant.
The Rashash passes away in Jerusalem and is buried on the Mount of Olives. His grave remains a site of pilgrimage for kabbalists.

Rabbi Zvi Hirsch (Hirschel) Levin (Berli.event: Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Levin is born in Rzeszów (Risha), Galicia, into a rabbinic family descended from the Chacham Tzvi.
Rabbi Levin is appointed Rabbi of the Great Synagogue of London, where he is known as Hart Lyon.
Rabbi Levin becomes Chief Rabbi of Berlin, navigating tensions between rabbinic authority and the Jewish Enlightenment (Haskalah).
Rabbi Levin endorses Moses Mendelssohn’s Pentateuch translation and commissions him to write Ritualgesetze der Juden for the government.
Rabbi Levin becomes embroiled in the controversy over Naftali Hertz Wessely’s educational reforms; he briefly resigns his post but later returns.
Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Levin passes away in Berlin after 28 years of service as Chief Rabbi.

Haim Yosef David Azulai (Hida).event: Haim Yosef David Azulai (Hida) is born in Jerusalem into the illustrious Azulai rabbinic family.
Hida begins his first emissary journey from Hebron, traveling through Italy, Germany, and Western Europe to raise funds and strengthen Jewish communities.
Hida visits Germany, meeting leading rabbis including the Pnei Yehoshua.
Hida embarks on his second emissary journey, traveling through Tunisia, Morocco, Italy, France, and Holland.
Hida publishes his seminal works Shem HaGedolim and Birkei Yosef in Livorno and Pisa, cementing his scholarly reputation.
Hida marries his second wife Rachel in Pisa and settles permanently in Livorno, Italy.
Hida dies in Livorno after decades of publishing, study, and leadership. He is buried there.
Hida's remains are reinterred on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem, fulfilling his final wish.

Rabbi David ben Hassin.event: Rabbi David ben Hassin is born in the Mellah of Meknes, Morocco.
At age 17, Rabbi David ben Hassin writes his first work Migdal LaDavid, a study on biblical interpretation and methods of Torah learning.
Rabbi David ben Hassin marries the daughter of his teacher, Rabbi Mordechai Birdugo, and continues his Torah and poetic work.
Rabbi David ben Hassin composes piyyutim that spread across Morocco and beyond, with themes of exile, persecution, consolation, and redemption.
Rabbi David ben Hassin passes away in Meknes on the 10th of Tammuz, 5552 (June 30, 1792).
Posthumously, Rabbi David ben Hassin's collection of poems Tehillah LeDavid is published in Amsterdam, spreading his works widely across the Jewish world.

Rabbi Raphael Hayyim Isaac Carregal.event: Rabbi Raphael Hayyim Isaac Carregal is born in Hebron, Ottoman Empire.
Rabbi Carregal begins his travels, spending two years in Constantinople (1754–1756).
Rabbi Carregal serves in Curaçao (1761–1763), where he appears to have held rabbinic duties.
Rabbi Carregal teaches at the Bet Midrash in London, earning a salary of £100 per year.
Rabbi Carregal spends a year in Jamaica before traveling to North America.
Rabbi Carregal sojourns in Newport, Rhode Island, where he befriends Ezra Stiles of Yale, preaches sermons in Spanish, and publishes the first Jewish sermons printed in America.
Rabbi Carregal arrives in Barbados, where he spends his final years.
Rabbi Raphael Hayyim Isaac Carregal passes away in Barbados on May 5, 1777.

Rabbi Aharon Perlov of Karlin (the Great.event: Rabbi Aharon Perlov is born in Yanova to Rabbi Yaakov of Kobrin and Perel.
Rabbi Aharon becomes a close disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch and establishes the Hasidic center in Karlin (today part of Pinsk, Belarus).
Rabbi Aharon, with Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, spreads Hasidism throughout Lithuania, becoming one of its foremost leaders.
Rabbi Aharon authors the famous Hasidic piyyut Ya Aksuf, later sung in many Hasidic courts on Shabbat.
Rabbi Aharon Perlov of Karlin passes away at the age of 36. His disciple Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin succeeds him and raises his son Rabbi Asher of Stolin, continuing the Karlin-Stolin dynasty.

Rabbi Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev (Kedus.event: Rabbi Levi Yitzchok is born in Husakiv (Yavoriv Raion, Ukraine) to Rabbi Meir and Sarah-Sasha Ruskov.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchok marries Perel, daughter of Rabbi Israel Peretz of Levertov, and soon becomes a disciple of the Maggid of Mezritch.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchok serves as rabbi in Żelechów, Pinsk, and other towns, gaining fame as a compassionate Hasidic leader.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchok settles in Berdichev, where he serves as rabbi and becomes renowned as the 'defense attorney of Israel.'
Kedushas Levi, his magnum opus commentary on Torah and Jewish holidays, is published for the first time.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev passes away on 25 Tishrei, 5570 (October 5, 1809) and is buried in Berdichev’s old Jewish cemetery.

Alter of Liadi.event: Became disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch
Died in Piena, Russia, while fleeing Napoleon's invasion

Rabbi Aryeh Leib Kahana Heller (Ketzos H.event: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Heller is born in Kalush, Galicia (today Ukraine), into a distinguished rabbinic family.
Rabbi Aryeh Leib Heller studies Torah under Rabbi Meshulam Igra of Tysmienica, becoming known as a prodigy in Talmud and halacha.
Ketzos HaChoshen is published, a halachic masterpiece on Choshen Mishpat that becomes a cornerstone of Talmudic study.
Rabbi Aryeh Leib Heller becomes rabbi of Stryi, Galicia, where he serves until his death in 1812.
Meshoveiv Nesivos is written in response to Rabbi Yaakov Lorberbaum’s 'Netivot ha-Mishpat,' continuing their halachic dialogue.
Rabbi Aryeh Leib Heller passes away in Stryi, remembered as one of Galicia’s greatest halachic authorities.

Rabbi Raphael Berdugo (Archangel Raphael.event: Rabbi Raphael Berdugo is born in Meknes, Morocco, into the famous Berdugo rabbinic dynasty.
At age 15, Rabbi Raphael Berdugo is orphaned. His Torah brilliance is revealed publicly during his father’s memorial.
Rabbi Raphael Berdugo becomes dayan in Meknes alongside his brother Rabbi Yekutiel and Rabbi Baruch Toledano.
After the death of his brother Rabbi Yekutiel, Rabbi Raphael Berdugo becomes head of the Beit Din of Meknes, recognized as one of the generation’s great poskim.
Rabbi Raphael Berdugo enacts communal regulations reducing excessive spending on celebrations, bringing relief to struggling families.
Rabbi Raphael Berdugo dies on Hoshana Rabbah at age 75, after completing study of the Idra from the Zohar. His rulings remain authoritative across Moroccan Jewry.

ר׳ אברהם דנציג.event: ר׳ אברהם דנציג is born in Danzig, now Gdańsk, to ר׳ יחיאל מיכל. Modern authorities normally give 1748, while several summaries allow 1747. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel catalogue.

At approximately fourteen, ר׳ אברהם דנציג enters the Prague yeshiva and studies with ר׳ יחזקאל לנדא and ר׳ יוסף ליברמן. His father reportedly required him to guard his traditional formation amid the city’s changing intellectual culture. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and My Jewish Learning.

After roughly four years of study in Prague, ר׳ אברהם דנציג settles in Vilna. Although qualified for rabbinic office, he follows his family principle of not deriving income from Torah and supports himself as a merchant. See Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

During his decades in commerce, ר׳ אברהם דנציג periodically travels from Vilna to the major Leipzig fairs while continuing intensive Torah study. His writings refer to these journeys, but their individual dates are not securely recorded; 1780 is a representative map marker only. See the Jewish Encyclopedia biography.

ר׳ אברהם דנציג also frequents the commercial fairs of Königsberg, an experience that helps explain the practical, household-centered orientation of his later codes. The surviving sources do not date particular trips; this representative year is approximate. See the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ אברהם דנציג begins issuing חיי אדם, his practical reorganization of the laws of אורח חיים for educated householders. Later expanded editions incorporate further correction and analysis, and organized חיי אדם study societies emerge in many communities. See the primary text on Sefaria and the publication history and cited references.

A military gunpowder-magazine explosion devastates ר׳ אברהם דנציג’s courtyard and home, kills thirty-one people and injures members of his family, who nevertheless survive. He establishes 15–16 Kislev as an annual family פולווער־פורים of fasting, thanksgiving, charity and a festive meal. Contemporary calendar conversion creates a 1803/1804 dating variation. See his account cited by the Jewish Encyclopedia and Simcha Fishbane’s modern study Beyond a Code of Jewish Law.

After the explosion contributes to the loss of his commercial fortune, ר׳ אברהם דנציג accepts service as a dayan in Vilna. His precise appointment year is not uniformly recorded, so 1804 is an approximate transition marker. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

An expanded Vilna edition of חיי אדם appears alongside its learned companion נשמת אדם. The combination makes practical rules accessible while preserving the deeper argumentation needed by scholars. See the bibliographic description of the 1809–1810 editions and נשמת אדם on Sefaria.

ר׳ אברהם דנציג publishes שערי צדק, systematizing laws dependent on the Land of Israel. In its introduction he connects the project to his vow and unrealized hope to settle in Jerusalem. See the Jewish Encyclopedia bibliography and the discussion in Beyond a Code of Jewish Law.

The mature חכמת אדם and its analytical companion בינת אדם circulate in Vilna, extending ר׳ אברהם דנציג’s codification principally to יורה דעה. Edition dates vary between 1812 and 1815. See חכמת אדם on Sefaria, the Jewish Encyclopedia bibliography and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ אברהם דנציג dies in Vilna on 4 Tishrei 5581 (12 September 1820). His codes remain central sources for later practical halakhah, while בית אברהם, his ethical testament, is published posthumously in 1821. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the National Library of Israel and My Jewish Learning.

ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין.place: Volozhin, Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; now Valozhyn, Belarus
ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין.event: ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין is born on ז׳ בסיוון תק״ט (24 May 1749) in Volozhin to ר׳ יצחק בן חיים, a communal leader, and Rivka daughter of Yosef Rapoport. See the Hebrew biographical entry and the National Library authority page.

As a young student, ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין studies for about two years with ר׳ רפאל זיסקינד הכהן, then rabbi of Minsk and later of Hamburg. The sources preserve the stage but not a secure starting year, so 1761 is approximate. See Hebrew Wikiyeshiva and the Idra source study.

In adolescence ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין studies under the town’s rabbi ר׳ אריה לייב גינצבורג, author of שאגת אריה. This relationship is well attested, although the exact year is reconstructed from later biographical accounts. See Hebrew Wikiyeshiva and the Idra study.

By the late 1760s or early 1770s, ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין begins travelling to Vilna to learn from ר׳ אליהו בן שלמה זלמן. Later sources variously place his beginning at age nineteen or twenty-five; the relationship is certain but 1770 is an approximate map anchor. See YIVO Encyclopedia and Hebrew Wikiyeshiva.

By 1782 ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין is formally appointed to the Volozhin rabbinate; surviving appointment letters from 1782 and 1785 provide firmer evidence than later claims assigning the office to 1774. See the description of the two appointment documents.

Around age forty, ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין accepts the rabbinate of Vilkomir (modern Ukmergė). Opposition within the community leads him to return to Volozhin after about one year. The move is attested, but 1789 is approximate. See Hebrew Wikiyeshiva and the document catalogue.

ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין circulates אגרת החיים, a public appeal asking communities to send capable students and finance a permanent centre of advanced Torah learning. See the National Library catalogue and Hebrew historical overview.

ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין.place: Yeshivat Etz Chaim, Volozhin, Russian Empire
ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין.event: Around 1803 ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין founds Yeshivat Etz Chaim. It recruits advanced students beyond the local community, supports them materially and maintains continuous study, becoming the institutional model for later Lithuanian yeshivot. See the YIVO Encyclopedia and Yeshivat Har Etzion.

A fire in 1815 destroys many responsa manuscripts belonging to ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין. The surviving legal material later printed in חוט המשולש is therefore only part of his halakhic output. See the Daf Yomi biographical dictionary and cross-reference.

ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין.place: Volozhin, Russian Empire; now Valozhyn, Belarus
ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין.event: ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין dies in Volozhin on י״ד בסיוון תקפ״א (14 June 1821) and is buried there. His son ר׳ יצחק מוולוז׳ין succeeds him as head of the yeshivah and publishes נפש החיים in 1824. See the National Library authority page, the Hebrew biography, and the documented gravestone photograph.

Rav.event: Rav Abba bar Aybo, later known simply as Rav, is born in Kafri in Babylonia.
Rav studies in the Land of Israel, learning from his uncle Rabbi Hiyya and becoming associated with the academy of Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi at Sepphoris.
Rav returns to Babylonia and begins teaching at Nehardea, where he serves as a lecturer and is appointed market supervisor by the Exilarch.
Rav moves to Sura and establishes an academy which becomes one of the great centres of Torah scholarship in Babylonia.
Rav dies in Sura after decades of teaching. His academy and disciples help establish Babylonia as the leading centre of rabbinic scholarship.

ר׳ נחמן מברסלב.event: ר׳ נחמן מברסלב is born in Medzhybizh on 1 Nisan 5532 (4 April 1772) to ר׳ שמחה and פייגא, a granddaughter of ר׳ ישראל בעל שם טוב. His paternal grandfather is ר׳ נחמן מהורודנקה. See the Oxford Bibliographies overview and YIVO Encyclopedia.

Shortly after turning thirteen, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב marries Sashia, daughter of ר׳ אפרים, and lives near her family for about five years while pursuing an unusually intense private devotional life. The broad sequence is documented by Oxford Bibliographies; the exact village identification varies in English transliteration, so the coordinates are regional.
ר׳ נחמן מברסלב moves to Medvedivka and begins functioning publicly as a Hasidic teacher, gradually attracting his first circle of followers. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica biography.

Traveling with ר׳ שמעון toward the Land of Israel, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב spends a difficult and deliberately inconspicuous interval in Ottoman Istanbul before securing passage onward. The journey is preserved in early Breslov sources and assessed in the National Library of Israel reconstruction.

ר׳ נחמן מברסלב lands at Haifa shortly before Rosh Hashanah 5559. He later treats setting foot in the Land of Israel as a transformative rupture in his spiritual development. See the National Library of Israel and Sefaria author profile.

In Tiberias, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב is received by ר׳ אברהם מקאליסק and spends much of his approximately three-and-a-half-month stay among the northern Hasidic community. He also visits the grave of his grandfather, ר׳ נחמן מהורודנקה. See the National Library account.

ר׳ נחמן מברסלב visits Safed and sacred sites in the Upper Galilee during his northern sojourn. Later devotional narratives elaborate these visits, but the broad itinerary is supported by the National Library of Israel reconstruction.

As Napoleon's campaign reaches the coast, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב reaches Acre amid an exodus of civilians and leaves aboard an Ottoman vessel on 17 March, two days before the siege begins. See the dated reconstruction by the National Library of Israel.

After mistakenly boarding a military rather than merchant vessel, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב and ר׳ שמעון endure a hazardous voyage and reach Rhodes, where the Jewish community helps redeem them from their predicament. See the National Library narrative.

Returning through Istanbul and the Black Sea, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב lands at Galați and continues overland home after further storms. The route is summarized by the National Library of Israel; details ultimately derive from Breslov travel traditions recorded by ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ.

After returning from the Land of Israel, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב settles briefly in Zlatopil. His challenge to the condition of contemporary Hasidism contributes to a fierce dispute with ר׳ אריה לייב משפולה. See YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ נחמן מברסלב moves to Bratslav and forms the distinctive community that takes the town's name. Here ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ becomes his closest disciple and principal recorder, preserving teachings, stories and conversations. See YIVO on ר׳ נחמן and YIVO on ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ.
Suffering from tuberculosis, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב travels to Lviv to consult physicians and remains there for several months before returning to Bratslav. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica biography.

The first part of ליקוטי מוהר״ן, the central collection of ר׳ נחמן מברסלב's discourses, is printed at Ostroh under the editorial care of his disciples. Its date and significance are documented by YIVO Encyclopedia; read the work on Sefaria.

Knowing his illness is terminal, ר׳ נחמן מברסלב moves to Uman, tells several of his major tales, teaches the ten-Psalm תיקון הכללי, and chooses burial near Jews killed in the 1768 massacre. He dies of tuberculosis on 18 Tishrei 5571 (16 October 1810) and is buried there. See Oxford Bibliographies, YIVO Encyclopedia and Sefaria.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ מברסלב.event: ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ is born in Nemyriv on 15 Shevat 5540 (22 January 1780) to ר׳ נפתלי הרץ in a prosperous, learned family opposed to early Hasidism. See YIVO Encyclopedia and the YIVO history of Nemyriv.

As a young teenager, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ marries Esther Shaindel, daughter of the prominent scholar ר׳ דוד צבי אוירבך, and continues intensive Talmudic and halakhic study. The exact domestic locations in early biographies vary; the marker represents his wife's family region. The autobiographical framework is preserved in ימי מוהרנ״ת, while his family and intellectual background are summarized by YIVO.
After unsatisfying visits to other Hasidic courts, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ meets ר׳ נחמן מברסלב in Bratslav and becomes his disciple despite family opposition. See YIVO Encyclopedia.

Traveling repeatedly between nearby Nemyriv and Bratslav, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ becomes the meticulous recorder and editor on whom ר׳ נחמן מברסלב increasingly relies for preservation of his discourses. See YIVO and the Breslov corpus on Sefaria.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ helps bring the first part of ר׳ נחמן מברסלב's ליקוטי מוהר״ן to print at Ostroh, an early landmark in his lifelong editorial mission. The publication is discussed in the YIVO biography of ר׳ נחמן; the text is available on Sefaria.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ attends ר׳ נחמן מברסלב during his final period in Uman and assumes responsibility for safeguarding the teachings after his death on 18 Tishrei 5571. He becomes the community's informal leader but never claims the title of rebbe. See YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ organizes the first annual Breslov Rosh Hashanah gathering at the grave of ר׳ נחמן מברסלב, establishing Uman as the movement's enduring pilgrimage focus. YIVO identifies him as the movement's post-1810 leader; the first gathering is also summarized in the YIVO profile and later pilgrimage historiography.

At Ostroh, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ publishes סיפורי מעשיות, preserving the symbolic tales told by ר׳ נחמן מברסלב in Hebrew and Yiddish. His editorial and publishing role is documented by YIVO; YIVO's history of Yiddish literature places the early edition in 1815–1816.

On his own hazardous pilgrimage to the Land of Israel, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ travels through Ottoman Istanbul during the Greek–Ottoman war. The trip is narrated firsthand in ימי מוהרנ״ת; its historical setting is summarized by the Breslov Research Institute.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ reaches Ottoman Palestine during his 1822 pilgrimage and enters through Acre before visiting Jewish communities and sacred sites. The route is reconstructed primarily from his own ימי מוהרנ״ת; the Breslov Research Institute confirms the 1822 pilgrimage.

In the Galilee, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ visits Tiberias, Safed and graves associated with earlier kabbalists and Hasidic immigrants, interpreting the journey through the teachings of ר׳ נחמן מברסלב. These stages derive principally from his travel memoir ימי מוהרנ״ת, so the marker is regional rather than a claim of continuous residence.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ reaches Jerusalem during the central phase of his pilgrimage, praying at holy places and recording the spiritual meaning of the visit. His firsthand source is ימי מוהרנ״ת; the date is corroborated by the Breslov Research Institute.

As the Rosh Hashanah gathering expands, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ raises funds for a dedicated prayer hall in Uman and composes prayers for use at the grave of ר׳ נחמן מברסלב. His role in developing the pilgrimage follows the scholarly overview in YIVO Encyclopedia and the movement's documented publication history.

During the anti-Breslov campaign led by ר׳ משה צבי מסאווראן, ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ is denounced to the authorities, briefly arrested, restricted and forced away from Bratslav to Nemyriv. YIVO dates the most severe campaign to 1835–1839 and records his Nemyriv residence in 1835–1838; see YIVO on ר׳ נתן and YIVO on Nemyriv.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ returns to Bratslav, rebuilds the embattled community and continues printing and circulating Breslov teachings with a press acquired for that mission. His leadership and publishing program are described by YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ dies in Bratslav on 10 Tevet 5605 (20 December 1844) and is buried in the Jewish cemetery there. He leaves Breslov without a successor-rebbe but with a durable textual, liturgical and pilgrimage infrastructure. See YIVO Encyclopedia.

Yaakov Tzvi Mecklenburg.event: Born in Lissa (Leszno), Province of Posen, Germany, into the family of Rabbi Gamliel.
Studied Torah under Rabbi Zechariah Mendel of Lissa, a close friend of Rabbi Akiva Eger.
Began independent Torah scholarship and business career.
After business difficulties, accepted position as Rabbi of Königsberg, East Prussia.
Together with the Malbim, opposed the Reform Judaism convention in Braunschweig.
Published Haketav Vehakkabbalah, his Torah commentary, in Königsberg.
Passed away in Königsberg after serving 34 years as Rabbi. Requested that no eulogies be given at his funeral.

Yehuda Aryeh Leon Bibas.event: Visited London and met Jewish philanthropist Sir Moses Montefiore
Met Judah Alkalai during his European tour and became an important influence on his proto-Zionist thought
Made aliyah and was welcomed by his students
Moved to Hebron, established a seminary and library, and died there shortly after his arrival

ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון (הרש״ש).event: ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון is born in Zaskevichi on 18 Heshvan 5554 (24 October 1793), according to the modern documentary reconstruction; older encyclopedias commonly print 1794. He is initially known as Zaskovitzer after his birthplace. The marker uses modern Zaskavichy, Belarus, the geographical identification supplied by gazetteers. See The Lost Library, YIVO Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel authority record.

At approximately thirteen, ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון marries Sarah, daughter of ר׳ דוד שטראשון, and joins her family in their village near Vilna. He takes the surname שטראשון; the precise modern identification of the village is uncertain, so this marker is a regional Vilna anchor rather than a claimed building location. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica. The year is approximate.

During Napoleon's invasion of 1812, the French army wrecks the distillery belonging to the family of ר׳ דוד שטראשון. The extended household moves into Vilna, where ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון becomes permanently rooted. Commercial activity supports his study while his wife takes a leading role in managing the business. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and YIVO Encyclopedia.

In the study house founded by his father-in-law, ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון devotes himself to intensive learning and studies with ר׳ אברהם דנציג, who cites him in בינת אדם and חכמת אדם under the name Zaskovitzer. The year is a representative early-Vilna marker, not a precisely dated commencement. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון joins other scholars in establishing Yeshivat ha-Arba'im, an ambitious but short-lived Vilna institution. He continues the rigorous Lithuanian scholarly culture associated with the circle and legacy of ר׳ אליהו מווילנה. See the YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe.

By the 1840s, ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון is delivering crowded daily Talmud lectures without payment at the synagogue on Popławska Street. Discussion in these sessions helps generate the notes later printed as הגהות הרש״ש. In 1843 his father-in-law dies, but Sarah and other relatives continue operating the family business so he can maintain his scholarly life. The exact synagogue building has not been securely identified, so the coordinate marks the historical district only. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Vilna editions of Midrash Rabbah issued in 1843–1845 publish annotations by ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון; further notes appear in 1855. His reputation spreads through both print and rabbinic correspondence, while he remains a communal leader and refuses the offered rabbinate of Suwałki. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel bibliography.

ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון dies in Vilna on 21 March 1872 (11 Adar II 5632). His glosses on almost the entire Talmud and Mishnah are subsequently absorbed into standard Vilna-style editions, making הגהות הרש״ש part of everyday advanced Talmud study. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, YIVO Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel.

Zvi Hirsch Kalischer.event: Born in Lissa (Leszno), Province of Posen, Prussia. Studied Talmud under Rabbi Jacob of Lissa and Rabbi Akiva Eger.
Settled in Thorn (Toruń), where he spent the rest of his life. Served over 40 years as Rabbinatsverweser (acting rabbi), refusing remuneration and living modestly.
Published 'Eben Bochan' (Krotoschin), commentary on Choshen Mishpat.
Published 'Emunah Yesharah' (Krotoschin), Jewish philosophy and theology, including a commentary on Job and Ecclesiastes.
Published parts I & II of 'Moznayim la-Mishpat' in Krotoschin and Königsberg, commentary on Choshen Mishpat.
Influenced Chaim Lorje to found the first 'Association for the Colonisation of Palestine' in Frankfurt. This was among the earliest proto-Zionist societies.
Published 'Derishat Tzion' in Lyck, calling for Jewish settlement in Israel, agricultural schools, and a Jewish guard force. Advocated self-help and natural redemption.
German translation of 'Derishat Tzion' published in Toruń by Poper. Second Hebrew edition issued in 1866 by N. Friedland.
Due to his influence, the Alliance Israélite Universelle founded the Mikveh Israel agricultural school in Palestine near Jaffa.
Died in Toruń after decades of rabbinic leadership and proto-Zionist advocacy. Remembered as a forerunner of modern Zionism.

Samuel David Luzzatto (Shadal).event: Born in Trieste, Italy (1 Elul 5560). Studied Talmud under Rabbi Abraham Eliezer ha-Levi, and languages and sciences with Mordechai de Cologna, Leon Vita Saraval, and Raphael Baruch Segré.
At age 11, won a prize copy of Montesquieu’s Considérations, sparking his critical thinking. Began writing Hebrew grammar in Italian and exegetical notes on the Torah.
Mother died; took over housework and helped his father’s turning trade while continuing studies and writing poetry (later collected in 'Kinnor Na’im').
Completed Ma'amar ha-Niqqud, a treatise on Hebrew vowels. Advanced in Biblical philology and exegetics.
Began writing 'Torah Nidreshet,' a philosophico-theological treatise, parts of which were later published in Hebrew and Italian.
Father died. Supported himself through private teaching and contributing to Hebrew journals such as Bikkure ha-Ittim.
Appointed professor at the Rabbinical College of Padua. Began his long career of teaching Bible and Hebrew philology.
Expanded literary work: critical studies in Hebrew, Italian, German, and French. Corresponded widely with European Jewish scholars.
Focused research on Biblical philology, Syriac, and Samaritan Hebrew. Critically emended Biblical texts and argued for the authenticity of Isaiah’s full book.
Published works opposing philosophical Judaism and rationalism; attacked Maimonides’ Aristotelianism, Ibn Ezra’s method, and Spinoza’s heresies.
Died in Padua on Yom Kippur (10 Tishrei 5626) after a career of more than 50 years in scholarship and teaching.

Nathan Marcus HaKohen Adler.event: Received doctorate at University of Erlangen and semikhah from Rabbi Abraham Bing in Würzburg
Appointed Chief Rabbi of the British Empire
Oversaw period of Jewish emancipation in Britain, including Sir David Salomons as first Jewish Lord Mayor of London
Helped establish the United Synagogue by Act of Parliament
Died and buried at Willesden United Synagogue Cemetery, London

ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד.event: ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד is born in 1804 at Ungvár, today Uzhhorod in Ukraine, to ר׳ יוסף. The National Library catalogue preserves an 1802 authority variant, while modern scholarly references and standard biographies use 1804. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, Sefaria and the National Library record.

After his father dies when he is eight, the gifted ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד comes under the guardianship of Ungvár’s rabbi and rosh yeshiva, ר׳ צבי הירש הלר. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica biography and the biographical synthesis.

At approximately fifteen, ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד follows his guardian and teacher ר׳ צבי הירש הלר to Bonyhád. He remains in the yeshiva for nearly a decade, continuing intensive Talmud study until ordination and marriage. See the biographical account and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

After marriage and rabbinic ordination, ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד briefly pursues commerce, including the wine trade, first around Homonna (Humenné) and then Ungvár. The year is approximate; the episode explains his later sensitivity to practical business law and the needs of working Jews. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the modern biography.

Leaving an unsuccessful commercial career, ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד accepts the rabbinate of Brezovica. He serves the community until 1849 and develops his program of clear, practical halakhic instruction. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

While serving in Brezovica, ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד publishes קסת הסופר, his practical code for scribes. ר׳ משה סופר endorses the book as essential knowledge for anyone receiving certification to write Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot. See קסת הסופר on Sefaria and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד returns to his native Ungvár as a dayan on its rabbinical court. Serving in the Orthodox leadership associated with ר׳ מאיר אייזנשטטר, he sees the need to equip ordinary households with reliable knowledge of practical halakhah. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Sefaria and the biographical synthesis.

ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד first publishes קיצור שולחן ערוך at Ungvár in 1864. Its concise Hebrew presents the laws of daily life to non-specialists; repeated editions, translations and classroom use rapidly make it one of the most influential Ashkenazi halakhic manuals. See Evyatar Marienberg’s peer-reviewed study, The 19th-century Kitzur Shulhan Arukh, Sefaria and the National Library collection.

At the 1869 Hungarian Jewish Congress in Budapest, ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד acts as a leading spokesman for Orthodox Jewry during the dispute over national communal organization and the relationship with the Neolog movement. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד dies in Ungvár on 30 July 1886, traditionally 28 Tammuz 5646, after serving its rabbinical court for nearly four decades. His קיצור שולחן ערוך continues to shape household practice and Jewish religious education internationally. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, Encyclopaedia Judaica and Chabad’s author reference.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Brody, Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria, Habsburg monarchy
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: ר׳ צבי הירש חיות is born in Brody on 20 November 1805 (28 Marḥeshvan 5566) into the prosperous scholarly family of ר׳ מאיר חיות. Brody provides the setting for both his intensive rabbinic education and unusually broad general learning. See the YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe and the National Library of Israel authority record.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Brody, Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria; education period approximate
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: During his youth in Brody, ר׳ צבי הירש חיות studies with Galician authorities including ר׳ אפרים זלמן מרגליות and develops competence in languages, history, philosophy, and contemporary scholarship. His later intellectual circle includes ר׳ נחמן קרוכמל and ר׳ שלמה יהודה רפפורט. The year is representative because surviving biographies do not provide a semester-by-semester itinerary. See YIVO and the biographical summary in Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Żółkiew (Zhovkva), Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: ר׳ צבי הירש חיות is appointed rabbi of the Żółkiew district in 1829 while still in his twenties. He remains there for more than twenty years, serving as communal rabbi while producing studies that combine traditional halakhic commitments with historical analysis of rabbinic literature. See the YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Żółkiew (Zhovkva), Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: While serving Żółkiew, ר׳ צבי הירש חיות publishes תורת נביאים, an early statement of his approach to tradition, rabbinic authority, and Talmudic method. Its appearance marks the growth of his reputation as a scholar who used modern organization and historical questions without abandoning halakhic authority. See Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Żółkiew (Zhovkva), Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: ר׳ צבי הירש חיות publishes מבוא התלמוד, his best-known independent work, offering a structured account of the Oral Torah, halakhah, aggadah, interpretation, enactments, and the composition of rabbinic literature. Publication is attached to his secure Żółkiew rabbinate rather than to later printing locations. See the National Library of Israel catalogue and YIVO.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Lwów (Lviv), Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: To comply with Austrian rules requiring district rabbis to demonstrate formal general education, ר׳ צבי הירש חיות travels to Lwów in the summer of 1846, passes external university examinations, and receives official permission to serve in the rabbinate. The evidence supports an examination certificate, not the doctorate sometimes claimed in popular accounts. See the YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Żółkiew (Zhovkva), Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: From Żółkiew, ר׳ צבי הירש חיות helps lead a circle of Galician rabbis and maskilim opposing the Reform rabbinical conferences in Germany and publishes מנחת קנאות. In the same period his responsa engage modern religious innovations while arguing from within traditional jurisprudence. See YIVO.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות is elected rabbi of Kalisz in 1852. The move gives him a major Polish communal post, but his tenure is marked by opposition from sections of the local community; he remains for approximately three years. See the YIVO Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.place: Lwów (Lviv), Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria; final return
ר׳ צבי הירש חיות.event: After becoming seriously ill in 1855, ר׳ צבי הירש חיות leaves Kalisz and returns to Galicia. He dies in Lwów on 12 October 1855, aged forty-nine. This follows YIVO’s account of his return and the Galician biographical tradition; some popular summaries instead list Kalisz as the death place. See YIVO and the Hebrew reference entry at Da’at.

שמשון רפאל הירש (Samson Raphael Hirsch).event: Born in Hamburg, then part of Napoleonic France, into a family with rabbinic lineage.
Studied in Mannheim under Rabbi Jacob Ettlinger; received semicha in 1830.
Appointed Landesrabbiner (chief rabbi) of Oldenburg. Wrote Nineteen Letters on Judaism (1836) and Horeb (1838).
Became rabbi of Emden, serving Hanoverian districts Aurich and Osnabrück. Founded a secondary school integrating Torah and secular studies.
Elected rabbi of Nikolsburg, Moravia. In 1847 became chief rabbi of Moravia and Austrian Silesia; active in Landtag advocating Jewish civil rights.
Accepted call to Frankfurt am Main to lead the Orthodox secessionist Israelitische Religionsgesellschaft (IRG). Established Realschule and schools promoting Torah im Derech Eretz.
Founded and edited the journal Jeschurun, publishing his philosophy and commentaries.
Promoted Austritt (secession) after German law permitted Jews to leave Reform-dominated communities; strengthened independent Orthodoxy.
Died in Frankfurt am Main. Buried there; left lasting influence through Torah im Derech Eretz philosophy.

ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (המלבי.event: ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר is born in Volochysk on 19 Adar II 5569 (7 March 1809). After his father ר׳ יחיאל מיכל dies during his childhood, he is educated by his stepfather ר׳ לייב מוולוצ'יסק and by ר׳ משה הלוי הורוויץ. See YIVO Encyclopedia and ויקיפדיה העברית.

At approximately thirteen, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר travels to Warsaw for advanced rabbinic study and becomes known as the ‘Volhynian prodigy.’ His early marriage and later divorce belong to this formative period; exact intermediate dates remain uncertain. See ויקיפדיה העברית and YIVO Encyclopedia.

In 1834, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר travels through European centers including Pressburg, Trieste, Amsterdam and Breslau to present the manuscript of ארצות החיים and obtain approbations. Breslau is used for this map stage because it became the work's publication center in 1837; the event does not imply continuous residence there. See YIVO Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel.

With the recommendation of ר׳ שלמה זלמן טיקטין, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר receives his first communal rabbinate at Wreschen around 1837–1839. He publishes ארצות השלום in 1839 but experiences financial strain and communal friction. See YIVO Encyclopedia and ויקיפדיה העברית.

Around 1841, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר becomes rabbi of the larger Kempen community, serving for approximately seventeen years and acquiring the sobriquet ‘the Kempener.’ In response to the 1844 Reform conference at Brunswick, he develops the program that becomes התורה והמצוה. See YIVO Encyclopedia and ויקיפדיה העברית.

In 1859, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר becomes chief rabbi and preacher of Bucharest. He strengthens kashrut supervision, education, Hebrew printing and the eruv, while opposing liturgical and institutional reforms promoted by sections of the communal elite. See YIVO Encyclopedia and ויקיפדיה העברית.

On 18 March 1864, Romanian authorities arrest ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר, take him through Giurgiu and expel him across the Danube to Ruse after accusations by his opponents. In Ruse he is hosted by ר׳ אברהם בן ישראל רוזאניס. See ויקיפדיה העברית and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

After his expulsion, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר petitions the Ottoman authorities in Constantinople without obtaining reinstatement, then spends roughly six months in Paris seeking diplomatic and communal assistance. The coordinate marks Paris, his longer documented stop. See Jewish Encyclopedia and ויקיפדיה העברית.

In spring 1865, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר accepts the Łęczyca rabbinate formerly held by his father-in-law ר׳ חיים אוירבך. Opposition from both modernizing and Hasidic constituencies makes this another short tenure. See ויקיפדיה העברית and Jewish Encyclopedia.

After leaving Łęczyca, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר serves for a short period as rabbi in Kherson. The precise starting year is not consistently reported; 1867 is an approximate map marker between his 1865 appointment and his move to Mogilev in 1870. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and YIVO Encyclopedia.

ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (המלבי.place: Mogilev on the Dnieper, Russian Empire
ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (המלבי.event: In 1870, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר becomes rabbi of Mogilev on the Dnieper. Conflict with affluent modernizers leads to denunciation as a political offender and an official order expelling him from the city. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Russian Jewish Encyclopedia.

By approximately 1875, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר serves as rabbi of Königsberg's Russian and Polish Jewish community. He remains there for about four years, continuing his writing amid further tensions with German Jewish reformers. See Russian Jewish Encyclopedia and Jewish Encyclopedia.

In 1879, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר visits Vilna and is considered for its rabbinate after the death of ר׳ יצחק אליהו לנדא. The governor blocks his appointment because of the earlier political accusation attached to his Mogilev expulsion. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and ויקיפדיה העברית.

While traveling to accept the Kremenchuk rabbinate, ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר becomes ill and dies in Kyiv on 1 Tishrei 5640 (18 September 1879), the first day of Rosh Hashanah. He is buried in Kyiv. See the Jewish Encyclopedia, ויקיפדיה העברית and the National Library of Israel.

Yisrael Salanter.note: Born in Žagarė, Lithuania (then Russian Empire)
Married Esther Fega Eisenstein; moved to Salant, studied under R. Hirsch Broda and R. Yosef Zundel
Appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Meile’s Yeshiva (Tomchai Torah) in Vilna
Established independent yeshiva in Zaretcha (suburb of Vilna)
Moved to Kovno; established Musar-focused yeshiva at the Nevyozer Kloiz
Left Lithuania for Prussia; lived with Hirsch brothers in Halberstadt
Edited and published journal 'Tevunah' in Königsberg
Lived for periods in Berlin; continued teaching Musar
Organized Russian Jewish immigrants into a community in Paris
Died in Königsberg (then East Prussia, now Kaliningrad)

ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.event: ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט is probably born in Białystok in 1812 (תקע"ב) to ר׳ יעקב אשר אייזנשטט and Rachel. Later sources often give 1813, but a source-critical comparison with the contemporary report of his age at death favors 1812. He descends from ר׳ מאיר אייזנשטט, author of פנים מאירות. See Hanan Yitzhaki's specialist study and ויקיפדיה העברית.

At approximately fifteen, ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט marries Yenta Reizel, daughter of Yehuda Leib HaKohen of Grodno, and remains in Białystok. She manages a stationery and paper-goods business while he studies in the beit midrash of ר׳ יחיאל נעכעס alongside ר׳ שמואל הלוי, author of בגדי ישע, and ר׳ גרשון חן טוב, author of מנחה חדשה. See המעין / מכון שלמה אומן and the cross-referenced English biography.

ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.place: Grodno, Russian Empire; now Hrodna, Belarus
ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.event: Around the early 1830s, after government offices that had patronized the family stationery business relocate, ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט and his household move from Białystok to Grodno. When the business fails there, he accepts service as a dayan to support his family. The year is necessarily approximate because the surviving biography says only that this occurred several years before his 1836 rabbinate. See Hanan Yitzhaki's biographical reconstruction.

ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.place: Bristovitz, Grodno Governorate; now Vyalikaya Byerastavitsa, Belarus
ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.event: ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט is appointed rabbi of Bristovitz in 1836. In the same year, following recovery from a serious illness, he publishes the first edition of פתחי תשובה on Yoreh De'ah in Vilna. The printing location documents publication, while Bristovitz is his evidenced residence and rabbinic post. See המעין and the contemporary-reference synthesis in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.place: Utyan, Kovno Governorate; now Utena, Lithuania
ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.event: In 1856 (תרט"ז), ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט accepts the Utyan community's invitation to become its rabbi and av beit din. He remains associated with Utyan through the rest of his working life while continuing the expansion of פתחי תשובה. See the dated appointment in Hanan Yitzhaki's study and the historical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.place: Königsberg, Kingdom of Prussia; now Kaliningrad, Russia
ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט.event: During the winter of 5628, the seriously ill ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט travels from Utyan to Königsberg for medical treatment. He dies there on Friday, 3 Elul 5628 (21 August 1868), aged approximately fifty-six, and is buried in the Königsberg Jewish cemetery near ר׳ יהודה אשכנזי of Tykocin and ר׳ יעקב צבי מקלנבורג. The 1868 date is confirmed by a contemporary Ha-Maggid notice and his son's family record, correcting a mistaken reading of the gravestone as 1865. See the documentary date analysis and ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.event: ר׳ עבדאללה סומך, also known by the Hebrew name ר׳ עובדיה אברהם יוסף סומך, is born in Baghdad in 1813 to ר׳ אברהם יוסף יחזקאל and Khatun. His family traced its ancestry to ר׳ נסים גאון. See the National Library of Israel authority record and the Hebrew biographical account.

ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.place: Baghdad, Ottoman Iraq; educational year approximate
ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.event: As a youth in Baghdad, ר׳ עבדאללה סומך studies under ר׳ יעקב בר יוסף הרופא, who later calls him his distinguished and discerning pupil, and under ר׳ משה חיים. The displayed year is an approximate educational marker because the sources do not provide an enrollment date. See the contemporary-oriented Jewish Encyclopedia and the Hebrew Wikiyeshiva biography.

ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.place: Midrash Abu Menashi, later Midrash Beit Zilkha, Jewish quarter of Baghdad
ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.event: After leaving commerce to teach young scholars without payment, ר׳ עבדאללה סומך receives the support of Ezekiel Reuben Manasseh, who purchases a courtyard and establishes Midrash Abu Menashi in 1840. The institution develops into Midrash Beit Zilkha, which ר׳ עבדאללה סומך heads until his death. The exact historic building coordinates are not securely published, so this marker uses Baghdad's former Jewish-quarter area rather than claiming a surviving building footprint. See the institutional history and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.place: Midrash Beit Zilkha, Baghdad; representative mid-career year
ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.event: By the middle decades of the nineteenth century, ר׳ עבדאללה סומך directs Baghdad's principal advanced rabbinic academy. Among the scholars formed in his circle are ר׳ יוסף חיים, ר׳ אליהו מני, ר׳ אברהם הלל, ר׳ יצחק מג׳לד, ר׳ ששון שמוחה and ר׳ שלמה בכור חוצין. The year marks a long teaching career rather than a single appointment. See the Hebrew biography and student list and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

A contemporary 1887 report describes ר׳ עבדאללה סומך as heavily occupied with questions sent to Baghdad from Persia and Central Asia, especially in divorce and marriage law. His responsa also reached Baghdadi communities in India and addressed the practical consequences of modernization. See the cited contemporary report and analysis in the Hebrew biography and the scholarly article on his halakhic response to change in Pe'amim.

During the 1889 cholera epidemic, ר׳ עבדאללה סומך falls ill while staying in a village near Baghdad and is brought back into the city for treatment. He dies in Baghdad on 18 Elul 5649 (13 September 1889). The village name appears in variant forms and cannot be geolocated securely, so no fabricated village marker is used. See the detailed Hebrew account and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.place: Traditional shrine of Joshua the High Priest and Jewish cemetery, Baghdad
ר׳ עבדאללה סומך.event: Because epidemic regulations close the regular cemetery, ר׳ עבדאללה סומך is first buried, with gubernatorial permission, in the courtyard traditionally associated with Joshua the High Priest, west of the Tigris. Local opposition triggers a violent confrontation, arrests of Jewish leaders and wider anti-Jewish attacks. After official intervention, his remains are transferred about three months later to Baghdad's Jewish cemetery. Exact nineteenth-century grave coordinates are uncertain, so the marker is placed only at Baghdad level. See the near-contemporary Jewish Encyclopedia and the full Hebrew burial narrative.

Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin (Netziv).note: Born in Mir, Belarus (then Russian Empire)
Began studies at Volozhin Yeshiva at age 11
Betrothed to Reina-Batya, daughter of R' Yitzhak of Volozhin
Began delivering lectures at Volozhin Yeshiva
Appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Volozhin after passing of R' Eliezer Yitzchak
Participated in Druskininkai Conference; appointed advisory trustee of Chovevei Zion
Closure of Volozhin Yeshiva under Russian government pressure
Died in Warsaw; buried in the Jewish Cemetery

Yitzchak Elchanan Spektor.note: Born in Ros (Rosh), Belarus, Grodno Governorate
Studied in Vilkovisk under R. Benjamin Diskin
First rabbinic position in Sabelin, Belarus
Appointed Chief Rabbi of Kovno, position held until death
Participated in St. Petersburg conferences after anti-Jewish riots

ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Nesvizh, Minsk Governorate, Russian Empire; now Belarus
ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק is born around 1820 in Nesvizh to ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and Rivka. His maternal ancestry connects him to ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין. The exact day is unknown. See the Hebrew biography and genealogical source study.

ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Volozhin, Minsk Governorate, Russian Empire; date approximate
ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: As a boy of about ten, ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק is sent to Volozhin for private study and then enters the yeshivah, developing the textual mastery that shapes his career. The year is approximate. See the Hebrew biographical account and bibliographic record for the scholarly biography.

While still a young scholar, ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק teaches in Minsk, associated in later accounts with Bluma’s kloyz and with replacing the local lecturer ר׳ גרשון תנחום. The episode is secure in the biographical tradition, but its precise year is not. See the genealogical-biographical study.

After the death of ר׳ אליעזר יצחק פריד, ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק joins ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין in leading the Volozhin Yeshiva. He serves as the Netziv’s deputy and delivers advanced Talmudic instruction until leaving in 1865. See the cross-referenced biography and the Hebrew rabbinic dictionary.

ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק becomes rabbi of Slutsk in 1865. He teaches advanced students including ר׳ יוסף רוזין and ר׳ זלמן סנדר שפירא, and communal accounts credit him with arranging meals for impoverished schoolchildren. See the biographical synthesis and the Hebrew biography.

ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Warsaw, Congress Poland; transition dated approximately
ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: After conflict with communal modernizers and Slutsk leaders, ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק resigns and moves to Warsaw, where he lives without a formal rabbinate and experiences financial hardship. Accounts date the resignation to 1874 or 1875; this map uses 1874 while preserving the uncertainty. See the biographical synthesis and Hebrew collected biography.

After ר׳ יהושע לייב דיסקין leaves Brisk for Jerusalem, the community appoints ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק as its rabbi. Sources place the beginning in 1877–1879; 1878 is a midpoint marker rather than a claimed exact inauguration year. He serves Brisk for the remainder of his life. See the Hebrew biography and cross-reference.

ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Brisk/Brest-Litovsk, Russian Empire; now Brest, Belarus
ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק dies in Brisk on ד׳ באייר תרנ״ב (1 May 1892) and is buried in the city’s Jewish cemetery. Contemporary reporting described the community’s public mourning; his son ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק succeeds him. See the Hebrew article quoting the funeral report and the Wikimedia portrait record.

ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין.event: ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין is born on 23 Shevat 5583 (4 February 1823) in Kreuzburg, now Krustpils in Latvia, to the Lithuanian rabbi ר׳ יעקב הכהן. See YIVO Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Orphaned as a young child, ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין is raised and educated by his uncle ר׳ יוסף בן אשר, a student of ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין. His early reputation gives rise to the designation 'the prodigy of Krynki.' See Encyclopaedia Judaica. The coordinates are regional because the surviving reference does not establish a precise residence.

ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין marries young into a wealthy family, allowing him to continue intensive study. A subsequent marital crisis leads him to seek an exceptional heter me'ah rabbanim from one hundred rabbis. YIVO and Encyclopaedia Judaica report the episode, but exact dates, allegations and itinerary are not secure; this is intentionally a regional marker.

During travels through Poland seeking rabbinic authorization, ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין reaches the Lublin region and encounters Hasidic teachers. This journey marks his transition from a Lithuanian non-Hasidic formation toward Hasidism. See Encyclopaedia Judaica; the year is approximate.

ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין becomes a disciple of ר׳ מרדכי יוסף ליינר מאיזביצה, whose radical exploration of providence, will, sin and divine purpose permanently reshapes his thought. See YIVO Encyclopedia, Encyclopaedia Judaica and his Sefaria author profile. The first year of discipleship is approximate.

After ר׳ מרדכי יוסף ליינר dies, ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין supports his friend ר׳ יהודה לייב איגר as leader of the Lublin Hasidic circle. For more than thirty years ר׳ צדוק studies, writes and lives in relative seclusion rather than claiming leadership. See YIVO and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Following the death of ר׳ יהודה לייב איגר, ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין reluctantly accepts leadership of the Lublin Hasidim. His public sermons from this final period are later collected in פרי צדיק. See YIVO Encyclopedia, Encyclopaedia Judaica and the digitized work.

In his final years, ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין continues teaching and writing but declines to publish most manuscripts during his lifetime, while indicating that they should appear after his death. Many unpublished manuscripts will later be lost in the Lublin ghetto. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the National Library of Israel catalogue.

ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין dies on 9 Elul 5660 (3 September 1900) in Lublin. Posthumous publication begins almost immediately: פרי צדיק starts appearing in 1901 and צדקת הצדיק in 1902. See YIVO, Encyclopaedia Judaica and צדקת הצדיק on Sefaria.

Aruch HaShulchan.event: Born in Bobruisk, near Vilna, in the Russian Empire (now Belarus).
Around this time, R'Yechiel Michel Epstein goes to study in Volozhin and stays there for two years. Married the sister of Rav Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin (the Netziv).
R'Yechiel Michel Epstein returns to Bobruisk and supports the Rav there.
R'Yechiel Michel Epstein was appointed Rav of Novozybkhov. This town had a large number of Chasidish Jews.
Appointed rabbi of Novogrudok, where he served for over three decades and composed his magnum opus 'Aruch HaShulchan'.
Died in Novogrudok. His 'Aruch HaShulchan' became a cornerstone of halakhic study and is widely used until today.

ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.event: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני is born in Jerusalem on 7 Cheshvan 5593 (1832) to ר׳ רפאל אשר אליהו מדיני and Kalu Vida. Older sources variously print 1833 or 1834, but the National Library authority record and Encyclopaedia Judaica use 1832. See the National Library of Israel, Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Hebrew HaChacham HaYomi biography.

ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.place: Jerusalem, Ottoman Palestine; educational date approximate
ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.event: As a young Jerusalem scholar, ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני studies under ר׳ יצחק קובו and ר׳ יוסף נסים בורלא. He marries Rivka at eighteen and receives rabbinic ordination at approximately nineteen; 1848 is an approximate educational marker because the references do not give a full year-by-year study record. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.place: Constantinople, Ottoman Empire; now Istanbul, Türkiye
ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.event: Following his father's sudden death, ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני moves with his wife, widowed mother and two sisters from Jerusalem to Constantinople. He supports the household partly by tutoring, teaches publicly without payment and devotes himself to study and writing during a fourteen-year residence. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and HaChacham HaYomi.

While living in Constantinople, ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני publishes his first work, מכתב לחזקיהו, containing Talmudic novellae and responsa. The book was printed in Smyrna, but the printing place is not treated as a personal move. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and the National Library of Israel catalogue.

ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.place: Karasubazar, Crimea, Russian Empire; now Bilohirsk, Ukraine
ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.event: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני accepts the rabbinate of Karasubazar in Crimea. During thirty-two years of leadership he establishes schools and yeshivot, introduces communal regulations, corrects practices he considers mistaken and works closely with the Krymchak Jewish community. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

From Karasubazar, ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני begins issuing volumes of שדי חמד, the encyclopedic halakhic project he has assembled through extensive reading and correspondence. Thirteen of its eighteen volumes appear during his lifetime; Warsaw is a printing location, not evidence that he relocated there. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Hebrew text at Wikisource and the National Library catalogue.

After more than three decades in Crimea, ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני returns to Jerusalem in 1899 and remains there for approximately two years. When his name is advanced for the Sephardi chief rabbinate, he seeks a quieter setting in which to continue his scholarship. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Community of Hebron biography.
