ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני moves to Hebron in 1901, hoping to study and complete his writings away from public office. He teaches from Beit Romano, where his study and library become a scholarly centre. See the Jewish Community of Hebron and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

After the deaths of Hebron's leading rabbis ר׳ אליהו מני and ר׳ חיים רחמים יוסף פרנקו, ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני reluctantly accepts communal leadership and serves as Hebron's rabbi until his death. The references place his Hebron move and ensuing rabbinate in 1901, without securely dating the interval between them more precisely. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Community of Hebron biography.

ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.place: Ancient Jewish cemetery, Hebron, Ottoman Palestine
ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני.event: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני dies in Hebron on 24 Kislev 5665 (1904) and is buried in the city's ancient Jewish cemetery. His library and correspondence dispersed after his death, while remaining portions and later editions of שדי חמד continued to appear. See the National Library of Israel, HaChacham HaYomi and the Hebron community biography.

Yisrael Meir ha-Kohen Kagan (Chofetz Cha.location: Dzyatlava, Grodno Governorate, Russian Empire (now Belarus)

Yisrael Meir ha-Kohen Kagan (Chofetz Cha.event: Moved for education after father's passing

Hermann Adler HaKohen.event: Born in Hanover, Germany, to Chief Rabbi Nathan Marcus Adler.
Studied at the rabbinical college in Prague.
Graduated PhD from University of Leipzig.
Received semikha (ordination) from Rabbi Solomon Judah Loeb Rapoport.
Appointed minister of Bayswater Synagogue, London.
Became assistant to his father, Chief Rabbi Nathan Marcus Adler.
Succeeded his father as Chief Rabbi of the British Empire.
Consecrated Dublin Hebrew Congregation synagogue; declared Ireland had never persecuted Jews.
Appointed Commander of the Royal Victorian Order (CVO).
Died and was buried at Willesden United Synagogue Cemetery, London.

Meir Simcha HaKohen of Dvinsk.event: Born in Butrimonys (Baltrimantz), Vilna Governorate, Russian Empire (now Lithuania).
Married at age 17 and moved to Białystok, supported by his wife while he continued Torah study.
Became Rabbi of the non-Hasidic community in Dvinsk (Daugavpils, Latvia), serving 39 years.
Helped expose Shlomo Friedlander’s forged 'lost' tractates of the Jerusalem Talmud, proving them fabrications.
Participated in founding meetings of Agudath Yisrael in Bad Homburg, Germany.
Published 'Ohr Somayach' on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah, which gained wide acclaim.
Opposed secular Zionism but supported Religious Zionism after the Balfour Declaration, declaring the 'Three Oaths' no longer applied.
Died in Riga while seeking medical treatment. Buried in Daugavpils. Left no living descendants.

Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter.event: Born in Warsaw, Poland; orphaned young and raised by his grandfather, Rabbi Yitzchak Meir Alter (Chiddushei Harim).
At age 10, visited the Kotzker Rebbe with his grandfather, leaving a deep spiritual impression.
Married Yocheved Rivka, daughter of Yehuda Leib Kaminer. Changed his name to Yehudah Aryeh Leib to avoid duplication.
Declined to become Rebbe after the death of his grandfather. Leadership passed to Rabbi Chanokh Heynekh Levin of Aleksandrów.
Accepted leadership of Ger Hasidim after Rabbi Chanokh Heynekh's death. Began teaching Torah discourses that became the 'Sfas Emes.'
Suffered personal loss with the passing of his wife. A year later, a fire destroyed his home and Beit Midrash. Later remarried Reizel, daughter of Rabbi Baruch Halberstam.
During the Russo-Japanese War, corresponded with Hasidim drafted into the army, encouraging their spiritual growth.
Passed away on January 11 (5 Shevat 5665) at age 57. Funeral drew around 20,000 people despite overcrowded trains. Buried in Ger.
Succeeded by his son Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Alter (Imrei Emes). Some Hasidim followed his brother-in-law Rabbi Pinchas Menachem Justman of Piltz.
Teachings published posthumously as 'Sfas Emes,' which became a cornerstone of Hasidic thought.

ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ.event: ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ is born in Plungė (Plungyan), Lithuania, into the family of ר׳ שלמה זלמן זיו הורביץ. His birth year is reported variously as 1847, 1848 or 1850; this map uses the well-attested 1847 chronology. See the Posen Library biography and the National Library of Israel authority record.

As an adolescent, ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ receives an intensive traditional education associated with Kurtuvėnai and the Kelmė milieu and is already teaching by about sixteen. His father served in Kurtuvėnai. The displayed year is an approximate educational marker. See the Posen Library and biographical synthesis with cited references.

At about eighteen, ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ marries the daughter of ר׳ יעקב שטיין and assumes responsibility for his father-in-law’s prosperous textile business in Švėkšna. The year follows the approximate age given in the surviving biography. See the documented biographical summary.

Around age twenty-seven, ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ meets ר׳ ישראל סלנטר in Memel. The encounter persuades him to leave commercial life and devote himself to Torah and mussar, the decisive turn in his biography. The year is approximate. See the biographical account and Novardok Research Center overview.

ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ enters the Kovno Kollel Perushim and studies in the circle of ר׳ יצחק בלאזר, ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם and ר׳ אברהם שנקר. Following his first wife’s death, he also undertakes an extended period of seclusion and mussar discipline in Kovno. See the biographical synthesis and Novardok Research Center; the year is approximate.

Seeking sustained self-scrutiny away from public honor, ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ establishes a simple retreat in woodland near Dzyatlava and spends long periods there over roughly twelve years. Sources preserve the retreat more securely than its exact beginning; both the year and regional coordinate are approximate. See the biographical account.

ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו urges ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ to redirect his intense private discipline toward public education. He consequently begins establishing kollelim and yeshivot across the region. The early 1890s date is supported by the Posen Library; see also the Novardok Research Center.

ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ establishes the yeshiva at Navahrudak that becomes the central institution and namesake of his mussar movement. Its students combine demanding Torah study with organized ethical work, radical bitachon and exercises intended to break dependence on social approval. See the Novardok Yeshiva history, Posen Library and Novardok Research Center.

ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ.place: Navahrudak and the western Russian Empire
ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ.event: From the Navahrudak center, ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ develops an unusually expansive network of Novardok yeshivot and kollelim, with institutions reported in cities including Dvinsk, Minsk, Warsaw, Berdychiv, Odessa and Lida. This is a representative network marker, not a claim that every foundation occurred in 1908. See the Posen Library and Novardok Research Center.

The First World War displaces the Novardok network eastward. ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ regroups students in Homel and continues founding and sustaining yeshivot despite hunger, epidemic and military disruption. Sources variously place the move in 1914 or 1915; this map uses 1915. See the biographical account and Novardok Research Center.

ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ reaches Kyiv amid revolution and civil war and establishes additional centers for displaced students. Accounts describe four yeshivot created in the city; the exact transition from Homel is variously dated 1917–1918. See the biographical synthesis and Novardok Research Center.

After personally tending students during a typhus epidemic, ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ contracts the disease and dies in Kyiv on 17 Kislev 5680 (9 December 1919). His teachings are subsequently preserved by disciples in מדרגת האדם. His remains were reinterred at Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem in 1963, a posthumous fact deliberately kept out of the movement chronology. See the biographical account, the National Library of Israel and the catalogued biography by ר׳ דב כץ.

R' Chaim HaLevi Soloveitchik (Rav Chaim.event: Born in Volozhin as the second son of Rabbi Yosef Dov (Beis HaLevi) Soloveitchik and Zirl née Efron.
As a youth, followed his father to Slutsk, where he studied under Rabbi Mendel of Slutsk.
Returned to Volozhin; at age 27 became Rosh Yeshiva as Deputy Netziv.
With the closure of the Volozhin Yeshiva, appointed rabbi of Brisk, where he led the community until his passing.
Passed away in Otwock, Poland; buried in the Jewish cemetery of Warsaw next to his wife's grandfather, the Netziv.

ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין.event: ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין was born on 4 Cheshvan 5616 (16 October 1855) in Kock, in the home of his maternal grandfather ר׳ מנחם מנדל מורגנשטרן. His father ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין was then supported in his father-in-law’s household. Some modern summaries misconvert the Hebrew year as 1856. Sochaczew memorial book; Sochaczew municipal history

At approximately eight years old, ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין moved with his family to Parczew when his father ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין accepted the town’s rabbinate. He received his education chiefly from his father and remained closely attached to him throughout their later moves. Hebrew biography; Sochaczew memorial book

ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין accompanied his father’s household to Krośniewice, another of the rabbinates in which his youth and intensive study under ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין unfolded. The precise year is approximate because accessible biographical summaries establish the sequence more securely than the date. Sochaczew memorial book; Polish-Jewish historical guide

ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין, by then married to Yuta Leah Litmanowicz, moved with his father’s household to Nasielsk when ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין assumed its rabbinate. His son and eventual successor ר׳ דוד בורנשטיין was born there. Sochaczew memorial book; Chronology of the father’s rabbinates

ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין settled with his family in Sochaczew when ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין became the city’s rabbi. He lived in a separate house near his father, taught disciples, and participated in the yeshiva and emerging Sochatchov court. Sochaczew memorial book; City of Sochaczew

Acting for his father, ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין travelled to Ottoman Palestine to investigate purchasing land for an observant agricultural settlement. The mission failed because Ottoman rules prevented the proposed acquisition by foreign subjects. The available account establishes travel to the Land of Israel but not every stop, so the marker is regional to Jerusalem rather than tied to an invented parcel. Herzog College pedagogy article

Following the death of ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין, ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין was installed as the second Sochatchover Rebbe and assumed leadership of the Sochaczew yeshiva. He initially hesitated because communal leadership would reduce his uninterrupted study, but senior disciples pressed him to succeed his father. Hebrew biography; City of Sochaczew

After wartime detention in Germany as a Russian subject and the German army’s destruction of Sochaczew, ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין could not restore his court in the devastated city and re-established it in Łódź. The unknown German detention site is not plotted as a separate movement. Hebrew biographical study; Dynastic chronology

Finding crowded industrial Łódź burdensome to his health and study, ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין moved his court to nearby Zgierz. The Sochatchov centre followed him there, and he established a study hall and later a yeshiva while continuing to hope for a return to Sochaczew. Polish-Jewish historical guide; Sochaczew municipal history

Because of declining health, ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין was taken to the resort town of Otwock, where he died on 24 Tevet 5686 (10 January 1926). His body was then returned to Sochaczew for burial beside his father; this marker represents the place of death. Hebrew biography; Sochaczew memorial book

ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין was buried in the Bornsztain ohel in the Jewish cemetery on Sierpniowa Street, Sochaczew, beside ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין. The cemetery and ohel were devastated during the Holocaust; the ohel was reconstructed in the early 1990s. The marker is cemetery-level rather than an asserted grave-level point. ESJF cemetery survey; International Jewish Cemetery Project

Joseph Rosen.event: Born in Rogachov (Rahachow, Belarus) into a Chabad-Kapust Hasidic family; educated in local cheder.
At age 13, studied under Rabbi Yosef Dov Soloveitchik (Beis Halevi) in Slutsk alongside Chaim Soloveitchik.
Continued studies in Shklov under Rabbi Yehoshua Leib Diskin (Maharil Diskin).
Appointed rabbi of the Hasidic community in Dvinsk (Daugavpils, Latvia), serving nearly 50 years. His counterpart was Rabbi Meir Simcha of Dvinsk.
Gained reputation as one of the greatest halachic authorities of the era, writing responsa rooted in Rambam and Rishonim.
Granted semicha (ordination) to leading rabbis across Europe and America, including future figures such as Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson.
Began publishing his magnum opus, 'Tzofnath Paneach', on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah, along with responsa volumes.
Died in Vienna on 5 March 1936 at a sanatorium; body transported to Dvinsk for burial.

Rabbi Baruch HaLevi Epstein.event: Born in Novogrudok to Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein (Aruch HaShulchan) and Michla, sister of the Netziv.
At age 13 began studies at the Volozhin Yeshiva, where he was considered a prodigy; studied for five years.
Married the daughter of Rabbi Elazar Moshe HaLevi Horowitz, rabbi of Pinsk, and settled there; studied Torah and general sciences in his father-in-law’s home.
Studied at the Academy of Commerce in Vienna, broadening his education.
Returned to Pinsk, worked as chief bookkeeper and later bank manager; continued writing and study of Torah.
Traveled to the United States to publish and distribute his writings; remained until 1926 before returning to Pinsk.
Died in Pinsk during the Holocaust; buried in Karlin cemetery.

Rabbi Shimon Yehuda Shkop.event: Born in Torez (then Russian Empire, today Ukraine).
At age 12 began study at Mir Yeshiva; remained there for 2 years.
Moved to Volozhin Yeshiva; studied under the Netziv for 6 years and joined Rav Chaim Soloveitchik’s chaburah.
Appointed rosh mesivta at Telz Yeshiva, serving 18 years and developing the 'Telz derech' in learning.
Appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Sha'ar HaTorah in Grodno.
Visited United States to raise funds; lectured at Yeshiva University and briefly served as Rosh Yeshiva at RIETS.
Returned to Grodno and resumed leadership of Sha'ar HaTorah.
Died in Grodno as Russian army approached; buried in Grodno Jewish cemetery.

Sholom Dovber Schneersohn.event: Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn is born in Lubavitch, the son of the fourth Chabad Rebbe, Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn (the Maharash).
Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn marries Rebbetzin Shterna Sarah, his cousin and granddaughter of the Tzemach Tzedek.
Following the passing of his father, Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, he gradually assumes increasing leadership responsibilities within the Chabad movement.
Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn formally accepts leadership as the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe.
He founds the famous Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in Lubavitch, creating the first major Chassidic yeshiva combining advanced Talmud study with systematic Chassidic learning.
The Rebbe Rashab establishes Jewish industrial and economic support initiatives to strengthen impoverished Jewish communities within the Russian Empire.
Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn becomes active in communal efforts to combat pogroms and support Jewish communities during the upheavals of the Russian Revolution of 1905.
As World War I approaches Lubavitch, the Rebbe Rashab relocates the Chabad leadership to Rostov-on-Don.
Following the Bolshevik Revolution, he begins organizing resistance to Communist attempts to suppress Jewish religious life.
Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn passes away in Rostov-on-Don and is succeeded by his son, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn.

Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz.event: Born in Slutsk (near Vilna region, present-day Belarus/Lithuania).
Became a student of Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik in Volozhin Yeshiva.
Served as rosh yeshiva in Halusk and later in Vilna.
Established the Kamenitz Yeshiva after World War I.
Passed away in Vilna just before World War II; his yeshiva students were later murdered in the Holocaust.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Iwye, Vilna Governorate, Russian Empire; now Iŭje, Belarus
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי is born on 9 Elul 5623 (24 August 1863) in Iwye. His father, ר׳ דוד שלמה גרודזינסקי, serves as the town’s rabbi for more than forty years, following an earlier family tradition of local rabbinic leadership. See the Association of Jews of Vilna biography, National Library of Israel authority record and Volozhin Yeshiva biography.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Eishyshok, Vilna Governorate, Russian Empire; now Eišiškės, Lithuania
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: At about twelve, ר׳ חיים עוזר leaves Iwye to study with the perushim, the advanced scholars of Eishyshok, and celebrates his bar mitzvah there. The move marks his entry into the wider Lithuanian Torah-study network. See the Association of Jews of Vilna and the Volozhin Yeshiva biography.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Volozhin Yeshiva, Volozhin, Russian Empire; now Belarus
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: At fifteen, ר׳ חיים עוזר enters the Volozhin Yeshiva. He studies in the circle of ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין and is accepted into the advanced shiur of ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, whose conceptual method profoundly shapes his later responsa. See the Volozhin Yeshiva biography and the Association of Jews of Vilna.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Vilna, Russian Empire; now Vilnius, Lithuania
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: Around age twenty, ר׳ חיים עוזר marries Leah, daughter of Vilna dayan ר׳ אליהו אליעזר גרודזינסקי and granddaughter of ר׳ ישראל מסלנט. He settles in Vilna and enters its dense network of batei midrash, rabbinical courts and charitable institutions. See the Association of Jews of Vilna biography and the Hebrew biographical compilation.

Following the sudden death of his father-in-law, ר׳ חיים עוזר joins the Vilna beit din as a dayan at roughly twenty-three. He eventually becomes its dominant halakhic authority, although Vilna’s fragmented communal structure makes the simplified title ‘chief rabbi’ historically imprecise. See the Association of Jews of Vilna and the CET–Yad Vashem educational biography.

ר׳ חיים עוזר establishes an advanced scholars’ kibbutz at the Gaon’s kloyz and supports the Ramailes Yeshiva. After the death of ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור, his role increasingly extends from local adjudication to international responsa and Russian Jewish communal policy. See the Hebrew biographical compilation and the Vilna Jewish association.

ר׳ חיים עוזר participates in Orthodox organizational discussions in Hamburg that precede the creation of Agudath Israel. The meeting reflects his effort to coordinate traditional communities across imperial borders amid Zionist, socialist and modernizing movements. See the Association of Jews of Vilna biography.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Kattowitz, German Empire; now Katowice, Poland
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: At Agudath Israel’s founding conference, ר׳ חיים עוזר becomes a central member of its Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah. His participation gives the new transnational organization Lithuanian rabbinic standing, though he continues to act through Vilna’s own institutions. See the Association of Jews of Vilna and the National Library of Israel.

The first volume of שו״ת אחיעזר appears in Vilna. Published volumes through 1939 establish ר׳ חיים עוזר as a major twentieth-century decisor, applying rigorous Talmudic analysis to ritual, civil, family and communal questions. See the Otzar HaHochma bibliographic catalogue, bibliographic record for אחיעזר and the Vilna biography.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Grodno, Second Polish Republic; now Hrodna, Belarus
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: At a rabbinical convention in Grodno, ר׳ חיים עוזר and ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן sponsor the Vaad Hayeshivot. He is appointed its leader, and its Vilna office coordinates fundraising, grants and oversight for dozens of yeshivot across the eastern Polish provinces. See the YIVO Archives finding aid and the Vaad Hayeshivot collection description.

After the Nazi takeover in Germany, ר׳ חיים עוזר issues an appeal describing the unprecedented danger and raising assistance for German Jewish refugees. His surviving letters document aid to individuals and communities as well as yeshiva finance. See his 21 November 1933 Call for the Assistance of the Refugees from Germany and the National Library of Israel archive description.

ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.place: Vilna, successively Polish, Soviet-occupied and Lithuanian territory
ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי.event: Following the German and Soviet invasion of Poland, ר׳ חיים עוזר urges yeshivot trapped in occupied eastern Poland to gather in Vilna, anticipating its transfer to neutral Lithuania. Thousands of refugees arrive; he and the Vaad distribute students among communities and organize food, lodging and institutional support. See the YIVO Vaad Hayeshivot records, the CET–Yad Vashem biography and the Vilna Jewish association.

As Soviet rule closes or threatens religious institutions, ר׳ חיים עוזר insists that yeshiva study continue and remains involved in refugee relief despite illness. He dies on 5 Av 5700 (9 August 1940) and is buried in Vilna’s new Jewish cemetery. See the CET–Yad Vashem educational biography, National Library of Israel and the Association of Jews of Vilna.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.place: Grīva, beside Dvinsk; now Daugavpils, Latvia
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.event: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק is born on 16 Elul 5625 (7 September 1865) in Grīva, across the Daugava from Dvinsk, to ר׳ שלמה זלמן קוק and Perel Zlata Felman. See the National Library of Israel and Rav Kook chronology.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.place: Volozhin, Russian Empire; now Valozhyn, Belarus
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.event: At about eighteen, ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק enters the Volozhin yeshivah and studies for roughly eighteen months under ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין. See the Rav Kook chronology and Yeshivat Har Etzion.
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק marries Batsheva, daughter of the Panevėžys rabbi ר׳ אליהו דוד רבינוביץ׳-תאומים (the Aderet), and continues advanced study near his new family. See the Rav Kook chronology.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק accepts his first communal rabbinate in Žeimelis and launches the rabbinic periodical עיטור סופרים. After Batsheva dies in 1889, he later marries Raiza-Rivka, daughter of the Aderet’s twin brother ר׳ צבי יהודה רבינוביץ׳-תאומים. See the National Library archive and Yeshivat Har Etzion.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק becomes rabbi of Bauska and remains there until his 1904 aliyah. His rulings and correspondence establish him as a distinctive halakhic and spiritual voice. See Yeshivat Har Etzion and the National Library of Israel.

In May 1904 ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק arrives in Jaffa as rabbi of the city and the surrounding Jewish agricultural settlements. He founds a yeshivah and develops rulings for renewed agricultural life in the Land of Israel. See the National Library archive and Yeshivat Har Etzion.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.place: Galilee agricultural settlements; representative marker at Merhavia
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.event: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק joins the first rabbinic tour of Jewish agricultural settlements, travelling through Galilee and the valleys to connect the rabbinate with largely secular pioneers. This marker represents a multi-stop journey, not a residence. See the National Library archive.

Travelling to Europe for the planned Agudat Israel conference, ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק is stranded by the First World War. Unable to return to Ottoman Palestine as a Russian subject, he spends the first phase of exile in St Gallen. See Mercaz HaRav and Yeshivat Har Etzion.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.place: Machzike Hadath, Brick Lane and Fournier Street, Spitalfields, London
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.event: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק becomes rav of Machzike Hadath, the Spitalfields Great Synagogue, serving until 1919 on condition that he may return to Jaffa after the war. He advocates publicly for a Jewish national home during the period of the Balfour Declaration. See the congregation’s official history and Encyclopaedia Judaica.
After the war, ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק returns to the Land of Israel and becomes Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Jerusalem. See the Rav Kook chronology and National Library of Israel.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק helps establish the Chief Rabbinate and becomes the first Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Mandatory Palestine, serving alongside Sephardi chief rabbi ר׳ יעקב מאיר. See the Rav Kook chronology and a National Library archival record.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.place: Beit HaRav, 9 HaRav Kook Street, Jerusalem
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.event: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק moves into Beit HaRav, which serves as his home, study hall and public headquarters from 1923 until his death. See the Beit HaRav–HaOrot foundation and site history.

At Beit HaRav, ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק founds the Central Universal Yeshivah, soon known as Mercaz HaRav, joining advanced Torah learning, Hebrew revival and preparation for religious national leadership. See the official Mercaz HaRav biography.

ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.place: Jerusalem and Mount of Olives Cemetery
ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק.event: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק dies in Jerusalem on 3 Elul 5695 (1 September 1935) and is buried in the Jewish cemetery on the Mount of Olives. His students continue publishing his notebooks, responsa and correspondence. See the Rav Kook chronology and National Library of Israel.

ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר (Imrei Emes).event: Born in Góra Kalwaria (Ger), Poland, son of the Sfas Emes (Rav Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter).
Succeeded his father, the Sfas Emes, as the Gerrer Rebbe, attracting tens of thousands of chasidim.
Led Ger through World War I; many chasidim displaced and Ger institutions suffered, but the Rebbe rebuilt the community.
Escaped Nazi-occupied Poland at the outbreak of World War II, fleeing through Lithuania and eventually reaching Palestine.
Settled in Jerusalem, reestablishing Ger Hasidut in Eretz Yisrael and leading Holocaust survivors.
Passed away in Jerusalem during Israel’s War of Independence; tens of thousands attended his funeral.

Chaim Elazar Spira.event: Born in Strzyżów, Galicia, Austria-Hungary, into the Spira rabbinic family.
Appointed Chief Justice of the Rabbinical Court in Munkács, serving alongside his father Rabbi Tzvi Hersh Spira.
Succeeded his father as Chief Rabbi of Munkács and the surrounding region.
Founded the 'Darchei Teshuva' yeshiva and Machzike Torah schools in Munkács.
Traveled to Mandatory Palestine; met privately with the kabbalist Rabbi Solomon Eliezer Alfandari for a week.
His daughter Chaya Fruma Rivka married Rabbi Baruch Yehoshua Yerachmiel Rabinowicz in a celebrated wedding attended by over 20,000 people.
Passed away on May 13 in Munkács; succeeded by his son-in-law Rabbi Baruch Yehoshua Yerachmiel Rabinowicz.

איסר זלמן מלצר (Isser Zalman Meltzer).event: Born in Mir, Lithuania (then Russian Empire).
Studied in the Volozhin Yeshiva under Rav Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin (Netziv) and Rav Chaim Soloveitchik.
Married and became Rosh Yeshiva in Slutsk, establishing a major Lithuanian yeshiva.
Immigrated to Eretz Yisrael; appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Etz Chaim in Jerusalem.
Published *Even HaEzel*, his monumental commentary on the Rambam’s Mishneh Torah.
Passed away in Jerusalem; buried on Har HaMenuchot.

R'Moshe Rosen.event: R'Moshe Rosen born in Brańsk, Grodno Governorate, Poland. He learns in various schools before studying on his own.
R'Moshe Rosen studies in Kovno Kollel and gets Smicha from R'Yizchak Elchanan Spektor and Moshe Danishevsky.
R'Moshe Rosen immigrates to the United States and becomes a teacher at Mesivta Torah v'Daat.
R'Moshe Rosen becomes a Rav in Brooklyn.

ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.event: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר is born in Baghdad around 1870 to ר׳ יצחק ברוך סופר and Esther. The displayed year follows the majority modern dating; the National Library authority allows 1869 or 1870, and some later traditions give 1867. See the National Library of Israel authority record and the German biographical summary.

ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.place: Beit Zilkha Yeshivah, Baghdad, Ottoman Iraq; year approximate
ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.event: In Baghdad, the young ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר studies at Beit Zilkha under ר׳ עבדאללה סומך and is shaped by the teaching and customs of ר׳ יוסף חיים, the Ben Ish Chai. The sources establish these teachers but not a precise enrollment year, so 1885 is an approximate educational marker. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography and biographical references collected here.

ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.place: Beit El Synagogue, Old City of Jerusalem, Ottoman Palestine
ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.event: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר travels from Iraq to Ottoman Palestine with Iraqi colleagues, visits holy sites and decides to settle permanently in Jerusalem. He joins the kabbalistic study circle at Beit El and is also associated with Rehovot HaNahar under ר׳ חיים שאול דוויק הכהן. See the biographical account and the study of the Ben Ish Chai's circle.

ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.place: Shoshanim LeDavid Synagogue and Yeshivah, 46 Rabbi Sonnenfeld Street, Jerusalem
ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.event: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר moves his principal study and teaching to the Iraqi synagogue and yeshivah Shoshanim LeDavid. He writes his major works here and serves as a leading scholar of Jerusalem's Babylonian community. The marker is placed on the building at 46 Rabbi Sonnenfeld Street. See the synagogue history and coordinates and his biography.

The first complete volume of כף החיים, covering Orach Chayim 1–88, appears in Jerusalem. Further Orach Chayim volumes follow in 1913, 1915, 1920, 1924, 1928, 1931 and 1933, making the work a sustained Jerusalem publishing project rather than a single-date publication. See the first-edition bibliographic description.

ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר publishes the first Yoreh De'ah volume of כף החיים. He dies before completing the next volume; it is later issued from his manuscript with a concluding section supplied by ר׳ עובדיה יוסף. See the edition record and the manuscript discussion.

ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.place: Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery, Jerusalem
ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר.event: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר dies in Jerusalem on 9 Sivan 5699 (27 May 1939), aged about sixty-nine, and is buried on the Mount of Olives. See the Hebrew biographical entry and the National Library authority record.

Joseph Herman Hertz.event: Born in Rebrín/Rebrény, Kingdom of Hungary (now Slovakia).
Emigrated with family to New York City.
Graduated as the first rabbinical graduate of the Jewish Theological Seminary of America.
Moved to Johannesburg, South Africa, as rabbi of Witwatersrand Old Hebrew Congregation. Advocated Jewish and Catholic civil rights.
Professor of Philosophy at Transvaal University College (later University of the Witwatersrand).
Returned to New York as rabbi of Orach Chayim Congregation.
Elected Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the British Empire.
Began his 'Imperial tour' — first visiting South Africa (66,000 Jews).
Visited Australia and New Zealand Jewish communities during his Imperial tour.
Concluded Imperial tour in Canada, addressing major communities in Montreal, Toronto, and Halifax.
After his tour, met King George V at Buckingham Palace to report on Jewish communities across the Empire.
Became vocal supporter of Zionism and strong opponent of Reform and Liberal Judaism.
Mobilized worldwide Jewish and Christian opposition to League of Nations calendar reform proposal.
Served as Acting Principal of Jews' College during WWII.
Co-founded the Council of Christians and Jews with Archbishop of Canterbury William Temple.
Died in office and was buried in Willesden United Synagogue Cemetery, London.

Elchonon Bunim Wasserman.event: Born in Biržai (Birz), Lithuania, to Naftali Beinish and Sheina Rakhel.
Family moved to Bauska, Latvia. At age 15 entered Telshe Yeshiva, studying under Rav Eliezer Gordon and Rav Shimon Shkop.
During school breaks in Bauska, attended shiurim from Rav Avraham Yitzchak Kook, rabbi of the city.
Studied in Brisk under Rav Chaim Soloveitchik for two years.
Married Michla Atlas, daughter of Rabbi Meir Atlas of Salantai. Lived in Salantai, dedicating years to Torah study.
Founded a mesivta in Mstislavl with Yoel Baranchik, earning reputation as a great teacher.
Joined the Chofetz Chaim’s Kollel Kodshim in Radin; studied intensely with Rav Yosef Shlomo Kahaneman.
Appointed rosh yeshiva in Brest-Litovsk at the urging of the Chofetz Chaim.
World War I scattered the yeshiva. Fled with the Chofetz Chaim and reestablished in Smilavichy, where he became rosh yeshiva.
Settled in Baranovichi, Poland, and became rosh yeshiva of Ohel Torah-Baranovich, which grew to nearly 300 students.
Spent 17 months in the U.S. raising funds and inspiring communities, collecting about $10,000 for his yeshiva.
Returned to Poland despite danger, unwilling to abandon his yeshiva. Criticized American institutions as spiritually weak.
Fled to Vilnius during Nazi invasion, continuing to lead his students in exile.
Arrested in Kaunas with 12 other rabbis. Murdered at the Seventh Fort on July 6, 1941 (11 Tammuz 5701). Urged repentance before death.
Remembered as spiritual heir to the Chofetz Chaim. His lectures circulated widely, and his surviving sons continued his legacy.

ירוחם ליבוביץ (Yerucham Levovitz).event: R' Yerucham Levovitz Born in Lyduokiai/Luban (near Kelm, Lithuania).
R' Yerucham Levovitz goes to study in Slabodka and becomes a talmid of the Altar of Slabodka.

R' Yerucham Levovitz goes to study in Kelm, after 6 years in Slabodka. He describes this period of time in detail in his shiurim and writings. He writes he wept for a whole night when the Altar of Kelm passed away shortly after and he felt his whole understanding came from then. He learns b'chavruta with R'Naftali Trop for 10 years.
R' Yerucham Levovitz goes to Uzvant to help his wife running a shop.
R' Yerucham Levovitz is hired as mashgiach for the Radun Yeshivah and becomes very popular for his charisma and shiurim.

R' Yerucham Levovitz leaves the Radun Yeshivah. He does so as there was a risk of him eclipsing the Chofetz Chaim, and out of his immense respect for the Chafetz Chaim he leaves. His Rebbeim in Kelm encourage him to take a position in Mir Yeshivah which also had recently become a mussar style Yeshivah.
R' Yerucham Levovitz moves with the Mir Yeshivah to Poltava. His family remains in Uzvant.

R' Yerucham Levovitz crosses at some point back to visit his family (on the German side). Sometime around this he meets the Altar of Novardok and they have a famous conversation. He is unable to return however and does not return to the Yeshiva for several years.
R' Yerucham Levovitz becomes Mashgiach in Ponovezh Yeshivah.
R' Yerucham Levovitz becomes Mashgiach in Slabodka building a new Yeshivah in the wake of the first world war chaos.

R' Yerucham Levovitz returns to Kelm to support the Yeshivah there. He debated there with R'Reuvan Dov Dessler whether Kelm should be kept elite or whether they should bring down the message to the lower level. R' Yerucham Levovitz moves on because of this debate.

R' Yerucham Levovitz returns to the Mir and tries to give the ideas he had learnt from Kelm and his wanderings to the students in the last 12 years of his life. These are often referred to as the golden age of the Mir Yeshiva.
R' Yerucham Levovitz passed away in Mir, Belarus.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Grajewo, Łomża Governorate, Russian Empire; now Poland
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן is born in Grajewo to Yaakov and Frida Lopian. The National Library authority record and most published biographies use 1876; an alternative tradition argues for 1872, so no exact civil birth date is asserted. The coordinate is town-level because the family home has not been securely identified. See the National Library of Israel authority record and ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Łomża, Łomża Governorate, Russian Empire; now Poland
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: When his family emigrates to the United States, the young ר׳ אליהו לופיאן chooses to remain in Łomża so that he can continue intensive Torah study. He studies first in the junior framework and then in the main Łomża yeshiva under ר׳ אליעזר שולביץ, enduring serious poverty. Sources variously say he was nine or ten, so 1886 is an approximate marker. See ויקישיבה and ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Kelmė, Kovno Governorate, Russian Empire; now Lithuania
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן enters the Kelm Talmud Torah and studies the disciplined Mussar method under ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו and ר׳ יצחק בלאזר. Since sources say that he studied with ר׳ שמחה זיסל for more than a year before the latter's death in 1898, 1897 is an approximate but evidence-based marker. He also marries Sarah Leah, daughter of ר׳ יצחק דוד רוטמן, a Kelm disciple. See ויקיפדיה העברית and Encyclopaedia Judaica's biographical entry.

During the First World War, ר׳ אליהו לופיאן remains in Kelm with students and continues teaching while much of the population disperses. After the war he travels among Lithuanian towns to give Mussar talks and persuade former students to return, helping re-establish the Kelm institution that he had led with ר׳ יוסף לייב ננדיק. See ויקיפדיה העברית and ויקישיבה.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Etz Chaim Yeshiva, Thrawl Street, Whitechapel, London
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן settles in London and joins Etz Chaim Yeshiva as its Mussar educator and senior rabbinic leader, working alongside ר׳ נחמן שלמה גרינשפן. Sources disagree over whether his appointment/arrival should be dated 1926 or 1928; the institution's Thrawl Street premises were consecrated in 1926, and reference works date his appointment to that year, while the standard English biography gives immigration in 1928. The marker is placed on Thrawl Street rather than at a generic London coordinate. See the Orthodox Union biography, Encyclopaedia Judaica, and the surviving 1940 Etz Chaim magazine.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן immigrates from Britain to Israel in 1950 and initially settles in Jerusalem. He delivers influential Mussar talks at the Zikhron Moshe and Kelilat Shaul synagogues and is associated with Kamenitz Yeshiva; contemporary newspaper notices also record his teaching activity in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv. See ויקיפדיה העברית and the surviving visa correspondence.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Knesses Chizkiyahu Yeshiva, Zikhron Ya'akov, Israel
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: At approximately seventy-five, ר׳ אליהו לופיאן accepts appointment as mashgiach ruchani of Knesses Chizkiyahu in Zikhron Ya'akov. Before accepting, he consults ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ, whose blessing 'עוד ינובון בשיבה' encourages him to continue public teaching in old age. See Dirshu's account and ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Knesses Chizkiyahu Yeshiva, Kfar Hasidim–Rekhasim, Israel
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: When Knesses Chizkiyahu transfers from Zikhron Ya'akov to its new campus beside Kfar Hasidim in April 1955, ר׳ אליהו לופיאן moves with the yeshiva and continues as its revered spiritual director. After the sudden death of rosh yeshiva ר׳ נח שימונוביץ, he helps stabilize the institution and supports the appointment of ר׳ אליהו מישקובסקי. The coordinate follows the documented yeshiva location, not the center of Haifa. See the institutional history and ויקישיבה.

In his final years, ר׳ אליהו לופיאן lives in Jerusalem's Bayit VeGan neighborhood with his daughter Chaya Ita and son-in-law ר׳ קלמן עזריאל פינסקי, while remaining closely identified with Knesses Chizkiyahu. The year is approximate because the source describes his last years without supplying a moving date. See ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.place: Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery
ר׳ אליהו לופיאן.event: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן dies in Jerusalem on 21 September 1970, corresponding to 20 Elul 5730, aged about ninety-four under the canonical 1876 chronology. He is buried in the Jewish cemetery on the Mount of Olives. See the National Library of Israel authority record, the Hebrew biography and contemporary newspaper reference, and the English biographical record.

R' Avraham Yeshaya Karelitz.event: Chazon Ish born in Kossow, near Grodno (present-day Belarus). His youth is spent with private teachers and individual study apart from a few unsuccessful stints in Yeshivah.
Chazon Ish spends a short stint in Vilna studying under R' Chaim Ozer Grodzinski.
Chazon Ish marries and settles in Kovidan, where his wife opens a fabric shop. He writes this period was his golden period of uninterrupted Torah study. His chavruta was R' Moshe Rozin
Chazon Ish with many other Jews flee from the battle areas and settle in Soybtz.
Chazon Ish moves to Minsk with his wife following soon after.
Chazon Ish immigrates to Eretz Yisrael; settles in Bnei Brak, becoming its spiritual leader.
Chazon Ish passes away in Bnei Brak; tens of thousands attend his funeral. Buried in Bnei Brak, revered as the guiding spirit of Torah Jewry in Israel.

Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Finkel.event: Born in Kelm, Lithuania, to Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel (the Alter of Slabodka).
Family moved to Slobodka, where his father established Yeshivat Knesset Yisrael.
Studied in Brisk under Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik.
Sent by his father to join the new Slutsk Yeshiva under Rabbi Yaakov Dovid Willowski (Ridvaz).
Married Malka, daughter of Rabbi Eliyahu Baruch Kamai, Rosh Yeshiva of Mir.
During WWI, led the Mir Yeshiva in exile in Poltava, Ukraine.
Became Rosh Yeshiva of Mir following the death of his father-in-law Rabbi Eliyahu Baruch Kamai.
Escaped war-torn Europe and settled in Jerusalem, reestablishing the Mir Yeshiva.
Passed away in Jerusalem; buried on Har HaMenuchot.

Rabbi Moshe Soloveichik.event: Born in Volozhin, Belarus, to Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik.
Appointed rabbi of Raseiniai, Lithuania, and dean of a yeshiva.
Moved to Warsaw; became director of Talmud studies at Tachkemoni Seminary.
Immigrated to New York; became Rosh Yeshiva at RIETS, Yeshiva University.
Passed away in New York City; funeral attended by 4,000 mourners.

ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר.event: ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר is born in Slabodka beside Kovno in approximately 1878 or 1879. Encyclopaedia Judaica and manuscript catalogues use 1879; JCR-UK gives 18 September 1878. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the JCR-UK minister profile and the National Library archive.

As a young scholar, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר studies in the Lithuanian yeshiva world. Biographical and manuscript sources connect him with ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור, ר׳ יצחק בלאזר and ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם; the displayed year is an approximate educational marker rather than a documented enrollment date. See the specialist Kedem manuscript description.

After migrating to Britain in 1910 or 1911, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר teaches Talmud in Manchester and is associated with the foundation or early leadership of its yeshiva. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates his settlement in England to 1911, while the National Library and manuscript sources use 1910. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, Kedem and the JCR-UK profile.

In July 1913, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר becomes rabbi of the West End Talmud Torah Synagogue in Soho, later known as the West End Great Synagogue. He will serve this immigrant congregation for more than forty years. See JCR-UK and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

During the First World War years in London, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר forms a close relationship with ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק. Their surviving correspondence reflects rabbinic cooperation and friendship; a 1921 recommendation from ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק is preserved in the archive. See the National Library of Israel archive description.

While serving in London, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר begins publishing כרם הצבי, his principal halakhic and aggadic commentary on the Torah. The first volume was printed in Vienna, but that publication location is not evidence that he personally relocated there. The Torah series continued through 1938. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the description of his autograph manuscript at Kedem.

ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר publishes בירור הלכה, addressing the halakhic consequences of civil marriage and divorce. Archival papers preserve the rabbinic controversy generated by the work, making this an unusually well-documented episode in his legal career. See the National Library of Israel archive.

Around 1947, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר drafts צהלת הצבי; portions are later printed in ספר המועדים (London, 1950). Surviving autograph leaves, drafts and letters reveal an active working scholar rather than only a public preacher. See the manuscript description and dating.

After more than four decades at the West End congregation, ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר retires in 1954 or 1955. The one-year discrepancy reflects differing institutional summaries, not a second appointment. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the JCR-UK profile.

ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר dies in London in November 1966 after a career joining Lithuanian rabbinic learning to the institutions of immigrant British Orthodoxy. Encyclopaedia Judaica and manuscript specialists give 1966; the National Library authority heading's 1967 endpoint is retained as a catalogue variant in this record's date note. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, Kedem and the National Library archive.

R'Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn.event: Born in Lyubavichi, Russian Empire, only son of Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (the Rashab).
At age 15, became secretary to his father and represented him at major Jewish conferences.
Married Nechama Dina Schneersohn, his second cousin and granddaughter of the Tzemach Tzedek.
Appointed head of Tomchei Temimim yeshiva network.
Organized kosher food and supplies for Jewish conscripts during the Russo-Japanese War.
Traveled to Germany and the Netherlands to persuade leaders to intervene against pogroms.
Between 1902–1911, arrested four times by Czarist police for Jewish activism.
Succeeded his father, becoming the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe.
Established the Tomchei Temimim in Warsaw.
Expelled from Rostov by Soviet authorities; settled in Leningrad.
Arrested by Soviet secret police, sentenced to death; commuted to exile in Kostroma, then released under international pressure. Departed for Riga.
Visited Palestine, then toured the U.S. to raise awareness for Soviet Jewry; met President Herbert Hoover.
Toured the U.S. to raise awareness for Soviet Jewry; met President Herbert Hoover.
He returned to Riga in 1930.
Settled in Warsaw, continued leadership and yeshiva activities until WWII.
Rescued from Nazi-occupied Warsaw through U.S. diplomatic intervention. Arrived in New York on March 19.
Established Lubavitch headquarters in Brooklyn; declared 'America is no different' and founded yeshivot and schools.
Arranged U.S. visa for his son-in-law, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, rescuing him from Nazi-occupied France.
Founded Kfar Chabad in Israel as a Chabad village near Tel Aviv.
Died January 28 in Brooklyn; buried at Montefiore Cemetery in Queens, later known as 'The Ohel.'
Succeeded by his son-in-law, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, as the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe.

ר׳ יחיאל יעקב וויינברג (Yechiel Yaakov W.event: Born in Ivie, Lithuania (then Russian Empire).
Studied in Slabodka Yeshiva under the Alter of Slabodka and became close with leading Lithuanian Torah figures.
Served as dayan in Vilna, earning reputation for halachic brilliance.
Appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary in Berlin, teaching a generation of European rabbis.
Arrested by Nazis and imprisoned; later released through international intervention. Survived the war in Switzerland.
Settled in Montreux, Switzerland, where he became a central halachic authority for post-Holocaust European Jewry.
Passed away in Montreux, Switzerland. Buried in Jerusalem; his responsa Seridei Eish became a cornerstone of 20th-century halachic thought.

ר׳ אריה לוין.place: Orla near Białystok, Russian Empire; now Poland
ר׳ אריה לוין.event: ר׳ אריה לוין is born on 22 March 1885 in Orla near Białystok to Binyamin Beinush and Ethel. The town then lay in the Pale of Settlement of the Russian Empire and is now in Poland. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center, the Lehi Heritage Association biography, and the National Library archival record.

ר׳ אריה לוין.place: Hlyusk, Minsk Governorate, Russian Empire; date approximate
ר׳ אריה לוין.event: After periods of study in Slutsk, Slonim, Brest and Pinsk, the young ר׳ אריה לוין studies in Hlyusk under ר׳ ברוך דב ליבוביץ. The source establishes his sequence of yeshivot but not a complete year-by-year itinerary, so 1899 is an approximate map marker. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center biography.

ר׳ אריה לוין.place: Volozhin, Russian Empire; now Valozhyn, Belarus
ר׳ אריה לוין.event: Having initially been refused because of his youth, ר׳ אריה לוין is accepted into the Volozhin yeshivah and studies under ר׳ רפאל שפירא. The exact admission year is not supplied by the heritage biography, making 1901 an approximate marker. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center.

ר׳ אריה לוין immigrates to Ottoman Palestine in 1905 and lands at Jaffa. There he meets ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק, beginning a close relationship that shapes his religious and communal life. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the Lehi Heritage Association.

Soon after arriving, ר׳ אריה לוין settles in Jerusalem, studies at Yeshivat Torat Chaim and marries Tzipora Chana, daughter of ר׳ דוד שפירא. Jerusalem remains his home for the rest of his life. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the Da'at biographical entry.
ר׳ אריה לוין receives rabbinic ordination from ר׳ חיים ברלין, ר׳ שמואל סלנט and ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the Da'at biography.

ר׳ אריה לוין becomes mashgiaḥ and spiritual educator at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah, a position he retains until his death. His work centres on children, including pupils from impoverished homes, rather than pursuit of a prestigious communal rabbinate. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the Lehi Heritage Association.

By the late 1920s, ר׳ אריה לוין regularly walks to Jerusalem's Central Prison on Sabbaths and festivals to pray with Jewish inmates, listen to them and maintain contact with their families. The work begins with criminal prisoners and later embraces imprisoned members of the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi, earning him the title אבי האסירים. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the Israel Ministry of Defense Underground Prisoners Museum.

ר׳ אריה לוין.place: Jerusalem hospitals and leprosy hospital in Talbiya
ר׳ אריה לוין.event: Alongside his prison ministry, ר׳ אריה לוין regularly visits patients across Jerusalem, including people isolated in the leprosy hospital in Talbiya; he also visits the related institution in Bethlehem. The displayed year represents a long-running practice, not its documented beginning. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the Lehi Heritage Association.

ר׳ אריה לוין.place: Jerusalem; identification of the Lamed-Heh remains
ר׳ אריה לוין.event: After the remains of the Lamed-Heh convoy are returned for burial and twelve cannot be conventionally distinguished, ר׳ צבי פסח פרנק asks ר׳ אריה לוין to conduct the traditional גורל הגר״א procedure. Its results are accepted by the bereaved families, the army and state authorities. This was a religious ritual accepted in its historical context, not modern forensic identification. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center.

After the establishment of Israel, ר׳ אריה לוין establishes Yeshivat Beit Aryeh in the courtyard of his modest Jerusalem home and appoints his son-in-law ר׳ אליעזר פלצינסקי to lead it. The precise opening year is not given, so 1950 is an approximate post-independence marker. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center.

ר׳ אריה לוין.place: Hadassah Medical Center and Sanhedria Cemetery, Jerusalem
ר׳ אריה לוין.event: ר׳ אריה לוין dies at Hadassah Medical Center on Friday, 28 March 1969, immediately before Shabbat HaGadol, and is buried that afternoon in Sanhedria Cemetery. The timing permits fulfillment of his request that no eulogies be delivered. See the Aryeh Levin Heritage Center and the National Library archival authority record.

יחזקאל אברמסקי.event: Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky was born in Dashkovichy, Grodno Governorate, Russian Empire (now Belarus), into a traditional Jewish family connected to Lithuanian Torah scholarship.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky studied in cheder in Mosty and became known for his exceptional mastery of Tanach at a young age.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky entered the Novardok Yeshiva after encouragement from תלמידי Novardok. There he encountered the influence of the Alter of Novardok and received early rabbinic recognition.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky continued his studies in the Telz Yeshiva, where he studied alongside future leading rabbinic figures including Rabbi Yosef Shlomo Kahaneman.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky moved to Vilna to study under Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski, becoming one of his close תלמידים.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky studied in Brisk under Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik, absorbing both his analytical learning style and approach to communal leadership.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky became rabbi of Smolyany in Belarus.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky became rabbi of Smalyavichy during the upheavals of World War I and maintained close ties with the Soloveitchik family.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky succeeded Rabbi Issur Zalman Meltzer as rabbi of Slutsk while Soviet anti-religious persecution intensified.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky was offered a rabbinic position in Petach Tikvah but Soviet authorities prevented him from emigrating.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky, together with Rabbi Shlomo Yosef Zevin, founded the underground Torah journal 'Yagdil Torah' to strengthen Torah observance under Soviet rule.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky was arrested by Soviet authorities for his religious activities, interrogated, tortured, and sentenced to hard labor in Siberia.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky endured imprisonment in a Siberian labor camp until international pressure helped secure his release.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky settled in London and became rabbi of the Machzikei Hadass community in the East End.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky was appointed Av Beit Din of the London Beth Din, becoming one of the leading rabbinic authorities in Britain.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky moved to Jerusalem, settling in Bayit Vegan while continuing to lecture and write Torah scholarship.
Dayan Yechezkel Abramsky passed away in Jerusalem after a lifetime of Torah leadership and scholarship.

Rabbi Isser Yehuda Unterman.event: Born in Brisk, Russian Empire (today Brest, Belarus)
At age 12 joined Etz Chaim Yeshiva in Maletz under Rabbi Zalman Sender Kahana Shapira
Briefly studied at the Mir Yeshiva, later returning to Maletz to learn under Rabbi Shimon Shkop
Studied at the Volozhin Yeshiva Kollel, ordained by Rabbi Raphael Shapiro
Founded a small yeshiva in Vishnevo and served as rabbi in Mohilev and Mstibovo (Lithuania)
After WWI served as rabbi in Lunovlya, later moving to Grodno
Moved to Liverpool, England; became city rabbi, founded Liverpool Academy for Torah Studies, and built a strong Mizrachi presence
Appointed Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Tel Aviv after Rabbi Moshe Avigdor Amiel’s passing
Elected to the Chief Rabbinate Council in Jerusalem
Elected Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel; served until 1972
Passed away in Jerusalem; buried on the Mount of Olives

Rabbi Yosef Shlomo Kahaneman.event: Born in Kuliai, Kovno Governorate, Russian Empire
Studied at Telshe Yeshiva under Rabbis Eliezer Gordon and Shimon Shkop
Studied at Raduń Yeshiva under the Chofetz Chaim and Rabbi Naftoli Trop
Became Rabbi of Vidzh after marrying the rabbi’s daughter
Appointed Rabbi of Ponevezh; built yeshivas, schools, and an orphanage
Trapped in Palestine during WWII; learned of destruction of Ponevezh Yeshiva and community
Re-established Ponevezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak; built Kiryat Ha-Yeshiva and orphanages
Declared Israel’s Six Day War victories 'obvious miracles'

ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Volozhin, Russian Empire; now Valozhyn, Belarus
ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק is born in Volozhin on 20 Tishrei 5647 (19 October 1886) to ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and Lifsha, daughter of ר׳ רפאל שפירא. His father is then teaching at the Volozhin yeshivah. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the National Library of Israel and Sefaria's authority record.

ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Brisk, Grodno Governorate, Russian Empire; now Brest, Belarus
ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: When ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק becomes rabbi of Brisk, the young ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק moves with the family to the city that will define his public identity. He studies principally under his father and absorbs the analytic method later called the Brisker derekh. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the scholarly bibliography at the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.place: Brisk, reborn Polish state; now Brest, Belarus
ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק.event: Following the death of ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק succeeds his father as rabbi and av beit din of Brisk; surviving communal correspondence documents his authority by 1920. He combines the rabbinate with highly selective Talmudic teaching. See Encyclopaedia Judaica and the 1920 signed communal letter.

ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and his brothers publish their father ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק's חידושי רבנו חיים הלוי על הרמב״ם in Brisk. The painstaking editorial process and introductory statement become key documents of the family's approach to exact formulation. See the first-edition description and the National Library bibliography.

The German invasion finds ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק away from Brisk at the health resort of Krynica. He and his son ר׳ יוסף דוב reach Warsaw but cannot return home; this begins the wartime flight that permanently separates him from Brisk and from family members later murdered in the Holocaust. See the documented chapter summary of The Brisker Rav and the historical account in Mishpacha.

From Warsaw, ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק escapes to Vilna, which has become a crowded refuge for Polish and Lithuanian yeshivot and rabbis. He teaches a small selected group while seeking a route out of Europe and receives certificates for entry to Mandatory Palestine. See The Brisker Rav, Mishpacha's historical account and the Kedem biographical note.

ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק reaches Mandatory Palestine with several of his children in 1941 and settles in Jerusalem. His wife Alte Hendel and children unable to escape from Brisk are later murdered. In Jerusalem he teaches a selected circle in his home rather than immediately founding a conventional public yeshivah. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, The Brisker Rav and a surviving telegram bearing his Press Street address.

During the formation of the State of Israel, ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק becomes an influential leader of Jerusalem's anti-Zionist Lithuanian Haredi public. He opposes incorporation of independent Torah institutions into state structures and intervenes through letters on education, conscription, Jerusalem and religious autonomy. See the scholarly Haredi Society Research Group bibliography and his documented 1947 Jerusalem letter.

ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק dies at his Jerusalem home on 9 Tishrei 5720 (11 October 1959), immediately before Yom Kippur, and is buried at Har HaMenuchot. Contemporary reporting records the death and public mourning; his sons and students subsequently publish his writings and institutionalize several Jerusalem Brisk yeshivot. See the contemporary JTA obituary, the National Library catalogue and Sefaria.

Joel Teitelbaum.event: Born on 13 January 1887 in Máramarossziget (Sighet), Hungary (now Romania), the youngest child of Grand Rabbi Chananyah Yom Tov Lipa Teitelbaum.
Married Chavah Horowitz, daughter of Rabbi Abraham Chaim Horowitz of Połaniec. They had three daughters, all of whom predeceased him.
Settled in Satmar (Szatmárnémeti) and opened a study hall, beginning to attract followers and later styling himself as the 'Rebbe of Satmar.'
Became rabbi of Ilosva (Irshava, Ukraine), establishing a local seminary and spreading Hasidism.
Appointed Chief Rabbi of Krula, serving until moving toward leadership in Satmar.
After years of disputes and elections, officially became Chief Rabbi of Satmar. His yeshiva grew into the largest in the city.
During a royal visit, King Carol II of Romania greeted Teitelbaum first, remarking on his spiritual presence.
After the death of his first wife, married Alte Faige Shapiro of Częstochowa, who later became a powerful force in Satmar leadership.
Deported to the Kolozsvár Ghetto, then placed on the Kastner train. Held in Bergen-Belsen before being released to Switzerland.
Arrived in Mandatory Palestine in September 1945, residing briefly in Jerusalem.
Moved to Williamsburg, Brooklyn, with a small group of Hasidim, laying foundations of the Satmar community in America.
His followers established Congregation Yetev Lev Satmar in Brooklyn, where he became supreme spiritual authority.
Appointed President of the anti-Zionist Edah HaChareidis in Jerusalem; became Chief Rabbi of its Rabbinical Court in 1953.
Founded the Central Rabbinical Congress, uniting anti-Zionist rabbinic voices under his leadership.
Suffered a debilitating stroke that left him partially paralyzed. His wife Alte Faige became a key figure in Satmar affairs thereafter.
Followers founded Kiryas Joel, a self-contained Satmar community in upstate New York, named in his honor.
Died on 19 August 1979 in New York. Over 100,000 attended his funeral in Kiryas Joel. Succeeded by his nephew, Rabbi Moshe Teitelbaum.

יצחק הלוי הרצוג (Yitzchak HaLevi Herzog).event: Born in Łomża, Poland, though raised in Leeds, England.
Became Chief Rabbi of Ireland; known as the 'Sinn Féin Rabbi' for his sympathy with Irish independence.
Succeeded Rav Kook as Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Mandatory Palestine.
Appealed to world leaders to rescue European Jewry during the Holocaust.
Became the first Chief Rabbi of the newly established State of Israel.
Passed away in Jerusalem. Buried on Har HaMenuchot.

ישראל אבוחצירא (Baba Sali).event: Born in Tafilalt, Morocco, into the illustrious Abuhatzeira rabbinic dynasty.
Began serving as a rabbinic leader in Morocco; became known for Torah scholarship and ascetic lifestyle.
Immigrated to Israel; initially settled in Jerusalem.
Moved to Netivot in the Negev; became famous as a miracle worker and spiritual guide for Jews across Israel.
Passed away in Netivot; his funeral drew hundreds of thousands, and his tomb became a major pilgrimage site.

Kalonymus Kalman Szapiro.event: Born in Grodzisk Mazowiecki, Poland (19 Iyar 5649), into the Grodzhisk Hasidic dynasty.
Married Rachel Chaya Miriam of Kozhnitz; they had two children, later killed in the Holocaust.
Appointed Rabbi of Piaseczno near Warsaw, where he began to gather Hasidim.
Founded the Da’as Moshe yeshiva in Warsaw, one of the city’s largest between the wars.
Published 'Chovas HaTalmidim,' a guide for youth in Torah study and spiritual growth.
Family tragedy: his only son, daughter-in-law, and sister-in-law killed in Nazi bombing of Warsaw. Soon after, he was confined to the Warsaw Ghetto.
Led clandestine Jewish life in the ghetto: synagogue, mikveh, kosher marriages, and encouragement of Hasidim.
Began delivering Torah discourses on suffering and faith under Nazi persecution, later known as 'Esh Kodesh.'
Buried his writings, including 'Esh Kodesh,' in a milk canister as part of the Oneg Shabbat Archive.
Deported to Trawniki labor camp after Warsaw Ghetto uprising; murdered November 3 during Aktion Erntefest.
'Esh Kodesh,' his ghetto sermons, published in Jerusalem and became a cornerstone of Holocaust-era Torah.

ר׳ ראובן מרגליות.place: Lemberg, Galicia, Austria-Hungary; now Lviv, Ukraine
ר׳ ראובן מרגליות.event: ר׳ ראובן מרגליות is born in Lemberg on 7 Kislev 5650, corresponding to 30 November 1889, to Moshe and Miriam Margolies. See ויקיפדיה העברית and the Encyclopedia of the Founders and Builders of Israel.

At approximately eleven, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות writes an early booklet on Choshen Mishpat. Although he studies with ר׳ משה זאב מזוזה and ר׳ דוד טוניס, his education becomes predominantly self-directed in the Zidichov Hasidic study house. The year is derived from his reported age. See ויקיפדיה העברית.

After his father dies when he is fourteen, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות leaves full-time formal study to manage the family shop while continuing intensive independent learning and beginning to publish in Hebrew periodicals. The year is approximate, based on his age. See ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ ראובן מרגליות publishes his first book, תולדות אדם, a biography and study of ר׳ שמואל אליעזר איידלס. The book inaugurates a publishing career that will exceed fifty volumes. See English Wikipedia's bibliography and the National Library of Israel authority record.

At twenty-four, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות receives rabbinic ordination from ר׳ מאיר אריק and ר׳ משה באב״ד. He nevertheless declines to make a salaried rabbinate his profession and develops a book business that becomes a scholarly meeting place. See ויקיפדיה העברית.

During the First World War, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות flees Lemberg for Vienna. After receiving an Austro-Hungarian conscription order, he hides for roughly two years and composes נפש חיה under severe conditions, sometimes studying by the glow of a stove to avoid detection. The displayed year is approximate within the wartime period. See his account as reproduced by ויקיפדיה העברית.

Back in Lwów, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות combines publishing and bookselling with leadership in Mizrachi and Zionist activity in Eastern Galicia, including religious-national education and Jewish National Fund work. He publishes קוי אור and טל תחיה, considering Jewish law in relation to renewed Jewish public life in the Land of Israel. See the contemporary Ha-Mitzpeh newspaper record and ויקיפדיה העברית.

Following the death of his first wife, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות immigrates to Mandatory Palestine in Tevet 5695 and settles in Tel Aviv. Although ר׳ מאיר שפירא, ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק and ר׳ בן ציון מאיר חי עוזיאל had proposed a communal rabbinate, he chooses scholarship and library work. See ויקיפדיה העברית and David Tidhar's contemporary biographical encyclopedia.

ר׳ ראובן מרגליות.place: Rambam Library, Tel Aviv, Mandatory Palestine
ר׳ ראובן מרגליות.event: From the period of his immigration, ר׳ ראובן מרגליות directs Tel Aviv's Rambam Library. During his tenure it grows from a very small collection into a research library of approximately 54,000 volumes, while he continues editing and publishing rabbinic works. The precise administrative start is sometimes described simply as 1934; 1935 marks his first full year in the country. See ויקיפדיה העברית and the National Library of Israel.

ר׳ ראובן מרגליות receives the Israel Prize for rabbinic literature, principally recognizing his pioneering annotated editions and comparative research on the Zoharic corpus. He donates the prize money to Mossad Harav Kook. See contemporary coverage in Davar and the detailed award account in ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ ראובן מרגליות retires after more than three decades directing the Rambam Library and receives the key to the city of Tel Aviv. ר׳ עזריאל הילדסהיימר succeeds him at the library. See the contemporary Ma'ariv report and ויקיפדיה העברית.

ר׳ ראובן מרגליות dies at Ichilov Hospital on 7 Elul 5731, 28 August 1971, aged eighty-one. His funeral leaves his home at 3 Yavne Street, and he is buried in Nahalat Yitzhak Cemetery. See the following day's obituary in Davar and the National Library authority record.

ר׳ אברהם חיים נאה (Avraham Chaim Naeh).event: Born in Hebron into a family connected to the Chabad community.
Moved to Jerusalem; studied under leading rabbis of the Old Yishuv, gaining a reputation for halachic expertise.
Became dayan and halachic authority of the Chabad community in Jerusalem; authored Kezot HaShulchan clarifying halachic rulings.
Published Shiurei Torah, establishing standardized shiurim (halachic measurements) widely adopted across the Jewish world.
Passed away in Jerusalem; buried on Har HaMenuchot. His rulings on shiurim remain a standard reference in halacha.

יעקב קמינצקי (Yaakov Kamenetsky).event: Born in Kalushkovo, near Kovno, Lithuania (then Russian Empire).
Studied in the Slabodka Yeshiva under the Alter of Slabodka (Rav Nosson Tzvi Finkel) and later in Slutzk under Rav Isser Zalman Meltzer.
Emigrated to the United States; became rabbi of Tzitevianer Shul in Brooklyn.
Appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Mesivta Torah Vodaath in Brooklyn; became one of the guiding lights of American Orthodoxy.
Published *Emes L’Yaakov*, his Torah commentary with halachic and hashkafic insights.
Passed away in New York; widely mourned as a fatherly leader of American Jewry.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: Svislach, then Russian Empire; now Belarus
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר, originally Aharon Pines, is born in Svislach in 1892 to ר׳ שניאור זלמן פינס קוטלר, the local rabbi. He later uses the surname Kotler, reportedly adopted from a relative to avoid Russian military conscription. The marker is town-level because the family home is not securely identified. See the National Library of Israel authority record and the Hebrew Yeshiva biography.

At about eleven, the orphaned ר׳ אהרן קוטלר is sent to Krynki to study under ר׳ זלמן סנדר כהנא שפירא. The year is approximate, calculated from the age reported by the source. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: Slabodka, Kovno; now Vilijampolė, Kaunas, Lithuania
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: After a period with relatives in Minsk, where ר׳ רפאל ראובן גרוזובסקי encourages him to attend Slabodka, ר׳ אהרן קוטלר enters Yeshivat Knesset Yisrael at about thirteen. He studies in the environment shaped by ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל and ר׳ משה מרדכי אפשטיין and rapidly gains a reputation as an exceptional scholar. The year is approximate. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography.

After marrying Chana Perel, daughter of ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר, ר׳ אהרן קוטלר joins the faculty of Yeshivat Etz Chaim in Slutsk. The marriage is placed at about age twenty-two; from 1917 he is documented as a regular maggid shiur. See the Da'at biographical entry and the Hebrew Yeshiva biography.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: Kletsk, Second Polish Republic; now Belarus
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: Facing Soviet repression, ר׳ אהרן קוטלר leads a substantial group of the Slutsk yeshiva across the frontier to Kletsk. He develops the institution into one of interwar Poland's important Lithuanian yeshivot; ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר joins it in 1923 before emigrating to Jerusalem in 1925. See the Da'at Jewish Encyclopedia.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: London and New York; fundraising journey
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר travels through England and the United States to raise funds for the Kletsk yeshiva. His American stay lasts many months and exposes him directly to the possibilities and limitations of advanced Torah study in the United States. This marker represents the London stage of a documented transatlantic journey. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography and Da'at.

After the destruction of independent Poland, the Kletsk yeshiva regroups first in Vilna and then in Jonava. ר׳ אהרן קוטלר continues teaching under Soviet rule until the authorities close the yeshiva in early 1941. The marker is placed in Vilna, the best-documented initial refuge and coordinating center. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography.

After traveling through Siberia and Japan, ר׳ אהרן קוטלר reaches the United States in 1941. Rather than mapping an undocumented Japanese building, this marker records his secure destination. He becomes a leading member of Vaad Hatzalah, working to rescue rabbis and yeshiva students trapped in Europe; the Yeshiva University archive preserves correspondence from his later chairmanship. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography, the Yeshiva University Vaad Hatzala archive, and the JDC wartime records guide.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: Beth Medrash Govoha, 617 Sixth Street, Lakewood, New Jersey
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר opens Beth Medrash Govoha in Lakewood with a small founding group, deliberately creating a setting for intensive full-time Torah study away from New York City's distractions. The coordinate is centered on the historic 617 Sixth Street campus nucleus, not merely on Lakewood town center. See the Hebrew Yeshiva biography and the BMG institutional catalogue.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: Lakewood and New York; support for Torah education in Israel
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר helps establish and becomes a principal American advocate and fundraiser for Chinuch Atzmai, founded in Israel in 1953. Because the evidence establishes organizational leadership but not his physical presence at a specific Israeli founding meeting, the marker remains at his Lakewood base rather than inventing a Jerusalem journey. See the history of the Independent Education System and the National Library authority record.

ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.place: Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center, New York City
ר׳ אהרן קוטלר.event: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר dies in New York on 29 November 1962, not in Lakewood as the former project record stated. Contemporary reporting identifies New York as the place of death. See the Jewish Telegraphic Agency death report and the contemporary Haaretz report in the National Library.

After major funeral observances in the United States, the remains of ר׳ אהרן קוטלר are flown to Israel and buried on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem. Contemporary JTA reporting records the Jerusalem burial and the large attendance. See the Jewish Telegraphic Agency burial report.

אליהו אליעזר דסלר (Eliyahu Eliezer Dessl.event: Born in Homel (Belarus, then Russian Empire), into a family of Musar scholars.
Entered the Kelm Talmud Torah, founded by R’ Simcha Zissel Ziv, where he absorbed the Musar tradition.
Settled in London and later Manchester, teaching Torah privately and working in business for support.
Appointed mashgiach of Gateshead Yeshiva in England, where he became a major Musar influence on postwar European Jewry.
Moved to Bnei Brak, Israel, serving as mashgiach of the Ponovezh Yeshiva until his death.
Died in Bnei Brak. His teachings were collected and published posthumously as 'Michtav Me’Eliyahu', shaping contemporary Jewish thought.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Uzda, Minsk Governorate, Russian Empire; now Belarus
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין is born on 7 Adar 5655 (3 March 1895) in Uzda, where his father ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין serves as rabbi. He receives his earliest Torah education from his father. See the Orthodox Union biography, contemporary JTA obituary and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Starobin, Minsk Governorate, Russian Empire; now Belarus; date approximate
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: When ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין transfers from Uzda to the rabbinate of Starobin, the young ר׳ משה פיינשטיין moves with his family and continues studying under his father. Sources document the family stage but do not uniformly date the move, so 1907 is retained as an approximate map marker. See the JTA obituary and the Orthodox Union biography.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Shklov, Mogilev Governorate, Russian Empire; now Belarus
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: After studying in the Slutsk yeshivah world, ר׳ משה פיינשטיין joins the yeshivah led by ר׳ פסח פרוסקין in Shklov. He later consistently regards ר׳ פסח פרוסקין as his principal rebbe; ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and his uncle ר׳ יעקב קנטרוביץ also influence his formation. See JTA, the Orthodox Union and the scholarly Hebrew Kotar study.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Mstislavl, Mogilev Governorate, Russian Empire; now Belarus
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין continues with ר׳ פסח פרוסקין's yeshivah after its transfer from Shklov to Mstislavl. The event corrects the former map coordinate, which placed Shklov at longitude 0.29 rather than in Belarus. See the biographical synthesis in the Orthodox Union profile and the JTA obituary.

After marrying Shima Kustanovich in 1920, ר׳ משה פיינשטיין becomes rabbi of Lyuban in 1921. For sixteen years he maintains communal religious life and answers halakhic questions under increasingly restrictive Soviet rule. See Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Orthodox Union and the Hebrew biographical study.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem, 145–147 East Broadway, New York City
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: In January 1937, ר׳ משה פיינשטיין, Shima and their children leave the Soviet Union and settle on New York's Lower East Side. He joins Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem to develop its advanced beit midrash and semikhah programme and becomes rosh yeshivah after ר׳ יוסף אדלר's death in 1938. See the JTA obituary, the New York Jewish Week institutional history and the Orthodox Union.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem, New York City
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין publishes the first volumes of אגרות משה in New York. The expanding responsa collection records answers sent to students, rabbis, institutions and individuals on ritual, marriage, medicine, technology, commerce and American communal conditions. See the University of California Berkeley library record, the National Library of Israel and the Hebrew Kotar study.

By the 1960s, ר׳ משה פיינשטיין is chairing Agudath Israel of America's Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah and serving in senior leadership of the Union of Orthodox Rabbis while advising Torah Umesorah and Chinuch Atzmai. The year is a representative marker for responsibilities extending over decades, not a single appointment date. See the contemporary JTA obituary and the Orthodox Union biography.

ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.place: Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem, New York City
ר׳ משה פיינשטיין.event: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין dies in New York on 13 Adar II 5746 (23 March 1986), aged ninety-one. More than 20,000 mourners gather around MTJ on East Broadway for the New York funeral before his coffin is flown to Israel. See the JTA obituary, the contemporary Los Angeles Times report and the New York Jewish Week photograph and history.

After transfer from New York, ר׳ משה פיינשטיין is buried at Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem near his teacher ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר. Contemporary reports describe an exceptionally large Jerusalem procession; numerical estimates vary widely and are not presented here as a settled figure. See the contemporary UPI report, the Los Angeles Times and the Har HaMenuchot history.

Sir Israel Brodie.event: Appointed Rabbi of Melbourne Hebrew Congregation, Australia.
Helped establish the Zionist Federation of Australia.
Returned to Britain; continued rabbinic and communal leadership.
Evacuated from Dunkirk during World War II.
Concluded service as Senior Jewish Chaplain of the British Forces (Forces Rabbi).
Appointed Chief Rabbi of Great Britain and the Commonwealth.
Founded the Conference of European Rabbis to rebuild Jewish life after the Holocaust.
Banned Rabbi Dr. Louis Jacobs from becoming Principal of Jews' College, sparking a major religious controversy.
Retired as Chief Rabbi and was knighted 'for services to British Jewry'.

Elazar Menachem Man Shach.event: Stayed with Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski before emigrating
Immigrated to Palestine; served as rosh yeshiva
Appointed rosh yeshiva at Ponevezh Yeshiva
Co-founded Shas political party with Rabbi Ovadia Yosef
Founded Degel HaTorah party after split with Shas and Agudat Yisrael
